Hello,
Thank you for your email correspondence to 's Immigration Representatives mailbox. Please consider that the Immigration Representatives Mailbox will only reply to general immigration program or policy related enquiries; therefore, no case-specific responses can be provided.
| Citizenship Canada| |
We appreciate your patience. Please find the answers to your questions below:
(1) If the student has both a study permit and an Iranian open work permit, can they study full time and work full time at the same time?
Response: The person would have to abide by the conditions of their study permit, which include being enrolled at a DLl and actively pursuing their studies. Actively pursuing their studies means being enrolled full-time or part-time during each academic semester (excluding regularly scheduled breaks) making progress towards completing their program's courses, and not taking authorized leave longer than 150 days from their study program An open work permit holder may work part- or full-time until the expiry date of that work permit.
Spring/summer is the student's scheduled break. However, this the spring/summer is the student's final semester, how many hours can they work by using their study permit?
Response: Students eligible to work without a work permit under paragraph R186(v) can do the following: work up to 20 hours per week during academic sessions once they have commenced their program of study work full time during regularly scheduled breaks between academic sessions regardless of their course load
If I understand right, given spring/summer is their final semester, they can only work up to 20 hours right?
The student has their study permit approved for Fall 2023 by using the offer of admission for Fall 2023. Their letter of introduction is still valid. They deferred their program start from Fall 2023 to
(3) Fall 2024 after their study permit's approval. Can they use their letter of introduction to come to Canada with their updated offer of admission? Do they need to apply for a new study permit?
Response: If the student defers their program start date, it should be formally approved by the DLI. In all deferral cases, students should obtain an updated letter of acceptance from the DLl. To enter Canada, they must have the port of entry letter of introduction from IRCC and a copy of a valid letter of acceptance from their school. If the letter of acceptance is not valid, they would need to apply for a new study permit.
If the deferral is approved by the school and they are issued a new letter of acceptance, they can come to Canada with their previous letter of introduction which is still valid right?
(4) If the student loses their passport but they did not lose their study permit, can they continue using that study permit with the lost passport number?
Response: They will need to apply for a new passport through their country's consulate or embassy and then apply for a new study permit which will reflect the new passport number.
I got the information from IRCC before that “Please note that the passport number indicated on your document has no impact on the information related to your current status." Do they have to apply for a new study permit after they get their new passport?
(5) A) If the student mistakenly uses the IRCC portal instead of IRCC secure account for their study permit extension, will they have maintained status by using IRCC portal?
Response: In order to have maintained status IRCC must have received a complete application before midnight UTC on the date the applicant's status expires. If the application was received after midnight UTC on the date of expiry, the applicant does not maintain their status under subsection R183(5).
If IRCC received a complete application, the applicant would have received an acknowledgement of receipt (AOR) letter (or email). If they haven't received a AOR letter, they will have to submit an application to restore their status and they are not able to continue under the conditions of their expired study permit (they can't study, nor work on or off campus). They have 90 days to apply for restoration of status from the date the study permit expired. If more than 90 days have passed, they will have to leave Canada or reapply from outside Canada for a new study permit.
It is important to note that the RCC secure account is used to extend a study permit while the IRCC portal is for a new application. Since a provincial attestation letter (PAL) is now required for new study permit applications, the student will not be able to proceed in using the IRCC portal for an extension because they won't have a PAL. They will need to submit a new application.
Given it is a new application for IRCC portal application instead of study permit extension, do they have maintained status?
B) They are still waiting for their study permit result of IRCC portal, but their study permit has already expired. What should they do?
Response: If they haven't received an AOR letter, they will have to submit a new application. They have lost their status and authority to study. They may not continue to study (or work) until their status and authorization have been restored and a new study permit has been issued. For more information please see Restoration of temporary resident status.
Does it mean that IRCC portal application does not grant maintained status?
(6) If the student has an open work permit, can they use their open work permit for their co-op terms? Do they need to apply for a co-op work permit?
Response: If a student holds an open work permit, they may work for an employer who is offering employment that is certified as part of the academic program offered at the designated learning institution. For more information please see Guide 5580 - Applying for a Work Permit-Student Guide-online application.
(7)Can you share how to apply for work permit for destitute students?
Response: Under section 208 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR), work permits may be issued to foreign nationals who cannot support themselves without working and who are study permit holders who have become temporarily destitute through circumstances beyond their control and beyond the control of any person on whom that person is dependent for financial support to complete their term of study.
The onus is on applicants to prove that they are unable to support themselves without public assistance. Evidence to assess the inability of the foreign national to support themselves may include, but is not limited to, the following: a letter or cheque stub from the provincial or territorial social service department bank statements letters from assistance groups or other related documentation.
Section R208 provides the opportunity for students to cover such difficult financial periods, should on-campus employment provided for under paragraph R186(f) or off-campus employment provided under paragraph R186(v), or co-op employment, if eligible, prove to be insufficient.
It should be noted that as per section R220, study permit holders are expected to have sufficient and available resources without working in Canada in order to pay their tuition, and maintain themselves and any family members. As such, the open work permit should only be provided in exceptional circumstances.
Information on applying for a work permit can be found here: You're a study permit holder who can no longer support yourself financially
A: Can students work on campus during the scheduled break? Response A: Students can work on campus full-time during scheduled breaks, such as winter and summer holidays, or a fall or spring reading week. They must meet all the requirements for working on-campus before they start working.
B: Do they need to be full-time student before and after break to work full-time on campus? They must be a full-time student both before and after the break to work full-time and they can't work during a break that comes before they start their very first school semester.
We trust this information will be useful.
Sincerely, The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

Question:

- Change their status (e.g., to visitor or worker), or
- Apply for a new study permit.

threads.answer:
Subject: RE: Clarification-mexican nationals with student visa and eTAs concurrently --REP-2024-0743-- Good Day, Thank you for your email correspondence to 's Immigration Representatives mailbox.
Question:
I am reaching out to get clarification regarding Mexican nationals who recently were added to the list of special countries that are visa-required but may be eligible to apply for an Electronic Travel Authorization (eTA).
I would like to clarify what options a Mexican national has if she/he has been approved to come to Canada as international student, has his/her student visa stamped in his/her passport but wants to visit for 1 week Canada months before the study program start date.
Option 1: Obtaining an eTA if the applicant complies with the requirements to enter with an eTA for tourism purposes. I did not find any regulation in the IRPA or IRPR or any bulletin or manual that specifically prohibits to have 2 authorizations concurrently (study permit and eTA). But I would like clarification if in any way getting a new eTA to be used before entering as international student may affect the SP approval process.
Option 2: Using the student stamped visa to enter Canada and explain to the CBSA officer that the applicant wants to enter for 1 week only in July when the study program starts in September. I understand that CBSA may use his/her discretion to allow this entry, but I would like to clarify if this is possible. The Mexican national will not be requiring the issuance of the study permit at this time unless it is mandatory to be issued at his/her entry.
Could you please confirm if both options are feasible or not?
Response:
As of 11:30 p.m. ET on February 29, 2024, Mexican citizens travelling to Canada need to meet new requirements to travel to Canada.
Before they can travel to Canada, they need to either
- apply and be approved for an electronic travel authorization (eTA) under the new rules, or
- apply and be approved for a temporary resident visa (TRV)
If a Mexican citizen already holds a valid TRV, they do not need to apply for an eTA to travel to Canada. However, if they only hold a valid eTA, they will need a TRV to travel to Canada using a non-air mode of transportation (e.g. car).
Furthermore, a TRV is an official document citizens from visa-required countries need to get to travel to and enter Canada. A foreign national will automatically get a TRV (or eTA if eligible) when they apply for their first study permit or work permit abroad and their application gets approved. A study permit or work permit is not an entry document, a permit allows a foreign national to work or study in Canada, and they will also need a TRV or eTA to travel to Canada.
While an eTA or a TRV is a required document to travel to Canada, they do not guarantee entry. A border services officer (BSO) of the Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) have the authority to use their discretion to grant entry into Canada and determine the length of stay allowed. When foreign national arrives at a Port of Entry (POE), it is the traveller's responsibility to satisfy the BSO of their purpose of travel to Canada.
We trust that this information will assist you.
and Citizenship Caneda
Sincerely,
Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.answer:
Hello, Thank you for your email correspondence to 's Immigration Representatives mailbox. We appreciate your patience.
QUESTION I am reaching out to seek clarification on the consequences for a study permit holder who, while concurrently holding a work permit (e.g. open work permit under the public policy for Iranian Nationals), experiences a gap in their study exceeding 150 days.
Could you kindly provide guidance on the following queries:
Question 1: Does a gap in study exceeding 150 days for a study permit holder with a concurrent work permit constitute non-compliance with study permit regulations?
Proposed Response: Yes, according to subsection R220.1(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR), study permit holders are required to actively pursue their course or program of study. Any leave from studies exceeding 150 days without authorization from the designated learning institution (DLl) is considered non-compliance with study permit conditions.
For further information, please visit our website
Question 2: If such a gap is considered non-compliant, what are the potential repercussions for the individual?
Proposed Response: Non-compliance with study permit conditions may result in enforcement action, including the issuance of an exclusion order subparagraph R228(1)(c)(v).
For further information, please visit our website
Question 3: Will individuals in this scenario still be eligible to apply for the Post-Graduation Work Permit (PGWP) after completing their studies?
Proposed Response: Individuals, who hold a study permit and a concurrent work permit, may still be eligible to apply for the Post-Graduation Work Permit (PGWP) after completing their studies provided the leave from studies was authorized. IRCC considers various factors when assessing PGWP applications, including the reasons for the gap in studies and whether the individual maintained their legal status in Canada during that time.
Work in Canada after you graduate: Who can apply-Canada.ca indicates:
You may not be eligible for a PGWP if:
- you take an unauthorized leave from your study program and we find that you didn't meet the conditions of your study permit by taking this leave.
There are a few cases where you may be able to take an authorized leave of up to 150 days from your study program and still meet the conditions of your study permit. You need to provide proof that your DLi authorized the leave when you apply for a PGWP. Find out what counts as an authorized leave from your studies
Question 4: Could this situation trigger an investigation into non-compliance, considering the individual's possession of another permit in Canada?
Proposed Response: Yes, officers have the authority to investigate compliance with study permit conditions, including situations where an individual holds another permit in Canada. If there are reasons to believe that the individual is not complying with their study permit conditions, an investigation may be initiated, and evidence of compliance may be requested (subsection R220.1(4).
For more information: Study Permits: Assessing study permit conditions-Canada.ca
Please be advised that the assessment of an application is based on a case-by-case basis, considering the particular circumstances in conjunction with the supporting documentation available to the officer. The onus is always on the applicant to provide sufficient documentation to satisfy an officer that they meet the requirements.
We trust that this information will assist you.
Sincerely,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

Answer: To calculate the hours per week for a period of work experience the total number of hours worked during that period are divided by the number of weeks in the period. Question: In a scenario wherein a student does not study full-time before and after a scheduled break, can you clarify whether they can still work up to 20 hours per week off-campus during that scheduled break if they choose to study full-time during the break?
For example, if a student studied part-time in the Winter semester so is not eligible to work full-time during the Spring scheduled break, can they still work 20 hours per week off-campus during the Spring months, if they study full-time during those Spring months?
Answer: International students can only work off campus without a work permit provided that all of the following statements are true:
They hold a valid study permit. They are full-time students enrolled at a designated learning institution (DLI). The program in which they are enrolled is a post-secondary academic, vocational or professional training program, or a vocational training program at the secondary level offered in Quebec. The program of study is at least 6 months in duration and leads to a degree, diploma or certificate.
Students must stop working off campus as soon as their full-time status becomes part-time during a regular academic session.
If a student did not maintain full time status for the duration of their program of study (excluding those who only require a part-time course load in their final academic session in order to complete their program of study) they are not eligible to work off nor on-campus. Please see Study permits: Off-campus work-Canada.ca for more information. We trust that this information will assist you.
Sincerely, Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.answer:
Hello,
Thank you for your email correspondence to 's Immigration Representatives mailbox. Please consider that the Immigration Representatives Mailbox will only reply to general immigration program- or policy-related enquiries; therefore, no case-specific responses can be provided.
We appreciate your patience. Please find the answers to your questions below:
1. If spring/summer is a student's final semester, they can only work up to 20 hours right? Response: They must be a full-time student both before and after a regularly scheduled break to work full-time during the break. In this situation they can only work up to 20 hours per week during the break. If the spring/summer period is not a regularly scheduled break, then students authorized to work off-campus can only do so up to 20 hours per week.
2. If a deferral is approved by the school and they issued a new letter of acceptance, can the student come to Canada with their previous IRCC letter of introduction which is still valid? Response: To enter Canada, they must have a valid port of entry letter of introduction from IRCC and the original and updated letter of acceptance from the same DLI. As long as they will be attending the same DLl, they do not need to reapply for a study permit. If a student changes their program of study to a different DLl after their visa is issued, they need to submit a new study permit application to IRCC. Students should immediately submit their new LOA to IRCC using the online web form if they made any changes to their program of study within the same DLl or to a different DLI while their study permit application is still in process.
3. I got the information from IRCC before that “Please note that the passport number indicated on your document has no impact on the information related to your current status." Do they have to apply for a new study permit after they get their new passport? Response: We apologize for the misunderstanding in our previous response. If they have a new passport, they do not need to change their study permit until it expires.
4. Given it is a new application for IRCC portal application instead of study permit extension, do they have maintained status? Response: Regardless of the system used, if IRCC received a complete application before the expiry date of their previous document, they would have maintained status until a decision is made on the new application. If the applicant hasn't received an AOR letter, they will need to submit a new application and pay the fees.
5. Does it mean that IRCC portal application does not grant maintained status? Response: Maintained status is only extended under R183(5) if IRCC receives a complete application before the period of authorized stay ends. If the applicant is not aware that IRCC has received a complete application, and their study permit has expired, they will need to apply to restore their status.
We trust this information will be useful.
Sincerely, The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

Answer: Thank you for your follow-up enquiry regarding lEC participation for Italian citizens.
As previously mentioned, foreign national youth are eligible to apply through an IEC recognized organization twice in their lifetime. These participations are separate from those allowed under the Youth Mobility Agreement (YMA). Repeat participations in the same category through a recognized organization are permitted. The two participations are cumulative across all recognized organizations, without any requirement for discontinuity.
Previous participation in an IEC country or territory under a YMA does not count towards recognized organization participations. Therefore, if a foreign national youth has exhausted their participations under a YMA with a specific country or territory, they may still apply through a recognized organization for up to the maximum number of lifetime participations.

Question: Where an individual and their spouse sponsor parents, and then one of the sponsors dies leaving the other with the financial burden, is there an option for them to voluntarily apply for default on their sponsorship application so that the parents can access social assistance? Or is there a different process for default?
Answer: As a result of signing the Application to Sponsor, Sponsorship Agreement and Undertaking [IMM 1344], both the sponsor and the co-signer have agreed to be financially responsible for their sponsored relatives for the length of the undertaking. The death of one (sponsor or co-signer) would not relieve the other from their obligations. There is no option for the sponsor or co-signer to default on their undertaking to allow the parents to access social assistance. If the parents access social assistance during the 20 year undertaking period, their sponsor(s) are responsible to repay those funds.
As specified in the Guide 5772 - Application to Sponsor Parents and Grandparents-Canada.ca if a sponsored family member receives financial support from a provincial, territorial or municipal social assistance program while the undertaking is still valid, the sponsor and co-signer will be considered to be in default of their obligations,
- must repay the government concerned any benefits (social assistance) the person(s) they sponsored received, and
- will not be allowed to sponsor other members of the family class until they have repaid the amount of these payments to the government concerned.
Both the sponsor and co-signer are liable if obligations are not performed.

Answer: As per R220.1 (1) the holder of a study permit in Canada is subject to the following conditions:
(a) they shall enroll at a designated learning institution and remain enrolled at a designated learning institution until they complete their studies; and
and Citizenship Caneda
(b) they shall actively pursue their course or program of study. There are a few cases where students may be able to take a leave of up to a maximum of 150 days, if authorized by their Designated Learning Institution, and still be considered to be actively pursuing their studies. However, if a student does not resume their studies within 150 days of their authorized leave, they should do either of the following:
- change their status (to visitor status or worker status)
- leave Canada
If they do not change their status or leave Canada, they are considered non-compliant with their study permit conditions. This may result in:
- a removal order (exclusion order) issued for non-compliance, per subparagraph R228(1)(c)(v), or
- impacts to the outcome of any future applications.
As per R222(1) a study permit becomes invalid upon the first to occur of the following days:
(a) the day that is 90 days after the day on which the permit holder completes their studies,
(b) the day on which the permit is cancelled under section 243.2; or
(c) the day on which the permit expires.
Furthermore, subsection 243.2(b) of the Regulations states that a foreign national's study permit is cancelled when a removal order made against them becomes enforceable.

Merci d’avoir soumis les questions suivantes pour clarification.
Question
Nous avons récemment pris connaissance de modifications sur le site d'IRCC qui rendraient inadmissibles certains de nos programmes au PTPD. Nous n'avons reçu aucune communication de la part d'IRCC à ce sujet et nous souhaiterions savoir ce que nous pouvons modifier pour rendre ces programmes admissibles au PTPD. Pilotage d'aéronefs-Pilotage intégré ATP (A) EWA.11 Le 1er septembre 2023
Pilotage d'aéronefs-Pilotage professionnel CPL (IR) EWA.1C Le 1er septembre 2023
Nous sommes très préoccupés pour nos étudiants qui ont commencé leur formation le 21 août 2023. Serait-il possible de nous indiquer comment rapidement rectifier le tir afin de ne pas pénaliser nos étudiants.
Réponse Un DLl est une école approuvée par un gouvernement provincial ou territorial pour accueillir des étudiants internationaux. La province de Québec a apporté les modifications suivantes à son PTPD qui pourraient avoir affecté votre établissement : Changement au permis de travail post-diplôme pour les EED au Québec Le 1er septembre 2023, les critères d’admissibilité au PTPD ont été modifiés pour certains programmes dans certains EED au Québec. Trouvez votre EED dans la liste ci-dessous et consultez sa page Détails pour savoir si votre programme est admissible au PTPD.
- Si vous avez complété votre programme d’études avant le 1er septembre 2023 et présentez votre demande de PTPD dans les 6 mois suivant la fin de vos études, vous aurez accès au PTPD selon les anciens critères.
L'information divulguée en vertu de la [oi sur l'accès à linformation
- Si vous commencez un programme d’études après le 1er septembre 2023, vous pourrez présenter une demande pour le PTPD seulement si vous êtes diplômé d’un programme d’études subventionné qui est demeuré admissible au PTPD après le 1er septembre 2023.
- Si vous étudiez dans un programme qui n’est plus admissible au PTPD après le 1er septembre 2023, la période précédant cette date durant laquelle vous avez étudié dans ce programme pourrait être comptabilisée pour l’obtention d’un PTPD.
Les provinces et les territoires conservent le droit de dicter quelles écoles et quels programmes peuvent devenir admissibles aux PTPD. Liste des établissements d'enseignement désignés-Canada.ca Bien qu'lRCC ait récemment modifié les conditions d'éligibilité au permis de travail post-universitaire, les exigences pour les ressortissants étrangers inscrits dans les écoles de pilotage n'ont pas été affectées.
Diplômés d’une école de pilotage Pour être admissible à un PTPD, un diplômé d’école de pilotage doit remplir tous les critères d’admissibilité susmentionnés en plus de l’un des critères suivants :
- avoir suivi un cours de pilotage dans un centre de formation d’EED et être titulaire d’une licence canadienne de pilote professionnel; ou avoir obtenu, ou être sur le point d’obtenir, sa qualification comme instructeur et avoir reçu une offre d’emploi à titre d’instructeur de vol d’un centre de formation au pilotage d’un EED.
Si les étudiants inscrits à votre programme répondent aux critères d'éligibilité énumérés ci-dessus, ils peuvent être éligibles à un permis de travail postuniversitaire. threads.subject: Parental Sponsorship question-Death of principal applicant-REP-2024-0954
threads.question:
Les Morley ### Dear Sirs & Mesdames
My client filed an “Interest to Sponsor” form in 2020, asking for the opportunity to sponsor her father (the principal applicant) and her mother (the dependent applicant). She has now received an invitation to apply to sponsor her parents, however between 2020 and the date of the ITÀ her father, the principal applicant, died.
Question 1: Can my client sponsor her mother, so that her mother fulfills the responsibilities of the principal applicant?
The Guide and the Checklist say “The information in your sponsorship application must match all the information you put on your 2020 Interest to Sponsor form", which suggests that the answer is “no”. However, the following passage, which is still posted on the IRCC website, suggests that the answer is “yes”:
CHANGE IN THE PRINCIPAL APPLICANT A change in principal applicant for a family class sponsorship can only occur in a sponsorship application for a parent or grandparent and their dependent spouse or common law partner. If the principal applicant passes away during processing of the application, an officer is authorized to process the surviving spouse or partner as the principal applicant. To qualify, that person must be a family class member in their own right, i.e. also be the sponsor's parent or grandparent.
When the surviving spouse or partner is a step-parent or step-grandparent of the sponsor, a processing office may examine the circumstances to determine if granting an exemption from membership in the family class is justified on humanitarian and compassionate grounds.
You can find the above passage here, which was posted on the IRCC webpage in 2019. Please note that my client is the natural daughter of her mother, who was married to the birth father, who was the principal applicant that died.
Question 2: Is it the position of IRCC that the officer “is authorized to process the surviving spouse or partner as the principal applicant”, but has the discretion not to do so? Is the discretion limited to determining if the surviving parent is “a family class member in their own right”, or are there other considerations as there are for stepparent or step grandparent? Is so, what are they?
Thank you for answering these questions.
| Citizenship Canada| |
Ruscito, Giovanni (IRCC/IRCC)

threads.answer:
# Good day,
Thank you for your email correspondence to 's Immigration Representatives mailbox. We appreciate your patience. Please find the answer to your question below:
1. Duration of validity of the TRP obtained at a port of entry or within Canada : According to the introduction letters issued to some of our clients, the duration of the validity for the TRP that will be issued would be one year. Could you please confirm, if these applicants could request a longer validity duration for the TRPs issued? Response: Officers hold the delegated authority to determine the validity period of temporary resident permits (TRPs), depending on the circumstances of the case. Under section 63 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR), an initial or subsequent TRP may be valid for a period of up to 3 years. TRP holders who are in Canada may remain longer by obtaining a subsequent TRP. They may submit the form Application to Change Conditions, Extend my Stay or Remain in Canada as a Visitor or Temporary Resident Permit Holder (IMM 5708).
2. Possibility of obtaining a multiple-entry TRP Some applicants have received a multiple-entry TRP visa, but their letters of introduction indicate that they will not be authorized to reenter Canada. As such, which information is correct between the visa and the introduction letter? Response: Clients should follow the instructions included in the letter of introduction. TRPs are not normally valid for re-entry to Canada; however, in compelling circumstances, re-entry may be authorized. A single-entry TRP is no longer valid if a TRP holder leaves Canada and does not have authorization to re-enter; clients would be required to apply for a new TRP or TRV overseas. If there is a discrepancy between the visa counterfoil affixed to the travel document and the letter of introduction, the Border Services Officer at the port of entry will make the final determination on whether to issue a single-entry or multiple-entry TRP status document. Would it be possible for these applicants to obtain multiple-entry TRPs at the port of entry considering their visa and/or personal circumstances (for example: to allow them to travel to a third country to visit a family member)? Response: Clients are unable to apply for a TRP at the port of entry. Once authorized to enter Canada, clients may apply inland for a subsequent TRP by completing and submitting the form Application to Change Conditions, Extend my Stay or Remain in Canada as a Visitor or Temporary Resident Permit Holder (IMM 5708).
3. Work permit/Study permit applications
Considering that TRP holders are eligible to apply for open work permits and study permits (s. 208 and 209 of the IRPR), would it be possible for them to apply at the port of entry for these permits (when they will be issued their TRPs) to avoid long processing times or will they have to apply online once they have entered Canada?
Response: Foreign nationals applying under the temporary public policy for foreign nationals who are family members of Canadian citizens and permanent residents who left Israel or the Palestinian Territories on or after October 7, 2023 or the temporary public policy for nationals of Israel and the Palestinian Territories who are in Canada as temporary residents must be in Canada with valid temporary resident status in order to be eligible to apply for fee-exempt study permits, work permits or extensions of temporary resident status. Clients applying under these temporary special measures are not eligible to apply for these permits at the port of entry.
Foreign national family members of Canadian citizens or permanent residents who arrive on or after October 7, 2023, will benefit from priority processing for their in-Canada applications for study permits and work permits. This is to ensure a reduced wait time between arriving, applying in Canada, and waiting for study and work permit applications to be processed to grant access to the labour market and a means of self-support.
4. Economic permanent residence applications Some Gaza nationals residing in Egypt (who applied for TRVs) have been issued TRPs as IRCC considered that they did not meet a requirement to obtain a TRV (ex. do not have sufficient financial means). In this case (and considering the absence of inadmissibility concerns), would these people be eligible to apply under "regular" economic permanent residence programs in Canada (example: "Express Entry", etc.)? Response: TRP holders may be eligible to apply under economic permanent residence programs, however they must meet all requirements of the program under which they are applying. More information on these programs is found at How Express Entry works-Canada.ca. Would they also be eligible to apply for "regular" work permits granting them temporary status (employer-specific work permit, etc.) if they meet all other requirements of the program? As such, are they only eligible to apply for open work permits under s. 208 b) of the IRPR. Response: The temporary public policy for nationals of Israel and the Palestinian Territories who are in Canada as temporary residents enables clients to apply for fee exempt open work permits and employer-specific work permits (if they meet all other requirements of the program); however, clients will maintain their status of a TRP holder for the duration of their stay in Canada. We trust that this information will assist you. Sincerely,
Immigration Representatives Mailbox

A TFW, who holds an employer specific work permit under the IMP: Canadian interests – Significant benefit as an ICT, is entitled to work for both the Canadian and foreign enterprise throughout the validity of their document.
Must take a position in Canada” under intra-company transferee provisions means that an employer-employee relationship with the Canadian branch of the company to which they are being transferred must exist. The essential element in determining this relationship is the right of the employer to order and control the employee in the performance of their work. While full-time employment by the Canadian branch is anticipated, there is no requirement that the foreign national perform full-time service in Canada. An executive, for example, could divide normal working hours between offices in Canada and the U.S. There is no requirement that the foreign national be paid from the Canadian entity; however, this is usually the case.
However, IRCC expects that the employer will continue to meet the employer compliance conditions on the work permit under the IMP, as per R209.2(1); this includes that they must provide the foreign national with employment in the same occupation as per the offer of employment, with wages and working conditions that are substantially the same as – but not less favourable than – those set out in the offer. As per the Employer compliance inspections PDI:
Acceptable changes
Employers are not required to inform IRCC of changes in working conditions. However, they must provide evidence of an acceptable justification [R209.2(3)] at the time of an inspection should there be differences between the working conditions offered and those found during the inspection.
If the change in working conditions (such as a reduction in hours or salary) negatively affects the worker, a new offer of employment and a new work permit are required before the change takes effect; otherwise, the employer risks being found non-compliant with the original job offer submitted to IRCC.
If the work being completed by the FN deviated from the offer of employment only in regards to when the worker was outside of Canada (resulting in them also being paid by the foreign company, since they weren't actually working for the Canadian company at the time), then this could be seen as an acceptable change of conditions since it does not negatively affect the employee.

(i) the offer is supported by a valid assessment — provided by the Department of Employment and Social Development at the request of the employer or an officer and on the same basis as an assessment provided for the issuance of a work permit — that the requirements set out in subsection 203(1) of the Regulations with respect to the offer have been met, (ii) the foreign national holds a valid work permit, the offer of employment is made by an employer for whom the foreign national currently works and who is specified on the work permit, the work permit was issued based on a positive determination made by an officer under subsection 203(1) of the Regulations with respect to the foreign national's employment with that employer in an occupation that is listed in TEER Category 0, 1, 2 or 3 of the National Occupational Classification and the assessment provided by the Department of Employment and Social Development on the basis of which the determination was made is not suspended or revoked, or (iii) the foreign national holds a valid work permit issued under the circumstances described in paragraph 204(a) or (c) or section 205 of the Regulations, the offer is made by an employer who is specified on the work permit and the foreign national works for that employer and has accumulated at least one year of full-time work experience, or the equivalent in part-time work, over a continuous period of work in Canada for that employer;
As per subparagraph 29(a)(ii), the applicant must have worked for at least one year for the employer specified on the work permit. If this is the case in this scenario, then the applicant should answer “yes" in order to obtain points for arranged employment. The subparagraph and the question in the Express Entry Profile Builder does not specify that the work experience must be under the same NOC. We’d recommend submitting a letter of explanation if you think an explanation of the situation is warranted.
Note that a work permit on its own is not a job offer, even if it is an open work permit. The job offer must also meet the other criteria to be valid under the Express Entry program the applicant qualifies for, listed on our website.
Please be advised that the assessment of an application is based on a case-by-case basis, considering the particular circumstances in conjunction with the supporting documentation available to the officer. Hello,

We strive to respond to all inquiries clearly and provide as many relevant links and resources as possible. However, due to the nuances in interpretation, there may be times when responses do not meet the requester's expectations.
To address your concerns, we’ve broken down your questions as follows:
Question: How do we ensure that if there is a compliance review, the client can be satisfied that they will not be found to be non-compliant if IRCC refuses to accept updates on the workers' files?
Response: In all cases, both companies should keep all documents about the merger or takeover in case of a compliance inspection. Documents about the employment of the temporary worker needs to be kept for 6 years from the date the work permit was issued. You can also fill out a Voluntary Disclosure form if the conditions in the offer of employment change.
Question: How can the workers ensure that, if there are concerns by CBSA at the border, they can demonstrate that their employment information says one thing, and the work permit says another?
Response: If the takeover organization is a successor in interest, in that it has substantially assumed the interests, obligations, assets and liabilities of the original organization (wholly or partially) and continues to operate the same type of business as the original organization, the takeover organization remains the “employer" for the purpose of the existing work permit as well. In this scenario, the temporary worker is not obligated to obtain a new work permit and will continue to be authorized to work in Canada for the duration of the period stated on the existing work permit as long as both of the following apply:
The takeover organization meets the requirements under which the LMIA-exempt work permit was issued (for instance, a qualifying relationship for intra-company transferee), or the takeover organization assumes the LMIA contract. •The worker's employment conditions as per the original offer of employment (for example, the wages, duties and location) have not changed.

threads.subject: Seeking guidance regarding situations in which the balance of the work duration approved in an LMIA can be recaptured in an extension application -- REP-2024-1039 - DUE 19-Jul-2024
threads.question:
Dear Immigration Representatives,
I hope you are well.
I am seeking guidance as to a foreign worker can use an existing LMIA to renew their work permit, even where its validity has passed, in a situation where their initial LMIA based work permit was issued for several years less than the LMIA work duration as I cannot find any guidance which addresses this point specifically. This scenario arises sometimes in the case of academics where the academic is in the final stages of securing their PhD when they commence their employment. In such cases, the university indicates this in its academic LMIA application and Service Canada approves a four or five year initial employment duration based on the university's request. The initial duration of employment requested usually aligns with the university's tenure review process timeline. In some schools it is four years, in others it is five. When the academic requests issuance of their work permit pursuant to the
LMIA, the work permit is typically issued for a shorter duration than the LMIA work duration. It is common for the initial work permit to be valid for two years instead of the full four or five so that the academic can provide proof that they did secure their PhD within 1-2 years of commencing their employment when they apply to extend their work permit. The employer entity has requirements of such academic employees also. If the PhD is not secured, as expected, within a certain timeframe, the academic's employment may come to an end. My question is whether a foreign worker in this scenario can apply to capture the balance of the work duration approved in an existing LMIA or if the employer in such instances must apply for a new LMiA to support the extension of the foreign worker's work permit despite that fact that the existing LMiA approves a longer work duration than was granted. As you may be aware, there is a variation to the advertising in the case of tenure stream academics where a second LMIA is being applied for such that no advertising is required. My point in raising this is that there would be no difference in terms of testing the labour market whether another LMIA is applied for in the above scenario or not. Had the work permit duration been limited due to the foreign worker's passport expiry date, the LMiA could be used for an extension application. IRCC's guidance makes this clear. There is no guidance for a scenario such as the one outlined above, hence my email to you.
Where the passport expires before the specified duration of work, the work permit must be issued for a shorter duration than identified in the LMIA. For example, if the LMIA work duration is 2 years but the foreign national's passport will expire in 1 year, the officer will issue a 1-year work permit. In cases where a shorter duration was provided due to passport expiry only, foreign nationals will be able to renew their work permits without obtaining a new LMIA if they have received a passport with longer validity. Even though the LMIA validity date has passed, the foreign national met the initial time frame for application, and his work permit can therefore be extended for the duration outlined in the initial LMIA, from the date of initial entry. Processing officers should record the reason(s) in the GCMS Case Notes view tab or in User Remarks when a work permit is issued for a shorter duration than is indicated in the LMIA. Many thanks for your guidance. Best regards,

Hello,
Please see our response to your question:
Response:
When reviewing work permit applications with an associated LMlA, officers ensure that the LMIA is valid at the time of the work permit application and that it has not been changed or suspended. Work permit applications received after the LMIA validity date has passed do not meet the requirement of section R200 (IRPR) for the issuance of a work permit. In such cases and before the worker can apply to extend or change their work permit, the employers must apply for a new LMIA when they anticipate that their need for TFWs will continue beyond the period covered by the initial work permit.
The new LMIA application should be sent at least 4 months prior to the expiry of the work permit to ensure Service Canada has sufficient time to process the application and for IRCC to process the work permit extension. However, applications received more than 6 months in advance of the job start date will not be accepted. [https://www.canada.ca/en/employment-social-development/services/foreign-workers/academic/after.html](https://www.canada.ca/en/employment-social-development/services/foreign-workers/academic/after.html) (source of the paragraph but not an IRCC link)

In summary, if the original LMiA is still valid, it can typically be used to extend the work permit to cover the remaining approved duration. However, if the LMiA has expired, a new LMiA application will likely be required before submitting a work permit extension application.

Question: Foreign nationals are required to disclose previous refusals when applying to Canada. However, the common practice of "flagpoling" requires an administrative refusal from the USA. Good afternoon,
All refusals must be disclosed when completing applications. It is even recommended that USA refusals be disclosed as that information can become available throughout the application process. Additional information can be found here: Temporary residents-Refusals overview-Canada.ca

threads.answer:
## Hello,
Please see our response to your question. QUESTION: I have a group of service industry employers wondering if they can hire TFWs under LMIA and bank their overtime hours during the busy season to pay out during a two month slow season where the worker would be off for two months. I have a handle on the employment law issues, but am not sure if this would comply with the 30 hour a week requirement for LMIA workers. For example, the TFW is hired in March. They work normal hours March to April. From May-August they work 50-70 hours a week. Any hours over 48 hours is “banked”. They work normal hours during shoulder season, September to December. Then they get all of January and February off, but is paid the overtime that was “banked” (assuming the math works out where pay equals 30 hours a week). RESPONSE: Temporary Foreign Worker Program (TFWP) compliance and specific employment standards are overseen by Employment and Social Development Canada (ESDC), rather than (IRCC). ESDC is responsible for assessing and issuing LMIAs, which includes ensuring that TFWs receive wages and working conditions that meet or exceed the minimum standards set by federal and provincial regulations. Under the TFWP, employers are required to ensure that TFWs work a minimum of 30 hours per week, unless specific exemptions apply. While banking overtime hours for future payout may comply with employment law regulations, it is essential to ensure compliance with LMIA requirements. Please contact the ESDC Employer Contact Centre.
and Citizenship Caneda
Thank you kindly, The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

L'information divulguée en vertu de la [oi sur l'accès à linformation
Good Day, Thank you for your email correspondence to 's Immigration Representatives mailbox. We appreciate your patience. Question: I have a client who is working in Canada on an LMIA based work permit (his LMIA was approved under the LMIA owner operator program). He is a 20% shareholder of the company and is paid a salary as per the wage mentioned on his LMIA approval. In another case, my client has a 51% shareholding in the company. Could you please clarify which experience out of the above (20% or 51% shareholding) gained in Canada will be counted towards CEC. Answer: A self-employed person who is owner or co-owner of a business that they are actively engaged in, is not able to elect' to employ themselves (or dismiss themselves) as is understood to be the case for an employer; which is what gives meaning to the value of the offer of employment. Neither would one of the co-owners be able to employ or dismiss' the co-owner, as is understood to be the case for an ‘employer'. Rather, they would need to create or dissolve a business partnership, which is not an employment relationship. The co-owners in this case have elected to be co-shareholders and directors, not 'co-employing employers' of each other. The intent of regulators, when drafting the Canadian Experience Class (CEC), was not so a self-employed person can meet the requirements of the class. The intent is that the worker enters the labour market, not the business community. It is the entry to the labour market which contributes to the assessment of their likelihood of economic establishment. This is why Section
87.1(3)(b) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations states, "any period of self-employment or unauthorized work shall not be included in calculating a period of work experience. Therefore, none of the experience claimed while owing a company (regardless of shareholder percentage) counts toward CEC. Please be advised that the assessment of an application is based on a case-by-case basis; each application will be considered on its own merits, with a final decision based on a review of all the information available to the officer at the time of decision. The onus is always on the applicant to provide sufficient documentation to satisfy an officer that they meet the requirements. We trust that this information will assist you. Sincerely, Immigration Representatives Mailbox

A study permit is not required for programs that are less than six months in duration and which will be completed in the period authorized for the foreign national's stay, as per R188(c).

Hello,
Question:

I would like to clarify with IRCC if officers take into consideration the time that the student took to complete their credential in order to determine the length of the student's PGWP. For example, if the student completed a one-year program in just 8 months, would this affect the length of the student's PGWP? Also, if a student used credits from a previously earned credential (1-year program) to complete another 1-year program in a shorter time, would that affect the length of the student's PGWP?
Response:
Determining the length of the post-graduation work permit details the guidelines officers follow when deciding the length of PGWPs. Specifically it says: "The length of the work permit should coincide with the length of the program" but "may not go beyond the applicant's passport validity date".
Further, the link provides information regarding accelerated studies: Accelerated studies If a student completes their studies in less time than the normal length of the program (that is, they have accelerated their studies), the post-graduation work permit should be assessed on the length of the program of study. For example, if the student is enrolled in a program of study that is normally 1 year in duration, but the student completes the requirements for the program of study within 8 months, they may be eligible for a post-graduation work permit that is valid for 1 year.
In other words, the length of the PGWP should be either the length of the study program or the time until the passport expires, whichever comes first. In terms of completing multiple programs, the aforementioned link states:
"The length of the work permit should combine the length of each program. If the combined length of the programs is 2 years or longer (or 1,800 hours or longer for a combination of a DVS with an AVS in Quebec), the work permit may be valid for up to 3 years (provided that the DVS program in Quebec is at least 900 hours in length)."
Thank you! The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.question:
In the Ministerial Instructions Respecting the Agri-food Immigration Class, 2023, the instructions identify a term with reference to the industry groups (NAlCS), which is "primarily engaged in activities set out for industry group xxxx".
Are there evidentiary/documentary standards that are used to demonstrate that an employer is primarily engaged in an activity? Is there a specific threshold of activities (a plurality, majority, etc.) or eligibility criteria to help establish when this standard is met?
Thank you for any assistance you can provide.
Sincerely,
and Citizenship Caneda
Ruscito, Giovanni (IRCC/IRCC)
threads.answer:
Good day,
Thank you for your enquiry on industry groups and their evidentiary standards.
In accordance with section 2(3) (c) and (f) of the Members of Class of the Ministerial Instructions Respecting the Agri-food Immigration Class ([https://canadagazette.gc.ca/rp-pr/p1/2019/2019-08-](https://canadagazette.gc.ca/rp-pr/p1/2019/2019-08-) 31/html/notice-avis-eng.html), a foreign national must demonstrate that they have received both work experience and an offer of employment that meets the following requirement among others:
- it is made by a single employer in Canada that is primarily engaged in activities set out for industry group 1114, 1121, 1122, 1123, 1124, 1129 or 3116 in the North American Industry Classification
System.
An employer is deemed to be primarily engaged in activities of a specific industry group if these activities represent the largest value-added for this business. For more information on how to determine the industry classification of a business, please refer to the NAICS website ([https://www.statcan.gc.ca/en/subjects/standard/naics/2022/v1/introduction#a11In](https://www.statcan.gc.ca/en/subjects/standard/naics/2022/v1/introduction#a11In)). In order to determine that an employer is engaged in a business with an eligible NAICS, IRCC will refer to the employer reference letter or offer of employment provided by the applicant. These letters should include a description of the main responsibilities and duties of the employee, as well as a description of the employer's principal business activities and the corresponding industry code. This is used to determine if the offer of employment is in an eligible NAlCS and NOC combination for the Agri-Food Pilot.
If the applicant would like to provide further supporting documents to help substantiate the principal business activities of the employer, they are welcome to do so, but this is not required.
Thank you, The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

Response: In regard to your inquiry on students changing their program of study at the same DLl, if students change their study program within the same DLl before traveling to Canada, this change would not affect their previously approved study permit application. If a student changes their program of study to a different DLl after their visa is issued, they will have to submit a new study permit application to IRCC.

threads.subject: Question regarding eTA vs visa for Mexican child of temp workers parents in Canada --REP-2024-0719-- DUE 31-MAY-2024
threads.question: On February 29th, 2024, Canada changed the requirements for Mexican nationals regarding their entry in the country, and, unless exempted, they should get a visa. [https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/campaigns/eta-work-visa-mexico.html](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/campaigns/eta-work-visa-mexico.html) If both Mexican parents currently hold valid work permits from 2023 to 2026 with valid eTA which remain valid following the change of February 29th, 2024, but a child (1 year old) who held a valid visitor record and submitted a renewal still in process. Would that child need a visa after getting the visitor record or the child will be able to obtain a new eTA since already in Canada and accompanying both parents in Canada who are temporary workers? There is no mention in the aforementioned link regarding the children of temporary workers in Canada who already hold valid eTAs. There is a mention about an exemption for Mexican who held a Canadian visa in the 10 previous years which could get an eTA, but nothing for a Mexican national who held a valid eTA and a visitor record.
threads.answer:
A temporary resident visa (TRV) is required to demonstrate at a port of entry that a person has met the requirements to enter Canada as a temporary resident. As a visitor record does not authorize re- entry, a child who is in Canada with a visitor record would require a temporary resident visa on their return to Canada in the event that they leave. A child is not exempt from the TRV requirement even if their parents are work permit holders with eTAs.
Thank you kindly, The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.answer:
Good morning,
Question:
I hope this email finds you well. I had a question about if the students in this scenario might need a work permit. in case if a US citizen or an international student studying at a US campus wants to do a remote COOP position for a Canadian DLl, do they need a work permit? Lets say the will be paid by their US university and will just for remotely as a part of their COOP. Also, in case they would like to visit the Canadian DLl for lets say a week for business meetings (but not work in Canada), can they do so while entering as a visitor? Thank you in advance for your help.
Response:
Please note that we cannot provide case-specific guidance. However, if a foreign national works in a country other than Canada, they do not need a Canadian work permit. There are 2 types of works permits in Canada: 1) Employer-specific work permits and 2) Open work permits (Work permit: About the process-Canada.ca). Both permits allow the foreign national to "work in Canada". Unless the foreign national is physically working inside Canada, there is no use for a Canadian work permit. Attending business meetings counts as working in Canada. As an American citizen, business visitors are covered under R186(a) and Appendix 1, Section B of the Canada-United States-Mexico Agreement (CUSMA) and do not require a work permit to attend business meetings.

threads.subject: Requirement to return to your home country -- REP-2024-1156 - Due 9-Aug-24
threads.question:
Hello, The individual would be applying for permanent residency under CEC or FSW.
Thank you
threads.answer:
Good Day, Thank you for your email correspondence to 's Immigration Representatives mailbox. We appreciate your patience. Question: Hello, I am wondering how IRCC deals with processing permanent residency for individuals that are in Canada, being paid by a foreign government, and required to return to their home country after completion of their work term. The individual would be applying for permanent residency under CEC or FSW. Answer: Considering that these positions are foreign-funded, i.e. no Canadian employer is paying them, they do not enter the Canadian labour market and therefore that activity they are performing in Canada may not be considered Canadian work experience for the purposes of Canadian Experience Class (CEC) or for Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) points. Currently, the system will award points based off the declared physical location of the work. Therefore, if you want to declare this activity as foreign work experience, you may data enter the location of the work to be the country who is paying them (provide an explanation with the letter of employment). Please note that if they are receiving a stipend or allowance, where the primary purpose is to cover expenses, this would not generally be considered wages (and therefore the work would not count for permanent residence). The onus is on the applicant to satisfy the officer that there was the payment of wages and that the employment constitutes Canadian work experience. Additionally, pursuant to Section R70(1)(b) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations, it must be established that the foreign national is coming to Canada to establish permanent residence. If they are required to return to their home country after completion of their work term then an officer may have concerns the applicant is not coming to establish permanent residence in Canada. Please be advised that the assessment of an application is performed on a case-by-case basis; each application will be considered on its own merits, with a final decision based on a review of all the information available to the officer at the time of decision. The onus is always on the applicant to provide sufficient documentation to satisfy an officer that they meet the requirements. We trust that this information will assist you.

Sincerely,

threads.answer:

Please find the answers to your questions below: Question: If a student has maintained full-time status for the duration of their program of study and only requires a part-time course load in their final academic session to complete their program of study, we understand that the student is allowed to work for no more than 20 hours per week during the academic session, however, we want to clear that whether the student is allowed to work full-time during the reading week? Regularly scheduled break: To be considered a regularly scheduled break, the break must be part of the DLl's academic calendar (for instance, winter and summer holidays, Reading Week). threads.answer:
Hello,
Thank you for your email correspondence to 's Immigration Representatives mailbox. We appreciate your patience.
Question: Hello, My question is if a client is working in Canada (on a work permit) but being paid by a foreign government (Saudi Arabia) can they claim this work experience under Federal Skilled Worker?
Answer: Please refer to our website to learn more about the work experience requirements under the Federal Skilled Worker Program (FSWP). The program does not have specific requirements regarding which entity remunerates the work experience required for meeting its minimum criteria, only that the experience must be remunerated by wages or commission. If the applicant is receiving a stipend or allowance, where the primary purpose is to cover expenses, such experience would not be considered “work" for the purposes of the economic programs for permanent residence, including FSWP, because a stipend or allowance is not considered a “wage". Please be advised that foreign-funded positions in Canada are not considered a part of the Canadian labour market and therefore may not be considered Canadian work experience for the purposes of Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) points. Currently, the system will award CRS points based on the declared physical location of the work. Therefore, if you want to declare this activity as foreign work experience, you may data enter the location of the work to be the country that is paying for the position. Please provide an explanation for this arrangement with the letter of employment when submitting an application.
Please be advised that the assessment of an application is based on a case-by-case basis, considering the particular circumstances in conjunction with the supporting documentation available to the officer. The onus is always on the applicant to provide sufficient documentation to satisfy an officer that they meet the requirements.
We trust that this information will assist you. Sincerely,

Question:
My question is regarding Canadian Experience Class (CEC) qualifying work experience, specifically in scenarios where brief periods of work are performed overseas but the applicant remains continually employed. It is understood that CEC work experience should be obtained for skilled work done in Canada, and I understand there is leeway for regular vacation time when calculating time periods claimed. However, what if an applicant's Canadian job and Canadian company require them to travel outside of Canada to complete their job duties? For example:
•Someone attending a conference in the USA for a week while still being paid by their Canadian employer.
- A long-haul truck driver for a Canadian company that is driving goods to delivery points in the USA.
- A software developer traveling overseas from their employer to perform software testing in person for 2 months.
Do these periods of work, despite being for a Canadian company and a necessary role for their Canadian job, need to be deducted from the qualifying Canadian experience? The context is where the applicant spends the majority of their time working in Canada, remains on the payroll of the Canadian company, and the job inherently requires some work to be performed outside of Canada.
I understand that fully remote jobs or those where the majority of time is spent working overseas do not qualify for CEC. However, where do officers draw the line?
If the applicant is not able to claim any hours for Canadian work experience obtained outside Canada while continuously employed by their Canadian company, would the applicant be expected to delineate all these periods of work experience where they were outside of Canada for the eligibility calculator to accurately deduct their Canadian work experience? I would imagine address or travel history would be able to accurately determine between Canadian Experience, and work performed overseas, but in the Express Entry eligibility questionnaire, applicants are unable to make that distinction.
Answer:
The policy intent of Canadian Experience Class requires that the work performed demonstrates to the Officer that the applicant has entered the Canadian labour market, and a Canadian entity paid the applicant for their work. It must also be evident to the Officer that the work would be considered a business activity that is competitive in the Canadian marketplace, and that this position would normally have been filled by a Canadian citizen or permanent resident. Entry into the Canadian labour market is a necessary element of work experience that demonstrates ones “ability to become economically established in Canada"” under R87.1(1) of the IRPR.
Officers would need to review the circumstances and decide if overall they are satisfied the usual place of work duties is in Canada, or elsewhere, AND whether the applicant maintained temporary resident status during the period of work. Factors that might go into that last assessment (TR status) might include whether they had that status, were physically present, and maintained residential ties (habitually resided) at a residence in Canada during the period of work.
While this is largely officer discretion (and there is no calculator available) a cautionary approach to the last scenario (software developer) might be to discount the 2 months residing and working outside Canada, as not meeting the TR status threshold, since the individual would need to be habitually sheltered outside Canada for those months, and accrue 2 additional months in Canada.
Overall, work that compels an employee to reside out of Canada for longer periods of time, and for which they would not require an authorization to work (since it is outside Canada's jurisdiction, in a foreign territory) and where they cannot be considered to have maintained status as a temporary resident, would need to be excluded from counting. That said, an applicant could conceivably satisfy an officer if for instance they remained a factual resident of Canada, etc. Factors that might complicate that could be that the applicant is an independent contractor of the Canadian employer, or employed by the foreign worksite while present, rather than being a wage-earning employee. There isn't a calculator and the officer would need to review to be satisfied the work was in Canada' as a temporary resident of Canada'.
Please be advised that the assessment of an application is performed on a case-by-case basis; each application will be considered on its own merits, with a final decision based on a review of all the information available to the officer at the time of decision. The onus is always on the applicant to provide sufficient documentation to satisfy an officer that they meet the requirements.

La personne principale demandant le permis de travail post-diplôme travaillait pendant ses études. Avant de terminer ses études, elle a eu un enfant et est actuellement en congé de maternité. La personne a reçu ses documents de fin d'études en juillet.
Ma question est la suivante : au moment de demander le permis de travail post-diplôme ainsi que le permis de travail ouvert pour le conjoint accompagnateur, peut-elle présenter la preuve qu'elle est employée (lettre d'emploi de son employeur) et les relevés de paiement des prestations parentales ? Ou est-il nécessaire qu'elle soit retournée au travail et qu'elle fournisse les relevés de paie de salaire?

threads.answer:
Bonne journée, Merci d’avoir soumis les questions suivantes pour clarification. Question Au moment de demander le permis de travail post-diplôme ainsi que le permis de travail ouvert pour le conjoint accompagnateur, peut-elle présenter la preuve qu'elle est employée (lettre d'emploi de son employeur) et les relevés de paiement des prestations parentales ? Ou est-il nécessaire qu'elle soit retournée au travail et qu'elle fournisse les relevés de paie de salaire?
Réponse
Les instructions suivantes figurent dans les informations destinées aux membres de la famille des travailleurs étrangers : Remarque : Le demandeur principal étranger peut être en congé autorisé de son emploi et toujours être considéré comme étant « employé ». Par exemple, si le demandeur principal étranger est une femme en congé de maternité et qu’il est prévu qu’elle retourne travailler pour le même employeur, on peut considérer que la personne est employée.
Ces instructions concernent à la fois les travailleurs hautement qualifiés et les travailleurs peu qualifiés. Il est donc raisonnable que la demanderesse principale présente la preuve qu'elle est employée avec une lettre d'emploi et de relevés de versement de prestations. Elle n'est pas tenue d'être retournée au travail ni de fournir des fiches de salaire pour que son conjoint obtienne son permis de travail ouvert.
Nous espérons que ces informations vous seront utiles. Pour plus d’informations, veuillez consulter la page Web suivante : Membres de la famille d'étrangers autorisés à occuper un emploi hautement spécialisé (FEER 0, 1, 2 ou 3) - [R205c)(ii) – C41 et C46] – Intérêt canadien – Programme de mobilité international (PMI) - Canada.ca
Membres de la famille d'étrangers autorisés à occuper un emploi peu spécialisé (FEER 4 ou 5) [R205c)(ii) – C47 et C48] – Intérêt canadien – Programme de mobilité internationale (PMI) - Canada.ca
Merci beaucoup, La boîte aux lettres des représentants en immigration

We appreciate your patience. Please find the answers to your questions below:
1. If spring/summer is a student's final semester, they can only work up to 20 hours right? Response: They must be a full-time student both before and after a regularly scheduled break to work full-time during the break. In this situation they can only work up to 20 hours per week during the break. If the spring/summer period is not a regularly scheduled break, then students authorized to work off-campus can only do so up to 20 hours per week.
2. If a deferral is approved by the school and they issued a new letter of acceptance, can the student come to Canada with their previous IRCC letter of introduction which is still valid? Response: To enter Canada, they must have a valid port of entry letter of introduction from IRCC and the original and updated letter of acceptance from the same DLl. As long as they will be attending the same DLl, they do not need to reapply for a study permit. If a student changes their program of study to a different DLl after their visa is issued, they need to submit a new study permit application to IRCC. Students should immediately submit their new LOA to IRCC using the online web form if they made any changes to their program of study within the same DLl or to a different DLl while their study permit application is still in process.
3. I got the information from IRCC before that “Please note that the passport number indicated on your document has no impact on the information related to your current status." Do they have to apply for a new study permit after they get their new passport? Response: We apologize for the misunderstanding in our previous response. If they have a new passport, they do not need to change their study permit until it expires.
4. Given it is a new application for IRCC portal application instead of study permit extension, do they have maintained status? Response: Regardless of the system used, if IRCC received a complete application before the expiry date of their previous document, they would have maíntained status until a decision is made on the new application. If the applicant hasn't received an AOR letter, they will need to submit a new application and pay the fees.
5. Does it mean that IRCC portal application does not grant maintained status? Response: Maintained status is only extended under R183(5) if IRCC receives a complete application before the period of authorized stay ends. If the applicant is not aware that IRCC has received a complete application, and their study permit has expired, they will need to apply to restore their status.

threads.subject: Does an American Citizen require a passport to apply for a work permit in Canada -- REP-2024-0268 Dear Sir or Madam, We kindly ask for clarification regarding a question that we obtained two different responses from Immigration Representatives. The question posed was: Question-Does an American Citizen require a passport to apply for a work permit in Canada? Specifically, a USA citizen with an enhanced driver's license should be able to apply without a passport as per Regulation 52(2). In this case the applicants enhanced ID number would be used in place of a passport number. Can you please confirm? On May 15th an answer from Immigration Representatives stated that: Response: Thank you for your inquiry, an enhanced driver's license typically cannot be used to apply for a work permit in Canada. Work permits generally require specific documentation such as passport along with other supporting documents depending on the type of work permit being applied for. An enhanced driver's licence can be used to enter Canada, but only for U.S. citizens who are coming either to visit or do business when a work permit is not needed (e.g., R186(a)). On June 28th an answer from Immigration Representatives stated that: Response: As a citizen of the USA the enhanced drivers license acts as a travel document and therefore can be used in place of a passport when applying for a work permit. However when entering Canada by air a passport will be needed as the enhanced drivers license is only used by land. “Enhanced Drivers Licenses (EDLs) are state-issued enhanced drivers licenses that provide proof of identity and U.S. citizenship when crossing the U.S. border in a vehicle" please see here for more information We kindly ask for clarification on whether or not a USA citizen can apply for a work permit using their enhanced drivers license instead of their passport. Please also find attached the two distinct email responses. Thank you for the clarification and continued cooperation.

Bonjour,
Je vous écris en tant que conseiller réglementé en immigration au Collège communautaire du Nouveau-Brunswick (CCNB). Nous offrons une formation de transition destinée aux infirmières formées à l'étranger, permettant de compléter les exigences nécessaires pour travailler au Canada.
Cette formation peut être suivie à distance à partir du Canada et varie en durée et en contenu selon l'évaluation académique préalable effectuée par l'Association provinciale des infirmières.
Nous avons récemment reçu des demandes d'admission de la part de personnes détenant un permis de travail. Pour assurer la conformité avec les régulations en vigueur, j'aurais besoin de clarifications sur les points suivants :
Formation de moins de 6 mois : Je voudrais une confirmation que les détenteurs d’un permis de travail peuvent suivre cette formation sans permis d’études. Est-ce applicable même si le permis de travail inclut la restriction « interdiction de fréquenter un établissement d’enseignement sans être autorisé » ?
Formation de plus de 6 mois : Je voudrais une confirmation que les détenteurs d’un permis de travail peuvent suivre cette formation longue, incluant un stage, en respectant toutes les conditions de la politique d'intérêt public temporaire. Est-ce applicable même si le permis de travail inclut la restriction « interdiction de fréquenter un établissement d’enseignement sans être autorisé » ?
Stage en milieu de travail : Je voudrais confirmer que le permis de travail permettra aux participants à la formation de plus de 6 mois d’effectuer leur stage seulement s’ils sont autorisés à travailler à l’endroit ou le stage aura lieu.
Je vous remercie d'avance pour votre collaboration et reste disponible pour toute information complémentaire.
Cordialement,
