## Bonjour,
Veuillez prendre note que nous ne pouvons répondre à des questions relatif à des cas spécifiques; ceci étant dit, nous avons inclus les informations suivantes pour vous guider.
QUESTIONS: Nous avons récemment reçu des demandes d'admission de la part de personnes détenant un permis de travail. Pour assurer la conformité avec les régulations en vigueur, j'aurais besoin de clarifications sur les points suivants :
1) Formation de moins de 6 mois : Je voudrais une confirmation que les détenteurs d’un permis de travail peuvent suivre cette formation sans permis d’études.
Est-ce applicable même si le permis de travail inclut la restriction « interdiction de fréquenter un établissement d’enseignement sans être autorisé »?
2)Formation de plus de 6 mois : Je voudrais une confirmation que les détenteurs d’un permis de travail peuvent suivre cette formation longue, incluant un stage, en respectant toutes les conditions de la politique d’intérêt public temporaire.
Est-ce applicable même si le permis de travail inclut la restriction « interdiction de fréquenter un établissement d’enseignement sans être autorisé »?
3) Stage en milieu de travail : Je voudrais confirmer que le permis de travail permettra aux participants à la formation de plus de 6 mois d’effectuer leur stage seulement s’ils sont autorisés à travailler à l’endroit ou le stage aura lieu.
RÉPONSES : Pour la ρolitique d’intérêt public temporaireLes permis de travail peuvent inclure la condition suivante : « interdiction de fréquenter un établissement d’enseignement ou de suivre un cours théorique ou professionnel à moins d’avoir une autorisation. » Pour les demandeurs admissibles, cette politique d’intérêt public donne l’autorisation à laquelle il est fait référence dans cette condition. Cette autorisation s’applique jusqu’à l’expiration du permis de travail dont il est question au point 1) ou associé à la demande dont il est question au point 2), le refus de la demande de permis de travail dont il est question au point 2), l’expiration de la politique d’intérêt public (27 juin 2026) ou la révocation de la présente politique d’intérêt public, selon la première de ces occurrences.

Question 1: Is there any correlation between the supported financial proof and the new permit validity? Can you confirm that if one student's projected to finish their program in one year, but they only have $10,000 in their proof of fund, assuming they meet other study permit conditions, might their new permit be issued for a shorter duration, such as 6 or 8 months?
Response 1: There is no correlation between the supported financial proof and the new study permit validity. Once an officer has determined that an applicant is a bona fide student and meets the requirements (including financial requirements), they are to issue a study permit for the length of studies plus 90 days or passport expiry, whichever comes first. If a student is expected to complete their program in one year but lacks sufficient funds, an IRCC officer will review the application and assess it based on its merits. Other factors, including academic progress and compliance with study permit conditions, also influence the decision. Study permits: Final decisions-Determining validity periods-Canada.ca
Question 2: How does IRCC evaluate different forms of available funds? Most students might use a combination of their Canadian bank savings, parents/sponsor savings together with sponsorship letter, and maybe their Canadian employment payments or their parents employment payments. Let's say a student needs to extend their study permit for one more year, required minimum living cost is $20,635 and required tuition is $10,000. Is it required to have in total $30,635 equivalent Canadian showing in theirs and their parents bank accounts to get the full length of study permit? Or alternatively, they have about $10,000 in all banking accounts, but can demonstrate approximately a combined of $20,000 annual income. Will this be accepted by IRCC, and the student can get the full length of the study permit?
Response 2: IRCC requires proof that the student has sufficient funds to cover both the minimum living cost and the tuition fees. They may accept combined income from various sources as proof of financial support to ensure that the total available funds, including income, meet or exceed the required amount. Study permit: Get the right documents-Proof of financial support-Canada.ca
Question 3
If a student needs to extend their study permit for more than one year, e.g., 20 months, are they required to show available funds for the entire period, or just for the first year? How about for a shorter period than one year, e.g., they only need to extend their study permit for 8 months, can they only show around $13,800 for living cost plus the remaining tuition amount, instead of $20,635 plus tuition?
Response 3: If a student extends their study permit for more than one year, they must provide proof of funds for living expenses and tuition fees for the first year of the extension, similar to the requirements for a new study permit. Officers should be satisfied that there is a likelihood of funding for the subsequent years. Each application is reviewed and assessed based on its own merits. Study permits: Assessing the application-Canada.ca-Financial sufficiency
Question 4: Once an officer decides the student has enough funding for the future projected length of studies, will another 90 days be added towards the new study permit validity? For example, a student's program is expected to be finished before Dec 31, 2025, and if they meet all study permit extension requirements together with the financial requirements, will the new permit be given to Mar 31, 2026? Is it recommended for the DLl's enrolment letter to include this 90-day period to cover students' graduation stage, so instead of Dec 31, 2025, we project the student will finish on Mar 31, 2026? If yes, should student provide even a higher amount of financial proof to cover the 3 months difference?
Response 4: When extending a study permit in Canada, the new permit typically includes an additional 90 days beyond the length of your study program. The extra 90 days gives you time to prepare to leave Canada or to extend your stay. All applications are reviewed by an IRCC officer and are assessed based on their own merit. The letter of enrollment should clearly indicate the end date of the program. Extend your study permit or restore your status: About the process-Canada.ca
Please be advised that the assessment of an application is based on a case-by-case basis, considering the particular circumstances in conjunction with the supporting documentation available to the officer. threads.question:
Subject: Re: Update of Work Experience Requirement under HCCP Pilot Dear Sir/Madam, I have clients who are working in Canada as Home Child Care Providers on Occupation restricted Open work permits since Jan 2024 issued under HCCP Pilot. They have applied under GAINING EXPERIENCE Category of HCCP. As per new policy of IRCC dated June/24/2024, these applicants now need 6 months of eligible work experience instead of 12 months before they can send proof of their eligible work experience to IRCC. As per checklist they need to send the following documents as proof of eligible Work Experience : T4 Slips, Notice of Assessment, Reference Letter from Employer and Job Offer, Payslips. My Question is, if applicants have started working in Canada since Jan 2024, they will not have T4 Slips and Notice of Assessments. In that case, should we update IRCC about applicant's work experience without T4 slips and Notice of Assessments or applicants have to wait for these documents and then update IRCC. Also, any additional documents may be required in this case? Waiting for your reply, Thanks & Regards,
Ruscito, Giovanni (IRCC/IRCC)
threads.answer:
Dear
Thank you for contacting the Immigration Representatives Mailbox.
For applicants that are claiming Canadian work experience and do not have the necessary tax information slips, you may still submit your work experience and documents including pay stubs, work contract or job offers. If an applicant is unable to provide a document, they must include a letter to explain why and include any other relevant proof of experience that they have performed the eligible work. Suggestions in lieu of a T4 or a NOA can include but are not limited to:
Bank statements showing salary deposits from the claimed work experience duration Pay stubs or other financial records to help verify payment
However, it is important to be aware that applicants only have one opportunity to submit their proof of work experience. If an applicant under the Home Child Care Provider or Home Support Worker pilots submits proof of work experience (foreign or Canadian), and an officer is not satisfied that this experience is eligible, the application for permanent residence (PR) will be refused. This means that their PR application will be closed and therefore, the applicant will not be able to submit any new or additional proof of work experience (foreign nor Canadian). If an occupation-restricted open work permit (OROWP) was issued before the proof was sent, the client would still be able to continue working under that work permit until its expiry, though any additional experience gained couldn't be used to support their now-refused PR application. There is a possibility, however, that the work experience might be used to support a future application for permanent residence for the recently announced new caregiver pilots (more information will be available before the full launch of the pilots, including full eligibility criteria).
Clients should make sure the work experience they wish to submit to satisfy the work experience requirement qualifies under the pilot they applied to. While foreign or Canadian work experience, or a combination, can be used to satisfy the work experience requirement, the work experience must have been obtained no more than 36 months before their application was made, and no more than 36 months after they get their OROWP. In addition, combined work experience must be in the same occupation and match the pilot under which they applied. Clients should review their documents carefully and make sure they're complete before sending them as proof of their work experience. It's up to the clients to decide at which point during their application process they want to send us their proof of experience, as long as it's not more than 3 years after they get their Occupation Restricted Open Work Permit.

threads.answer:
Good day,
Thank you for reaching out to IRCC with these questions.
1. How does the Federal EMPP program define "living outside of Canada" for applicants? Specifically, we are interested in understanding if this requirement excludes individuals who have temporarily lived in Canada, such as those who have held a study permit, work permit, or other forms of temporary resident status, but have since left Canada. The Federal EMPP states that the principal applicant must be “outside of Canada" at the time of application for permanent residence is received. This means that the principal applicant must be physically outside of Canada when submitting the application. This requirement does not exclude individuals who have temporarily lived in Canada, including those who have held a study permit, work permit, or other forms of temporary resident status, as long as they are physically outside of Canada at the time of application for permanent residence.
2. Is it possible for an individual to apply for the Federal EMPP program while holding a valid temporary resident status and being physically present outside of Canada? Yes, it is possible for an individual to apply for the Federal EMPP program while holding a valid temporary resident status and being physically outside of Canada. The principal applicant must ensure they are outside of Canada at the time of submitting the application for permanent residence.
Thank you kindly,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

I am writing to you to seek clarification on the length of study permits issued for a graduate program that is offered primarily online with some in-Canada components. Below is the tentative course schedule for your reference.
Program: Two-year Master's program (Starting Sep. 2025 - Aug. 2027) Delivery method: Primarily online with the exception of three weekends (2-3 days) of classes (Aug. 2025, Jul. 2026 and Jul. 2027)
We understand that International students enrolled in a study program for more than six months, including an in-Canada component, require a study permit. Our understanding is also that the study permit will only be issued for the duration of the in-Canada portion. (*1)
With the above in mind, we were wondering how to best advise our international students taking this program to ensure they meet IRCC requirements as international students in Canada.
Q1. Could a 2-year study permit be issued based on the letter of acceptance for a 2-year master's program that includes three weekends of classes in Canada? Q2. If a 2-year study permit is not issued, does this mean international students are expected to apply for study permits for each visit? (three different occasions)
IRCC-Distance learning can be through e-learning, correspondence, or internet courses. Distance learning is a process by which technology is used in ways where the student does not have to physically be in the place where the teaching is taking place. Since by definition distance learning does not require one to be in Canada, a study permit cannot be issued for this type of course. For example, if a foreign national authorized to work in Canada is prohibited from engaging in studies as per a condition of their work permit, they are allowed to engage in distance learning courses.
However, some distance learning courses include an in-Canada portion to the program (e.g., special tutorials or the writing of final exams). If the overall course of study is greater than six months, then the student requires a study permit for the in-Canada portion of the program, even if the in-Canada portion is less than six months. The duration of the study permit should be for the duration of the in-Canada portion only.
Study permits: Other considerations-Canada.ca

Thank you in advance for your kind assistance.
Warm regards,
| Citizenship Canada| |

Question 1. Could a 2-year study permit be issued based on the letter of acceptance for a 2-year master's program that includes three weekends of classes in Canada? Response 1: Based on the current guidelines from (IRCC), a study permit for a primarily online program that includes some in-Canada components would typically be issued only for the duration of the in-Canada portion of the program. This means that it is unlikely for a 2-year study permit to be issued for such a program. The study permit is generally valid for the period when the student needs to be physically present in Canada.
Question 2. If a 2-year study permit is not issued, does this mean international students are expected to apply for study permits for each visit (three different occasions)? Response 2: International students would likely need to apply for a study permit for each visit to Canada. Each application would need to demonstrate the necessity of the student's presence in Canada for the specific portion of the program. This approach aligns with IRCC's guidance that a study permit is required for the in-Canada portion of a distance learning program that exceeds six months in total duration, even if the in-Canada portions are individually less than six months. Study permits: Other considerations-Canada.ca
Please be advised that the assessment of an application is based on a case-by-case basis, considering the particular circumstances in conjunction with the supporting documentation available to the officer. The onus is always on the applicant to provide sufficient documentation to satisfy an officer that they meet the requirements.

Question: Can an applicant include their work experience in their Express Entry Profile if they were not on employer payroll and instead received wages on their own corporation and claimed HST for it ?
Many transport truck drivers earned their salary on their corporation number, so can they claim the work experience in their Express entry profile or that will be considered as self employment?
Answer: Please follow the instructions when completing the Express Entry (EE) profile: all work experience must be declared accurately, regardless if the work experience is eligible for EE or not. It is an obligation for the applicant to declare all information truthfully and accurately. Failure to provide truthful and accurate information may result in misrepresentation. Under EE, Canadian work experience may not be accumulated while engaged in self-employment. This means that periods of self-employment in Canada are not eligible to meet the minimum criteria of the Canadian Experience Class and may not be awarded Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) points for work in Canada. For your information, our internal guidance to determine whether an applicant was an employee or a self-employed individual during their period of qualifying work experience in Canada can be found on our website. It should be noted that consultants or contractors engaged in a contract for services business relationship and individuals who hold substantial ownership and/or exercise management control of a business for which they are also employed are generally considered to be self-employed. Each application will be considered on its own merits, with a final decision based on a review of all the information available to the officer at the time of decision. Self-employment in Canada or abroad may count towards the minimum criteria of the Federal Skilled Worker and the Federal Skilled Trades Program if it meets the respective requirements of those programs.
Please be advised that the assessment of an application is based on a case-by-case basis, considering the particular circumstances in conjunction with the supporting documentation available to the officer. threads.answer:
Hello,
Question: I am trying to clarify IRCC's instructions on the public policy from June 27, 2023 allowing eligible foreign workers to study without a study permit.
The shorter public policy announcement, linked here indicated that the eligibility included those who held a valid work permit issued based on an application that was received by IRCC prior to or on June 7, 2023, OR an application to renew a work permit was received on or before June 7, 2023 and the person is authorized to work per 186(u) (maintained status).
When we go to the more detailed policy information in the first link above, it says that only those with a valid work permit issued before June 7, 2023, OR had a letter authorizing them to work while processing the application that was issued before June 7, 2023 are eligible.
Can someone who applied for a work permit prior to June 7, but received the work permit after June 7, qualify under this policy, if they never received a letter of authorization to work before the permit was received?
Would this policy apply to someone who had applied for a work permit, from having a visitor record prior to their application that was submitted before June 7?
Response: If a foreign national applied for their first work permit prior to June 7, 2023 and the work permit was issued after June 7, 2023 they do not meet the eligibility for the public policy from June 27, 2023 allowing eligible foreign workers to study without a study permit. The applicant must hold the valid work permit before June 7, 2023 as stated in the public policy announcement, unless they are seeking to renew a work permit and are on maintained status as of July 7, 2023..
If a foreign national had a visitor record and applied for an initial work permit before June 7, 2023 but the work permit was not issued before June 7, 2023, they are not eligible to study without a study permit under this public policy.

Good day, Thank you for your email correspondence to 's Immigration Representatives mailbox. We appreciate your patience. Please find the answer to your question below: Question We have a question regarding LOS/s (Letter/s of Support) which were issued by a Designated Organization for the Startup Visa Program, prior to April 29 2024. A company (Qualifying Business) has two members, both essentials, have obtained the LOS from a Designated Organization, valid for six months. At the time and within the initial LOS validity, only one of the members were able to submit their PR and work permit applications, with the initially issued LOS. As the initial LOS was expiring, we applied for a LOS renewal, a new LOS was issued for the same business and for both members, valid for additional six months. Questions: 1- How IRCC treats LOS renewal? LOS Renewal-is treated as extension or as a new LOS application? 2- Should we update the first member's PR application with the renewed LOS, even though his application was submitted within the first LOS validity?
Note: The work permit has already been issued for the first applicant with initial LOS.
3- Would the fact that one member sent the application with one LOS and the second member with a renewed one affect the outcome of the work permit (second applicant) or PR applications for any of the applicants? Response
According to the current program delivery instructions (PDl) a commitment certificate (CC) and letter of support (LOS) are considered valid as long as the applicant submits a complete application for PR under the SUV program on or before the expiry of the CC and LOS (Economic classes: Procedures at the Centralized Intake Office for applications (non-Express Entry) - Canada.ca).
Changes can be made to the CC and LOS anytime before it expires and anytime before the first applicant submits their PR application. The receipt of the first PR application in the same business group will serve as the 'lock-in' date for the CC and LOS at which time no further changes can be made (Assessing the application (start-up business class) - Canada.ca).
If there are changes to the business group that requires changes to be made to the CC and LOS after the 'lock-in' date, the applicants that have submitted their application must withdraw it and re-submit new applications along with the new LOS and a new CC must be submitted by the Designated Organization (DO).
In your given situation, since one of the business members of the business group has submitted their application for PR under the SUV program, there is no need to provide an updated CC / LOS if there has been no major changes where the business no longer fits the requirements of the SUV program.
The CC and LOS must have the same validity and information, hence it could cause complications to the processing if one of the LOS is updated without updating the CC and the other LOS.
Please note that there is a cap of ten (10) commitment certificates (CC) per designated entity. SUV PR applications submitted after April 30, 2024 and linked to CCs issued after April 30, 2024, are subject to the cap. (Economic classes: Procedures at the Centralized Intake Office for applications (non-Express Entry) - Canada.ca) (Immigrate with a start-up visa: Who can apply-Canada.ca).
Please be advised that the assessment of an application is based on a case-by-case basis, considering the particular circumstances in conjunction with the supporting documentation available to the officer. The onus is always on the applicant to provide sufficient documentation to satisfy an officer that they meet the requirements.
We trust that this information will assist you.
Sincerely,

threads.subject: Experience considered under CEC-REP-2024-0980- REP-2024-1208 - Due 15-Aug-24
threads.question:
Good day,
Thank you for your prompt response.
Could you please confirm whether the self-employment experience gained in Canada can be counted towards the Federal Skilled Worker (FSW) program?
Thanks, Harit
Outlook for iOS-Sent from my mobile device
threads.answer:
Good Day, Thank you for your email correspondence to 's Immigration Representatives mailbox. We appreciate your patience. Question: Could you please confirm whether the self-employment experience gained in Canada can be counted towards the Federal Skilled Worker (FSW) program? Answer: Work experience as a self-employed person is not explicitly excluded from the Federal Skilled Workers (FSW) Class nor is it excluded as applicable experience to be included in Category Based Selection (CBS). If the applicant is self-employed, documentary evidence of their work experience can include articles of incorporation or other evidence of business ownership, evidence of self-employment income and documentation from third-party individuals indicating the service provided along with payment details (self-declared main duties or affidavits are not acceptable proof of self-employed work experience). It is imperative that you declare this work experience accurately in your profile by clicking the button for “self-employment” next to the experience. This will ensure it is scored properly. While a period of self-employed work experience can be calculated towards membership of an occupation-based category, self-employed work experience is still excluded from calculating the period of work experience for the Canadian experience class (CEC) [R87.1(3)(b)] and for Canadian work experience under the ministerial instructions respecting the Express Entry system. Please note as well that a self-employed person cannot elect to give themselves a job from the company that they own. Meaning arranged employment points cannot be awarded either in this case. Arranged employment is defined in subsection 82(1) of the Regulations: In this section, arranged employment means an offer of employment that is made by a single employer other than an embassy, high commission or consulate in Canada or an employer who is referred to in subparagraphs 200(3)(h)(ii) or (iii), that is for continuous full-time work in Canada having a duration of at least one year after the date on which a permanent resident visa is issued and that is with respect to an occupation that is listed in TEER Category 0, 1, 2 or 3 of the National Occupational Classification.
As per the Ministerial Instructions respecting the Express Entry system, a "qualifying offer of arranged employment” means any offer of employment referred to in subsection 29(2).
A self-employed person who is owner or co-owner of a business that they are actively engaged in, is not able to elect' to employ themselves (or dismiss themselves) as is understood to be the case for an employer'; which is what gives meaning to the value of the offer of employment. Neither would one of the co-owners be able to employ or dismiss' the co-owner, as is understood to be the case for an employer'. Rather, they would need to create or dissolve a business partnership, which is not an employment relationship. The co-owners in this case have elected to be co-shareholders and directors, not co-employing employers' of each other.
The intent of regulators, when drafting the Selection Criteria for the Federal Skilled Workers Class (FSW), where the definition of arranged employment is defined (R82), was not so a self-employed person can benefit from the arranged employment factor. The intent as per the Regulations Amending the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulation is that the worker enters the labour market, not the business community. It is the entry to the labour market which contributes to the assessment of their likelihood of economic establishment.
Please be advised that the assessment of an application is performed on a case-by-case basis; each application will be considered on its own merits, with a final decision based on a review of all the information available to the officer at the time of decision. The onus is always on the applicant to provide sufficient documentation to satisfy an officer that they meet the requirements.
We trust that this information will assist you.
Sincerely,
Immigration Representatives Mailbox

Answer: Please note that we do not answer case specific inquiries. For more information on what qualifies as a job offer for those on an LMIA work permit please visit our website. Documents for Express Entry: LMIA-exempt job offers-Canada.ca
It is imperative that you declare this work experience accurately in your profile by clicking the button for “self-employment" next to the experience. This will ensure it is scored properly.
While a period of self-employed work experience can be calculated towards membership of an occupation-based category, self-employed work experience is still excluded from calculating the period of work experience for the Canadian experience class (CEC) [R87.1(3)(b)l and for Canadian work experience under the ministerial instructions respecting the Express Entry system.
Please note as well that a self-employed person cannot elect to give themselves a job from the company that they own. Meaning arranged employment points cannot be awarded either in this case.
Arranged employment is defined in subsection 82(1) of the Regulations:
In this section, arranged employment means an offer of employment that is made by a single employer other than an embassy, high commission or consulate in Canada or an employer who is referred to in subparagraphs 200(3)(h)(ii) or (iii), that is for continuous full-time work in Canada having a duration of at least one year after the date on which a permanent resident visa is issued and that is with respect to an occupation that is listed in TEER Category 0, 1, 2 or 3 of the National Occupational Classification.
As per the Ministerial Instructions respecting the Express Entry system, a “qualifying offer of arranged employment" means any offer of employment referred to in subsection 29(2).
A self-employed person who is owner or co-owner of a business that they are actively engaged in, is not able to 'elect' to employ themselves (or dismiss themselves) as is understood to be the case for an ‘employer’; which is what gives meaning to the value of the offer of employment. Neither would one of the co-owners be able to ‘employ or dismiss' the co-owner, as is understood to be the case for an 'employer’. Rather, they would need to create or dissolve a business partnership, which is not an employment relationship. The co-owners in this case have elected to be co-shareholders and directors, not ‘co- employing employers' of each other.

threads.question:
Hi,
Do Mexican nationals whose eTAs were automatically cancelled by operation of law on February 29, 2024, need to declare this as a refused visa application, or anywhere else in the statutory declarations of forms?
Would it be misrepresentation if they do not disclose it?
Sincerely,
Ruscito, Giovanni (IRCC/IRCC)
threads.answer: Good Day, Thank you for your email correspondence to 's Immigration Representatives mailbox. We appreciate your patience and apologize for the delay. Question: Do Mexican nationals whose eTAs were automatically cancelled by operation of law on February 29, 2024, need to declare this as a refused visa application, or anywhere else in the statutory declarations of forms? Would it be misrepresentation if they do not disclose it? Response: As per the question that appears on the eTA or TRV applications, it is explicitly asked whether the foreign national has ever been refused a visa or permit, denied entry to, or ordered to leave Canada or any other country/territory. As such, a Mexican national who had an eTA cancelled during the imposition of visa requirements does not need to disclose this as it was an administrative action taken due to regulatory changes which made them no longer eligible to hold an eTA, but their application was not refused. However, if the individual's eTA was not a part of this administrative action and was refused an application instead, they must disclose the details surrounding the refusal. It does not matter the type of refusal, foreign nationals should disclose all instances of refusals. Individuals should always be fully truthful when providing information to officers, be it IRCC or CBSA. If a foreign national answers yes to such a question, they will not be automatically refused, applications are assessed by officers on a case by case basis. Details surrounding each declared previous refusal must be provided to allow officers to assess the individual to ensure the health and safety of Canadians and maintain the security of Canadian society. Please note that not being fully transparent about such information may lead to a refusal under A40(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act. We trust that this information will assist you. Sincerely, Immigration Representatives Mailbox

To immigrate to Atlantic Canada through the AIP program, you must be either be:

2. a skilled worker (see Work Experience requirements below)
Work experience
In the last 5 years, you must have worked at least 1,560 hours. This is the number of hours you would have worked in 1 year if you were working 30 hours per week.
To calculate your hours
Count hours worked in part-time and full-time jobs. Count only paid hours of work. Volunteering or unpaid internships don't count. Don't count hours when you were self-employed. Count hours worked inside or outside Canada. You must have been legally authorized to work in Canada as a temporary resident. Count hours that were accumulated over a period of at least 12 months. This work should be at one of these National Occupational Classification (NOC) 2021 Training, Education, Experience and Responsibilities (TEER) categories
TEER 0 (management jobs such as restaurant managers or mine managers) TEER 1 (professional jobs that usually need a degree from a university, such as doctors, dentists or architects) TEER 2 (technical jobs and skilled trades requiring at least 2 years of college or apprenticeship, or occupations with supervisory or safety responsibilities such as police officers and firefighters) TEER 3 (technical jobs and skilled trades requiring less than 2 years of college or apprenticeship; or more than 6 months of on-the-job training) TEER 4 (intermediate jobs that usually call for high school and/or several weeks of job-specific training, such as industrial butchers, long-haul truck drivers, or food and beverage servers)
Your work experience must include
the actions in the description of your NOC most of the main duties of your NOC

The Embassy of Ukraine to Canada (Ottawa, ON) and Consulates General of Ukraine (Toronto, ON; Edmonton, AB) continue to provide consular support and services to Ukrainian nationals living in Canada, including passport extension services. Pour plus d’informations, veuillez consulter la page Web suivante : Permis de travail postdiplôme (PTPD) [R205c) - C43] - Programme de mobilité internationale-Canada.ca
Question 3 Sinon, est-ce qu’un étudiant peut :
- Quitter le Canada dès la fin des cours
- Attendre la délivrance du diplôme et soumettre la demande de PTPD de l’extérieur du Canada avec un formulaire IMM-1295 Retourner au Canada avec la preuve que la demande de PTPD est déposée et commencer à travailler jusqu’à ce qu’elle soit approuvée.
Réponse 3
Pour bénéficier du droit de travailler dans l’attente de la décision, est-ce que la demande de permis de travail post diplôme doit avoir été soumis de l’intérieur du Canada?
Pour bénéficier du droit de travailler dans l’attente de la décision selon alinéa 186w) du RIPR, la demande de permis de travail post diplôme doit avoir été soumis à l’intérieur du Canada.
L’étudiant peut quitter le Canada et soumettre leur demande de PTPD à l’extérieur du Canada avec le formulaire IMM 1295, mais ils ne pourront pas retourner au Canada et travailler à l’attente d’une décision.

Hello,
Question: I am writing to seek guidance on behalf of my client, an employee who was recently impacted by a severe incident. My client was employed under a Labor Market Impact Assessment (LMIA) based work permit at a bakery, which unfortunately suffered extensive damage due to a fire. As a result of this unforeseen event, my client, along with other employees, is currently without work. Given that my client has only been employed for approximately two months, he does not meet the eligibility criteria for Employment Insurance due to insufficient hours worked. We are exploring options that would allow him to continue working and sustaining himself in Canada during this challenging period. Upon reviewing the information on your website, we understand that an Open Work Permit for Vulnerable Workers is available; however, it appears to be limited to individuals who have faced abuse in their workplace. Considering my client's situation stems from a workplace disaster rather than abuse, I seek clarification on whether he might still qualify for this permit or any other form of relief or permit available under such circumstances. Could you please provide advice on the best course of action for my client? Are there alternative permits or provisions for workers affected by non-abuse-related workplace disruptions?
Response: We are so sorry to hear of the situation your client and their colleagues are facing.
A temporary foreign worker on an employer-specific work permit is only eligible for an Open Work Permit for Vulnerable Workers (OWP-V) in cases of abuse in the context of their employment. A Foreign National outside of this scope is not eligible for an OWP-V.
If your client was impacted due to the 2024 Wildfires across Canada, IRCC does have immigration, passport and citizenship measures in place for affected clients. This includes measures for an Open Work Permit. We encourage you to consult the 2024 Wildfires in Canada: Temporary immigration, passport and citizenship measures webpage for all details.
If the Wildfire context does not apply to your client, unfortunately, a dedicated Open Work Permit option for a non-Wildfire situation is not be available at this time. That said, Temporary Foreign Workers (TFWs) may be eligible to extend or change conditions on their current work permit.
| Citizenship Canada| |
TFWs can apply to extend their current work permit or change the conditions of their existing permit to allow them to work for another employer. This process requires them to have a job offer from a new employer who may need to obtain a Labour Market Impact Assessment (LMiA) unless exempt. Specifically, workers on employer-specific work permits can leverage the Changing Employers Public Policy which allows workers to apply from within Canada to change their jobs more quickly. The public policy allows foreign nationals to obtain interim work authorization with a new employer expediently from the date of application, instead of waiting for their work permit application to be finalized. This measure ensures workers can begin working with their new employer with minimal delay. Resource: Extend or change the conditions on your work permit: About the process-Canada.ca
Thank you kindly, The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

As such, students, workers, and visitors are all examples of foreign nationals. However, a foreign national must respect all of the conditions listed on their work permit. If their PGWP states that they may not attend any educational institution or take any academic, vocational, or professional training course, they must refrain from doing so. If a spouse of an international student, that is a holder of an open work permit, decides to pursue studies in Canada and decides to apply for a study permit. The question are: 1-In the case that the applicant applies before the expiration date of his/her open work permit to change of status to study permit, can he or she continue to work until the decision is made? 2-Does he or she have to stop working during the time after the expiration of the open work permit and before getting the decision of the study permit? If the applicant applies to extend or change the conditions of their work permit before the permit expires, maintained status allows them to remain in Canada and continue working until their work permit expires; it does not allow them to study before a decision is made on their study permit application.

If you meet all of these requirements, you can start looking for a job with a designated Atlantic employer.
Work experience
In the last 5 years, you must have worked at least 1,560 hours. This is the number of hours you would have worked in 1 year if you were working 30 hours per week. To calculate your hours
- Count hours worked in part-time and full-time jobs.
- Count only paid hours of work. Volunteering or unpaid internships don't count.
- Don't count hours when you were self-employed.
- Count hours worked inside or outside Canada. You must have been legally authorized to work in Canada as a temporary resident.
- Count hours that were accumulated over a period of at least 12 months.
- Count work experience acquired while studying, as long as the work hours don't exceed what was authorized.
This work should be at one of these National Occupational Classification (NOC) 2021 Training, Education, Experience and Responsibilities (TEER) categories
- TEER 0 (management jobs such as restaurant managers or mine managers)
- TEER 1 (professional jobs that usually need a degree from a university, such as doctors, dentists or architects)
- TEER 2 (technical jobs and skilled trades requiring at least 2 years of college or apprenticeship, or occupations with supervisory or safety responsibilities such as police officers and firefighters) TEER 3 (technical jobs and skilled trades requiring less than 2 years of college or apprenticeship; or more than 6 months of on- the-job training)
- TEER 4 (intermediate jobs that usually call for high school and/or several weeks of job-specific training, such as industrial butchers, long-haul truck drivers, or food and beverage servers)
Your work experience must include
- the actions in the description of your NOC
- most of the main duties of your NOC
International graduates
You do not need to meet the work experience requirements if you're an international graduate who
- has a degree, diploma, certificate, or trade or apprenticeship certification that 0 took at least 2 years of studies 0
is from a recognized post-secondary institution in 1 of the 4 Atlantic provinces (New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island, or Newfoundland and Labrador) was obtained within 24 months prior to the date you applied for permanent residence
- was a full-time student for the entire time you were studying
- lived in one of the following provinces for at least 16 months during the last 2 years before you graduated ONew Brunswick 0 Nova Scotia
Newfoundland and Labrador or Prince Edward Island
- had the visa or permit you needed to work, study or get training while you were in Canada
Educational requirements
You must have one of these:
- If you have a job offer at the NOC 2021 TEER 0 or 1 category, you must have a one-year Canadian post-secondary educational credential or higher, or the equivalent from outside Canada.
- If you have a job offer at the NOC 2021 TEER 2, 3 or 4 category, you must have a Canadian high school diploma, or the equivalent from outside Canada.
However, if you studied outside Canada, you need an educational credential assessment (ECA) to confirm that your studies are equal to or higher than the required level of education for your job offer.
- Your ECA report must be less than 5 years old on the date we receive your application.
Thank you! The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

My general inquiry relates to the following Super Visa requirement as per IRCC guidelines, [https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-manuals/temporary-residents/visitors/super-visa.html](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-manuals/temporary-residents/visitors/super-visa.html) "Eligibility criteria and documentation requirements The Super Visa offers eligible parents and grandparents of Canadian citizens and permanent residents the possibility of visiting Canada for 5 years on each entry. An applicant is eligible for a Super Visa if they apply from outside Canada, meet the requirements for temporary residence in Canada as a visitor and provide the additional supporting documentation demonstrating that they meet the requirements in the Ministerial Instructions."
Our question is whether an applicant can be a visitor in Canada (on a valid TRV) at the time of the submission of the Super Visa application, as long as the application is submitted to be processed OUTSIDE OF CANADA.
Thank you for your guidance on this matter.
Kind regards,
and Citizenship Caneda
Ruscito, Giovanni (IRCC/IRCC)
threads.answer:
Hello,
Question Our question is whether an applicant can be a visitor in Canada (on a valid TRV) at the time of the submission of the Super Visa application, as long as the application is submitted to be processed OUTSIDE OF CANADA.
Approved Response: This information is provided as general policy guidance and is not a directive for individual case files. For case specific enquiries, applicants can contact the Department by submitting the RCC Web form.
As per A16(1), an applicant must truthfully answer all questions put to them, which includes correctly indicating which country they are currently residing in. This includes visitors, if they have been lawfully admitted to that country.
As per the Ministerial Instructions for super visas, a foreign national must apply for a super visa from outside Canada. If their application is approved, and they receive a super visa in their passport (the visa must be printed outside Canada), then they may travel to Canada. At the port of entry, a Border Services Officer (BSO) will examine the foreign national as per R180. If the BSO grants entry, then the foreign national is authorized to stay in Canada for 5 years.
A foreign national who holds a valid visitor visa may travel to Canada while their super visa application is being processed. Their authorized period of stay will be 6 months or any other period that is fixed by an officer, as per R183(2).
Please note that it is important for Super Visa holders to ensure that their passport and health insurance are valid while they are in Canada.
We trust that this information will assist you.

While there is nothing preventing an out of status spouse or common-law partner from applying for a Temporary Resident Permit (TRP) should they feel it is warranted, they would not require a TRP to apply under the spouse or common-law partner in Canada Class (SCLPC) or to be considered under this public policy. The public policy serves as a method for out of status spouses and
It uses A25(1) to exempt a foreign national from having to meet the requirements in A21(1) and R72(1)(e)(i), only as they relate to inadmissibility for lack of status (and related documents), and R124(b), so as to enable such foreign nationals to become permanent residents if and only if they meet all other requirements of the Spouse or Common-law Partner in Canada class and are not
persons who have entered Canada without a valid passport or travel document (provided valid documents are acquired by the time CiC seeks to grant permanent residence).
Once an individual has made an application under the SCLPC and is subject of a sponsorship undertaking that is made by their spouse or common-law partner, eligibility for the public policy, including the exemption from having to meet the admissibility and eligibility requirements as they relate to lack of status, will be assessed and determined by an officer on a case-by-case basis when processing the application. If any additional information is needed the officer will send a request to the applicant.
When it comes to removals under this public policy, an applicant can only benefit from an administrative deferral of removal if the SCLPC application is submitted before the applicant is deemed removal ready by the Canada Border Services Agency (i.e. called/requested to attend a pre-removal interview with the CBSA). Some exceptions to this may exist in limited circumstances outlined in the public policy for transitional cases.
Section F of the public policy further outlines circumstances where a deferral will not be granted.
For cases that qualify, the CBSA has agreed to grant a temporary administrative deferral of removal to applicants who qualify under this public policy.
For those applicants who submitted their spouse or common-law partner in Canada application prior to the applicant being deemed removal ready and are receiving a pre-removal risk assessment (PRRA), the administrative deferral for processing applicants under this H&C public policy will be in effect for the time required to complete the PRRA (R232). Applicants who have waived a PRRA or who are not entitled to a PRRA will receive an administrative deferral of removal of 60 days.
CBSA will contact IRCC to request that a step one decision be rendered on a priority basis. IRCC will make best efforts to process spousal sponsorship cases to a “step-one" or “approval in principle" decision within the 60-day period. (A step-one decision occurs after IRCC has received an application which contains evidence that the applicant is in a genuine marriage or common-law relationship with an eligible sponsor, is living with that sponsor and that the sponsorship submitted is a valid one.).
After a positive step-one decision, the R233 stay will be invoked until such time as IRCC makes a final decision on whether to grant permanent residence. Should a step-one decision not be made within the deferral period, the applicant may be removed from Canada until such time a step-one decision is made and the R233 stay of removal is invoked.
It should be noted that a TRP is not a legal impediment to removal. As a result, it is possible for an out-of-status spouse or common-law partner to be removed from Canada, even if they are a TRP holder. Please also note that there is no processing time service standard for TRP applications.

I hope this message finds you well. I have a couple of questions regarding the definition of work in specific scenarios that I would appreciate your guidance on:

threads.answer:
Good Morning,
Please see our responses to your queries below.
1. Off-Campus Work Hour Limit: “Work” is defined in the Regulations as an activity for which wages are paid or commission is earned, or that competes directly with activities of Canadian citizens or permanent residents in the Canadian labour market. A student helping with chores around the residence would be considered incidental to their stay there. Temporary Foreign Worker and International Mobility Programs: What is work? - Canada.ca
2. Experiential Course and Co-op Work Permit: Please note that if there is any volunteering or participation aspect anticipated as part of this course, a co-op work permit may be required. Please see here for more information: Study permits: Off-campus work-Canada.ca. Depending on the current situation of a student, if they meet the requirements noted in the following policy they can work at a co-op placement while awaiting the decision on their new co-op work permit application: Work related to a research, educational or training program -exemption codes C31, C32 and C33 (International Mobility Program) - Canada.ca. Students who are already in Canada and have applied for a co-op work permit may begin their co-op placement using their on-campus and off-campus work authorization, provided they meet all the eligibility requirements. For off-campus work authorization, as per paragraph R186(v), students can work a total of 20 hours per week during an academic term or semester while they are waiting for their co-op work permit; however, the 20 hours must include both the hours worked at their co-op job and those worked at their regular paid job (if they have one). They can work full-time during the regularly scheduled breaks. If the co-op work permit application is refused, they must stop their co-op work immediately. We hope you found this information helpful. Thank you kindly, The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

Question: Could you clarify if the language test results of the spouse of the main applicant expires, whether the express entry profile of the main applicant could become ineligible? Or is it only the language test result of the main applicant expires the profile gets expired?
Answer: Language test results for the spouse are optional, and not an eligibility requirement for any Express Entry program. threads.subject: Clarity on Employment Agreement requirement for Employers-REP-2024-1272-Due 23-Aug-24
threads.question:
Dear Immigration Representative,
I am an immigration lawyer based in BC and I would be much obliged for your input.
Under the IMP and the TFWP, employers are required to provide an employment agreement that is in official language of the foreign worker's choice and that includes occupation, wages and working conditions.
Context: Having an actual employment agreement for immigration application may run contrary to the pre-existing employment contract particularly if the foreign worker is in a collective bargaining position. Also, in some situations, foreign workers are hired in permanent positions and the employment agreement does not have an end date whereas the foreign worker's work permit application will require a specific end date for the temporary application.
Question #1: Can employers remedy the potential conflict with employment considerations by simply using the Offer of Employment form or the LMIA application form? Does having the foreign worker and employer both review the Offer of Employment and sign it instead of an employment agreement, still satisfy the legal requirement of providing the foreign worker with a copy of the written employment agreement on or before the start date?
Question #2: In order to ensure that the immigration context (such as having an end date for the temporary work permit application) does not lead to a legal employment law implication, can the employer include a wording on the actual copy of the Offer of Employment form / LMIA form, before the foreign worker and employer sign it, such as " A new employment agreement has not been entered into for the purposes of the work permit application and the pre-existing employment agreement will continue to be in full effect". Does having a clause like this on the Offer of Employment (before employer and foreign worker sign it), disqualify the employer from meeting the legal requirement of providing the written employment contract to the foreign worker?
3: At the time of an IMP inspection, will it suffice for the employer to provide a copy of the signed Offer of Employment? OR do they have to still show the employment contract (such as a pre existing one) which may not have the same terms and conditions as the Offer of Employment?
Thank you so much for your valued advice!
Sincerely,
and Citizenship Caneda
Ruscito, Giovanni (IRCC/IRCC)
threads.answer:
Hello,
Please see our response to your questions.
Question #1: Can employers remedy the potential conflict with employment considerations by simply using the Offer of Employment form or the LMIA application form?Does having the foreign worker and employer both review the Offer of Employment and sign it instead of an employment agreement, still satisfy the legal requirement of providing the foreign worker with a copy of the written employment agreement on or before the start date?
Answer: Paragraph R209.11(1)(e) requires employers to provide the temporary worker with a signed employment agreement with the same occupation, wages and working conditions as those set out in the offer of employment before submitting the offer of employment.
The employment agreement must be in the official language chosen by the temporary worker. For inspection purposes relating to paragraph R209.2(1)(b)(i) and the accuracy of the information provided under section R209.11, officers should be aware that in the context of contract for services, the Canadian company (not the foreign company) is the entity who must provide the worker with a signed agreement. This is because it is the Canadian company that creates the need for the temporary worker to enter Canada, even if it is the foreign company that pays the temporary worker.
The intent of the employment agreement is not to establish a standard employee-employer relationship as normally understood in the labour force; rather, it aims to make the Canadian company responsible for providing the worker with the same occupation, wages and working conditions as those set out in the offer of employment.
Question #2: In order to ensure that the immigration context (such as having an end date for the temporary work permit application) does not lead to a legal employment law implication, can the employer include a wording on the actual copy of the Offer of Employment form / LMIA form, before the foreign worker and employer sign it, such as " A new employment agreement has not been entered into for the purposes of the work permit application and the pre-existing employment agreement will continue to be in full effect". Does having a clause like this on the Offer of Employment (before employer and foreign worker sign it), disqualify the employer from meeting the legal requirement of providing the written employment contract to the foreign worker?
Answer: Including a clause in the Offer of Employment or LMIA form that clarifies the continuity of the pre-existing employment agreement may help address potential legal implications related to employment law. However, such a clause should be carefully drafted to ensure it does not conflict with the requirements of the IMP or TFWP. The key consideration is that the foreign worker must still be provided with a written document that clearly sets out the terms of employment relevant to the temporary work permit, including any necessary end date.
Employers should ensure that any language used does not negate or reduce the clarity of the terms of employment as required under immigration regulations. While the inclusion of such a clause does not inherently disqualify the employer from meeting legal requirements, the document provided must still meet the standards expected by IRCC. The work permit application might be refused if the requirements associated with submitting an offer of employment are not met. Employers are responsible for ensuring that all the information submitted in their offer of employment and all documents submitted during work permit processing are accurate and complete at the time of submission.
For more information on this, please visit the following webpages: [https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/work-canada/permit/temporary/work-permit.html](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/work-canada/permit/temporary/work-permit.html) and Verifying the accuracy of information provided.
Question# 3: At the time of an IMP inspection, will it suffice for the employer to provide a copy of the signed Offer of Employment? OR do they have to still show the employment contract (such as a pre existing one) which may not have the same terms and conditions as the Offer of Employment?
Answer: Officers can request specific documents or information or ask the employer to provide whatever documents the employer determines are sufficient as proof of their compliance with the conditions. A list of documents that could be provided as proof is available in Documents that may be used to verify employer compliance
Employers may be required to submit a copy of the jointly signed agreement during an inspection to demonstrate compliance.
Paragraph R209.11(1)(e) requires employers to provide the temporary worker with a signed employment agreement with the same occupation, wages and working conditions as those set out in the offer of employment before submitting the offer of employment.
For more information, please consult the following webpages: Compliance conditions imposed on employers and Employer compliance inspections (ci.gc.ca)

threads.answer:
immigration κepresentatives / κepresentants immigration (IRCC)
Hello,
Thank you for your email correspondence to 's Immigration Representatives mailbox. We appreciate your patience.
Question: In an Express Entry Profile, Can an Applicant claim 50 points for pre approved Imia without applying closed work permit?
Answer: The Ministerial Instructions respecting the Express Entry system, specifically section 29 concerning arranged employment, dictates that the applicant must have a qualifying offer of employment that is one of the following:
(a) an arranged employment as defined in subsection 82(1) of the Regulations, if
(i) the offer is supported by a valid assessment — provided by the Department of Employment and Social Development at the request of the employer or an officer and on the same basis as an assessment provided for the issuance of a work permit — that the requirements set out in subsection 203(1) of the Regulations with respect to the offer have been met, (ii) the foreign national holds a valid work permit, the offer of employment is made by an employer for whom the foreign national currently works and who is specified on the work permit, the work permit was issued based on a positive determination made by an officer under subsection 203(1) of the Regulations with respect to the foreign national's employment with that employer in an occupation that is listed in TEER Category 0, 1, 2 or 3 of the National Occupational Classification and the assessment provided by the Department of Employment and Social Development on the basis of which the determination was made is not suspended or revoked, or (iii) the foreign national holds a valid work permit issued under the circumstances described in paragraph 204(a) or (c) or section 205 of the Regulations, the offer is made by an employer who is specified on the work permit and the foreign national works for that employer and has accumulated at least one year of full-time work experience, or the equivalent in part-time work, over a continuous period of work in Canada for that employer;
Note that a work permit on its own is not a job offer, even if it is an open work permit. The type of work permit (open or closed) is not specified in the Ministerial Instructions for the purposes of obtaining 50 or 200 CRS points. Work authorization (work permit) is not a requirement under this subparagraph. The job offer must also meet the other criteria to be valid under the Express Entry program the applicant qualifies for, listed on our website.
Question: Do we need to provide a Police clearance certificate for non-accompanying spouses in PR Application?

Question: I hope this message finds you well. I have a question regarding the Canadian Experience Class eligibility and CRS points related to Canadian work experience.

Individuals who are accredited foreign representatives to Canada (for example, diplomatic, consular or official personnel) and their accredited family members can't become permanent residents while they are still accredited. Their privileges and accredited status must have ended before they may be issued a visa or confirmation of permanent residence.

From Dear Sir/Madam,
My name is and I am a Regulated Canadian Immigration Consultant (RCiC) member in good standing with the College of Immigration and Citizenship Consultants (CICC). My registration number is I represent several clients who seek open work permits based on the Facilitative measures to support Israeli and Palestinian nationals in Canada, started on December 21, 2023 and extended to July 31, 2025[https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-manuals/service-delivery/facilitative-measures-israeli-palestinian.html](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-manuals/service-delivery/facilitative-measures-israeli-palestinian.html).
According to this policy, a national of Israel who is in Canada with valid temporary resident status (regardless of the date of their arrival) and who applies to change the conditions of their temporary stay as a worker may be eligible for a fee-exempt open work permit, and to change the conditions of their temporary stay.
Please clarify whether Primary Applicants are allowed to include their spouses and common-law partners, as well as their children as dependents under the framework of this policy, if the spouses, common-law partners, and dependent children are not citizens of Israel or Palestine.
1. Are foreign spouses of Israeli nationals who are not Israelis eligible for an open work permit under this program?
2. Are dependent children of Israeli nationals who are not Israelis eligible for an open work permit/study permit under this program? Thank you for your attention to this matter. We look forward to your quick reply and any clarification you can give. Best Regards,
and Citizenship Caneda
Ruscito, Giovanni (IRCC/IRCC)
threads.answer:
Good day,
Thank you for reaching out to IRCC.
Foreign national family members currently in Canada with valid temporary resident status who do not hold a passport or travel document issued by Israel or the Palestinian Authority are not eligible to apply for a fee-exempt open work permit or study permit, or to extend their to extend or change the conditions of their temporary stay under the Temporary public policy for nationals of Israel and the Palestinian Territories who are in Canada as temporary residents.
Only foreign national family members of Canadian citizens or permanent residents who left Israel or the Palestinian Territories on or after October 7, 2023 are eligible for in-Canada measures under the Temporary public policy for foreign nationals who are family members of Canadian citizens and permanent residents who left Israel or the Palestinian Territories on or after October 7, 2023. If clients meet the eligibility requirements for these measures, they can refer to our Web page for further information: Crisis in Israel, the West Bank and the Gaza Strip-Canada.ca.
Foreign national family members who don't meet the eligibility requirements of the public policies can apply under regular pathways for a work permit, study permit, or extension of temporary resident status. These applications are subject to standard fees and must be submitted through regular IRCC inland channels.

Under the Express Entry, work experience obtained during a period of full-time studies may not be awarded Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) points for work in Canada regardless of the type of work authorization. Such provisions apply separately to both: principal applicants and their accompanying spouses. The opposite is true – an accompanying spouse may be obtaining eligible work experience in Canada while the principal applicant is a full-time student if they meet all the requirements.
The definition of full-time studies is determined by each educational institution and graduates must have proof of program completion from their institution in order to begin accumulating work experience in Canada.

Question: I would like to get a policy clarification on the following scenario: A Start-Up VISA PR application is pending with PR file and AOR. If the founder (essential) member decides to change his/her status from essential to other members due to medical or other reasons, can this be done during the pending PR application? Answer: The Start-Up Visa (SUV) program requires that the essential member, typically the founder or key individual associated with the start-up, remains actively involved throughout the application process and after receiving Permanent Residency (PR) status. If the essential member withdraws themselves, all the applications linked to the same SUV business will be refused. If the essential member changes their status from essential to non-essential, it could potentially impact the eligibility of the start-up business under the program. The assessment of any change in circumstance related to the status of the essential members will be dealt with on a case-by-case basis. The applicants must promptly notify the designated entity (DE), and have a comprehensive plan and explanation. The DE is required to update the Commitment Certificate (CC) and Letter of Support (LOS) for all of the applicants in the SUV business. Subsequently, the DE should issue the revised CC and LOS, and provide the updated CC to IRCC. Please be advised that the assessment of an application is based on a case-by-case basis, considering the particular circumstances in conjunction with the supporting documentation available to the officer. Must take a position in Canada" under intra-company transferee provisions means that an employer-employee relationship with the Canadian branch of the company to which they are being transferred must exist. The essential element in determining this relationship is the right of the employer to order and control the employee in the performance of their work. While full-time employment by the Canadian branch is anticipated, there is no requirement that the foreign national perform full-time service in Canada. An executive, for example, could divide normal working hours between offices in Canada and the U.S. There is no requirement that the foreign national be paid from the Canadian entity; however, this is usually the case.

Acceptable changes
Employers are not required to inform IRCC of changes in working conditions. However, they must provide evidence of an acceptable justification [R209.2(3)] at the time of an inspection should there be differences between the working conditions offered and those found during the inspection.
If the change in working conditions (such as a reduction in hours or salary) negatively affects the worker, a new offer of employment and a new work permit are required before the change takes effect; otherwise, the employer risks being found non-compliant with the original job offer submitted to IRCC.
If the work being completed by the FN deviated from the offer of employment only in regards to when the worker was outside of Canada (resulting in them also being paid by the foreign company, since they weren't actually working for the Canadian company at the time), then this could be seen as an acceptable change of conditions since it does not negatively affect the employee.

Regardless of the listed scenarios, once an applicant has received an invitation to apply for Express Entry, they have 60 days to respond. Instructions on how to respond to the invitation if their CRS score may have changed can be found on our website.
Question# 1 : If they apply to change their conditions to visitor, do they maintain their ability to work until a decision is made on their visitor record? Or they immediately lose their status as a worker, but are authorized to remain in Canada? As they have now lost their status as a worker, are they expected to restore their status and pay $229 to apply for a work permit within 90 days of losing work status, or are they eligible to apply under the public policy, visitors to workers?
Answer:
| Citizenship Canada| |
If an applicant applies to change their status from worker to visitor, they maintain their ability to continue working only as long as their work permit remains valid. They would not be authorized to work while awaiting a decision on their visitor record, if their work permit is expired; there is no maintained status work authorization for a foreign national who has submitted an application to change their status from worker to visitor. Nevertheless, they would still be authorized to remain in Canada by operation of law under R183(5).
If a foreign national (FN) applies to extend their stay in Canada before the end of their authorized period of stay and meets the eligibility requirements as a visitor, the IRCC officer may issue a visitor record, which serves to legally extend a foreign national's temporary resident status in Canada. However, the FN does not have the authority to work as a visitor.
If the FN is able to find a new job or new employer before the expiry of their current work permit, they could apply for a new work permit from inside Canada, and via the Change of Employers Public Policy, begin working in that new job while IRCC finalizes their application.
If the work permit of a foreign national expires before they submit an application to extend their stay in Canada, they have 90 days to submit an application to restore their temporary resident status and authorization to work. Foreign nationals applying for restoration have lost their status and authority to work or study. They may not continue to work or attend school until their status and authorization have been restored and a new work or study permit has been issued.
For more information on restoration of status, please visit Restore your status and get a work permit-Canada.ca. Please note that, as of August 28th, 2024, the visitor to worker public policy has ended.
Question#2: They could apply for a work permit extension; however, it won't be complete until they receive their e-APR, R204 support letter, or LMIA. Does IRCC expect the applicant to submit an incomplete BOWP, an incomplete work permit extension (PNP), or incomplete LMIA based work permit (based on LMIA being submitted only), and then update the application via webform with the proper documentation? Answer: Concurrent Processing for in-Canada work permit applications allows for applications to be submitted in-Canada as per section R199, to ensure that foreign nationals do not fall out of status. IRCC will allow 60 days from the date of submission for the applicant to provide a positive LMIA, if they provide proof that their work permit expires in 2 weeks or less their prospective employer has submitted a complete application for an LMIA 0with sufficient lead time to have the LMIA processed (i.e.: submitted LMIA application far enough in advance of the published processing times 0no decision on the LMIA application has been made.
Applications will be held by IRCC for 60 days, after which a final determination regarding the work permit will be made. If the LMIA or CAQ are not provided within 60 days, the application will be refused unless the applicant submits a request for an extension (with evidence that more time is needed to get the LMIA).
For more information please visit the following webpage: I want to extend my expiring work permit, but I don't have a new LMIA or CAQ yet. What should I do? (canada.ca)
Question#3: They could apply for the work permit extension to maintain their status and authorization with a letter of explanation that they intend to complete it as soon as they can, and then apply for a second (complete) work permit application. When the first application is refused, they will lose the authorization to work, but have extended their time to stay in Canada until a decision is made on the second application based on the guidance. Does this mean their second application could be refused because it doesn't include the restoration fee? Or are they considered to have maintained their status in this case? Is the second application considered based on the conditions when they applied or at the current conditions?
Answer: The FN does not need to pay the restoration fee since they are not applying for restoration in this case. If the applications are refused, then the applicant has 90 days to apply for restoration. The applicant needs to wait for the decision on their work permit extension applications to determine if they are in or out of the status. Once the decision is made by IRCC, and if the application is refused, the foreign national has 90 days to submit a request for restoration of temporary resident status and authorization to work.

However, if the first application is withdrawn and the original work permit expired before the second application was received, then there would be no continued authority to work.
The restoration fee is to be paid when an application for restoration is submitted. Applicants must apply within 90 days of having lost their status. Foreign nationals applying for restoration have lost their status and authority to work or study. They may not continue to work or attend school until their status and authorization have been restored and a new work or study permit has been issued.
Please visit the following webpages for more information: 0Restore your status and get a work permit-Canada.ca 0Restoration of temporary resident status-Canada.ca

Answer: The foreign national will need to apply for restoration of temporary resident status and authorization to work.

0Restore your status and get a work permit-Canada.ca CRestoration of temporary resident status-Canada.ca

Question#7 Also, from the guidance, I see that if a work permit application is rejected (for being incomplete), it's as if the application was never submitted, so their status would immediately expire, back to the date their original status expired.
