threads.question:
We have a question related to the remark "authorized to work at multiple locations across Canada".
We often receive a work permit issued from the in-land extension process that has a location restriction even though we had requested that the applicant be authorized to work at multiple locations across Canada throughout our submissions. For instance, we submit a work permit extension application for an employee and make a note of "multiple locations across Canada" in the employer compliance application and the employer support letter as well as on the work permit extension application form; however, we receive a work permit with the condition "not authorized to work at any location other than above" without the remark "authorized to work at multiple locations" added. In these cases, we submit an amendment request to IRCC to receive a new work permit.
Our question is-does the employee's wage need to meet/exceed the Canada-wide median wage for their work permit to include the remark, especially if the employee's work permit was issued under the Reciprocal Employment (C20) category? Does the answer change if the work permit application was submitted under a different category such as the ICT category or the CUSMA Professionals category.
We don't believe that is correct, especially under the Reciprocal Employment category as the "median wage" is not one of the considerations for this category. In addition, we have the following guidance from the IRCC guidelines on conditions and validity period on work permits:
Location of work (mandatory imposition) Location of work must be imposed as a condition where an LMIA has been issued or where it is a requirement of the LMIA exemption [R185(b)(iii)] For example, when an employer has several franchise locations but indicates only one location on the offer of employment submitted through the system, the work permit should reflect the physical location of work and restrict the work to that location. However, if the employer indicates in the offer of employment that the worker will be working at multiple work locations, the officer should not restrict the work permit to a single location and should indicate in the "Remarks" field that the worker is authorized to work at the various locations across Canada.
Any guidance will be greatly appreciated!
threads.answer:
If the work permit is LMIA supported, officers impose the location of work to match the destination on the LMIA. This is to ensure that the temporary worker is working in the same labour market area assessed by Employment and Social Development Canada. For LMIA-exempt work permits, location must be imposed where the location of work is important to the exemption (such as for provincial nominees or specific “significant benefit to Canada" situations).
Additionally, there are conditions related to location of work that may be imposed on the employer (based on the offer of employment) OR the worker (on their work permit):
Worker conditions: The foreign national may have specific conditions imposed on them with the work permit. These conditions may include “not authorized to work at any other location". If this condition is imposed and a location is specified, the worker will need a new work permit (including a new offer of employment in case of an LMlA-exempt work permit) in order to change locations.
Employer conditions: "Location" is normally considered as part of the condition that the employer must provide the “same working conditions". The change in work location can't be less favourable to the employee. In addition, the location can't be changed if the location was part of the LMiA exemption requirement or justification (for instance, provincial nominees). (IRCC) does not require proactive notification of changes, but the employer is required to maintain any documentation regarding the changes and provide it as justification at the time of inspection. Employers who believe that they are not meeting conditions can use the voluntary disclosure process.
Please see this page for additional information: Conditions and validity period on work permits (temporary workers) - Canada.ca

Your question indicates child below 22 years of age, please note that child under 22 years of age refers to the definition of a dependant child (which does not seem to be the case here). In Canada, each province or territory defines the age of majority. The age of majority is 18 in Alberta, Manitoba, Ontario, Prince Edward Island, Quebec and Saskatchewan. The age of majority is 19 in British Columbia, New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Labrador, Nova Scotia, the Northwest Territories, Nunavut and the Yukon. D'une manière générale, si une personne présente une demande de prolongation de permis de travail plusieurs mois d'avance (avant l'expiration de son permis), si elle décide de sortir du Canada (faire un voyage) durant le traitement de la demande de prolongation je me demande quelle option s'applique :

threads.answer:
Bonjour, Merci d’avoir communiqué avec nous. Prendre note que ne pouvons répondre à des questions relatifs à des cas spécifiques, ceci étant dit, nous avons joins l’information ici-bas comme référence. QUESTION: si une personne présente une demande de prolongation de permis de travail plusieurs mois d'avance (avant l'expiration de son permis), si elle décide de sortir du Canada (faire un voyage) durant le traitement de la demande de prolongation je me demande quelle option s'applique : Option A: À son retour, elle peut rentrer au Canada comme travailleur étant donné que le permis de travail actuel n'est pas encore arrivé à sa date d'expiration bien qu'une demande de prolongation soit en traitement, le permis de travail actuel reste donc valide. Option B : À son retour, elle ne pourra pas rentrer au Canada comme travailleur parce que la demande de prolongation viendrait invalider le permis de travail actuel. RÉPONSE : Oui, le résident temporaire, après avoir fait une demande de prolongation de permis de travail, peut quitter le Canada. Dans l’éventualité que le résident temporaire revient avant que le permis de travail actuel expire, il peut continuer à travailler jusqu’à temps qu’une décision sur la demande de prolongation soit émise. Si le résident temporaire revient au Canada après que le permis de travail actuel expire et qu’une décision sur la demande de prolongation de permis de travail n’a pas encore été rendu, il aura maintenu son statut en vertu du R183(5), mais il ne pourra pas continuer à travailler car il ne répondrait plus aux conditions du R186(u). Pour plus d’informations, veuillez visiter la page web suivante : Résidents temporaires : Statut conservé au cours du traitement (qui portait anciennement le nom de statut implicite) - Canada.ca Merci beaucoup, La boîte aux lettres des représentants en immigration

Hello,
Thank you for your email correspondence to 's Immigration Representatives mailbox. We appreciate your patience.
Question: Just to clarify, can an owner of a company under ICT-Work Permit C62 gain arranged employment (200 or 50 points) as well?
Based on the attached article, “There is nothing in the Ministerial Instructions that provides that an offer would not be valid for arranged employment if the applicant owns a majority of the employer, making them self-employed. IRCC has in fact confirmed this understanding in a couple of communications with the Immigration Representatives Mailbox.
Answer: Thank you for your follow up inquiry.
For the purposes of Section 29 of the Ministerial Instructions respecting the Express Entry arranged employment is defined in Subsection 82(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations. The Regulations prescribe that an offer of employment must be made by an employer, meaning that there is a an arrangement between an employer and an employee. A self-employed person may not meet this requirement. The onus is on the applicant to satisfy that their offer of arranged employment meets the definition of an employer-employee relationship and all the other requirements.
We trust that this information will assist you.
Sincerely,
Immigration Representatives Mailbox

Hello, Thank you for your email correspondence to 's Immigration Representatives mailbox. We appreciate your patience.
Question: I understand that a self-employed individual with an LMIA-exempt such as a C62 work permit could claim points for arranged employment (200 or 50 points) under Express Entry after one year of work in Canada. Nothing in the Ministerial Instructions provides that an offer would not be valid for arranged employment if the applicant owns a majority of the employer, making them self-employed.
However, self-employment can't gain points under Express Entry for Canadian Experience.
Could you kindly confirm whether this is still correct?
Answer: To be assigned Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) points for arranged employment pursuant to section 29 of the Ministerial Instructions respecting the Express Entry system (Ml), the applicant must be an employee in an employer-employee relationship, and the offer itself must be made by an employer to an employee, and must meet all the other requirements. A self-employed person cannot make an offer of arranged employment to themselves. Likewise, an offer of arranged employment cannot be made by a business partner, such as a co-proprietor, to another business partner.
A period of self-employment is not to be included in calculating CRS points for a period of work experience in Canada, as per the paragraph 15(7)(b) of the MI with the exception of providing publicly funded medical services under select occupations.
Please be advised that the assessment of an application is based on a case-by-case basis, considering the particular circumstances in conjunction with the supporting documentation available to the officer. The onus is always on the applicant to provide sufficient documentation to satisfy an officer that they meet the requirements.

threads.answer:

Question:
IRPR 186 A foreign national may work in Canada without a work permit
- (w) if they are or were the holder of a study permit who has completed their program of study and
(i) they met the requirements set out in paragraph (v), and (ii) they applied for a work permit before the expiry of that study permit and a decision has not yet been made in respect of their application; or

Subsequent clarification provided: My question was relating to maintained status and being allowed to continue working after their studies in the same fashion as when they apply for a PGWP Can a student of a non-PGWP program apply for a LMIA or LMIA exempt closed work permit and be allowed to continue working R186(w)
Answer:
A Student permit holder may work in Canada without a work permit if they meet the following criteria:
IRPR 186(w) if they are or were the holder of a study permit who has completed their program of study and
•(i)they met the requirements set out in paragraph (v)*, AND (ii) they applied for a work permit before the expiry of that study permit and a decision has not yet been made in respect of their application;
*IRPR 186(v) if they are the holder of a study permit and
- (i) they are a full-time student enrolled at a designated learning institution as defined in section 211.1, (ii) the program in which they are enrolled is a post-secondary academic, vocational or professional training program, or a vocational training program at the secondary level offered in Quebec, in each case, of a duration of six months or more that leads to a degree, diploma or certificate, and •(iii) although they are permitted to engage in full-time work during a regularly scheduled break between academic sessions, they work no more than 20 hours per week during a regular academic session;
Students who have applied for a work permit and do not meet the requirements outlined above, cannot work without a permit and must wait to work until the work permit application is approved. [https://ircc.canada.ca/english/helpcentre/answer.asp?qnum=475&top=4](https://ircc.canada.ca/english/helpcentre/answer.asp?qnum=475&top=4)
Therefore, under maintained status, the applicant must continue to observe the same conditions stipulated in their original permit until the original permit expires or a decision is made on the new application.

I'm waiting for my post-graduation work permit. Can I travel
outside Canada?
You can leave Canada and return, as long as your visa or Electronic Travel Authorization (eTA) is still valid. Your permit (study or work) is not a visa and doesn't allow you to travel back to Canada. If your visa or eTA is expired, you have to get a new one before you return to Canada. When you return to Canada: •You may enter as a student if your study permit is still valid.
- If we approve your post-graduation work permit while you're away, you may enter as a worker.
- If we're still processing your post-graduation work permit, you may enter as a visitor, and you can work without a work permit until we make a decision on your application.
A border officer will have some questions for you when you arrive back in Canada. The officer may ask you for proof that you applied for a post-graduation work permit, such as a copy of your application or the fee payment receipt. If the officer believes there is reason to refuse your re-entry, you won't be able to enter Canada.
Travel outside Canada
A temporary resident whose period of authorized stay has been extended as per subsection R183(5) who leaves Canada will be examined on re-entry and may be allowed to 會 re-enter Canada as a temporary resident pending a decision on the extension of their study permit or work permit in Canada
- apply for a new work or study permit at the port of entry, if eligible
Re-enter Canada as a temporary resident Applicants may be allowed to re-enter Canada as a temporary resident pending a decision on the extension of their study permit or work permit in Canada, provided they are temporary resident visa (TRV) exempt as per section R190 or hold a valid multiple-entry visa. The border services officer will set the period of authorized stay on entry.
Temporary residents from TRV-required countries whose period of authorized stay has been extended under subsection R183(5) and who are seeking re-entry to Canada following a visit solely to the United States or St. Pierre and Miquelon are considered to be TRV exempt, as per subparagraph R190(3)(f)(ii). This interpretation of the legislation is consistent with paragraph 30 of the Federal Court decision De Brito v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2003 FC 1379. If a TRV-required national has travelled anywhere other than the United States or St. Pierre and Miquelon, regardless of whether their period of authorized stay was extended under subsection R183(5), they are not TRV exempt. Regardless of the De Brito decision, the authorization to work and study without a permit under paragraph R186(u) or section R189 while pending a decision on an application ends on departure from Canada. If the new study or work permit has not been issued prior to the applicant's return, they may not resume work or study in Canada until their application for renewal has been granted. Those not able to resume work must satisfy the border services officer that they have sufficient means of support and that they will not study or work without authorization.

Thank you for your enquiry concerning the document requirements for non-accompanying dependent children under the Agri-Food Pilot.
In accordance with section 10(2)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (justice.gc.ca), all immigration applications are required to provide information on the applicant and all the family members of the applicant, whether accompanying or not. A family member is defined in section 1(3) as:
(a) the spouse or common-law partner of the person;
(b) a dependent child of the person or of the person's spouse or common-law partner; and
(c) a dependent child of a dependent child referred to in paragraph (b).

- police certificate
- adoption certificate (if applicable)
- digital photos

Thank you for your email correspondence to 's Immigration Representatives mailbox. We appreciate your patience.
Question: Does modifying or updating an Express Entry profile alter the original timestamp of the profile submission?
For example, during the recent Express Entry draw on August 7,2024, the CRS score of lowest-ranked candidate invited was 507. Tie-breaking rule: June 5, 2024. My client's CRS score is 507 and her profile was created on April 23, 2024 with a score of 504. We updated her profile on August 23, 2024 due to her new IELTS score and her CRS score became 507.
According to your website, 'if more than one candidate has the lowest score, the cut-off is based on the date and time they submitted their Express Entry profiles. It should not be based on the date we amended/updated her profile, right?
Answer: Modifying or updating an Express Entry profile does not affect the original time and date of the profile submission. Even if the candidate's CRS score and/or qualifications change, it is the original date of entering the pool for that active profile that is used for the tie-breaker. Please note that the tie-breaking rule for the round of invitation of August 27, 2024 was updated on our website to reflect the correct value. The actual tie-breaker for the round was April 17, 2024 at 20:11:20 UTC.

threads.question:
Dear IRCC
I have a question, which I hope you can answer:
Scenario: Company obtains a Global Talent Stream LMIA approval for a 1 year contract. Post-graduate work permit holder submits application to extend and change conditions to an LMiA work permit. While the work permit is in process, the company provides a permanent job offer. Worker updates Express Entry profile to state they have a permanent job offer, that an LMiA has been approved, and that they do not hold an employer specific work permit. The Express Entry gave 50 points for arranged employment.
Questions:
Does a worker on a non-employer specific work permit, with an LMIA approval that was not issued for a job offer that is at least one year in length after getting PR yet has an updated offer for such a length get the arranged employment points? Or must they wait to have their LMIA work permit, plus the revised job offer for at least one year after getting PR, to get these points?
Does a worker on a non-employer specific with work permit, with an LMiA approval of 3 years under the high-wage or GTS program, get the arranged employment points without yet holding an LMIA work permit, provided the employer can also confirm the offer is for at least 1 year after getting PR?
Thank you
Ruscito, Giovanni (IRCC/IRCC)
threads.answer:
Good Day,
Thank you for your email correspondence to 's Immigration Representatives mailbox. We appreciate your patience.
Question: Scenario: Company obtains a Global Talent Stream LMIA approval for a 1 year contract. Post-graduate work permit holder submits application to extend and change conditions to an LMIA work permit. While the work permit is in process, the company provides a permanent job offer. Worker updates Express Entry profile to state they have a permanent job offer, that an LMiA has been approved, and that they do not hold an employer specific work permit. The Express Entry gave 50 points for arranged employment.
Does a worker on a non-employer specific work permit, with an LMIA approval that was not issued for a job offer that is at least one year in length after getting PR yet has an updated offer for such a length get the arranged employment points? Or must they wait to have their LMIA work permit, plus the revised job offer for at least one year after getting PR, to get these points?
Does a worker on a non-employer specific with work permit, with an LMiA approval of 3 years under the high-wage or GTS program, get the arranged employment points without yet holding an LMIA work permit, provided the employer can also confirm the offer is for at least 1 year after getting PR?
Answer: Section 29 of the Ministerial Instructions respecting the Express Entry system, dictates that the applicant must have a qualifying offer of employment that is one of the following:
(a) an arranged employment as defined in subsection 82(1) of the Regulations, if
(i) the offer is supported by a valid assessment — provided by the Department of Employment and Social Development at the request of the employer or an officer and on the same basis as an assessment provided for the issuance of a work permit — that the requirements set out in subsection 203(1) of the Regulations with respect to the offer have been met, (ii) the foreign national holds a valid work permit, the offer of employment is made by an employer for whom the foreign national currently works and who is specified on the work permit, the work permit was issued based on a positive determination made by an officer under subsection 203(1) of the Regulations with respect to the foreign national's employment with that employer in an occupation that is listed in TEER Category 0, 1, 2 or 3 of the National Occupational Classification and the assessment provided by the Department of Employment and Social Development on the basis of which the determination was made is not suspended or revoked, or
(iii) the foreign national holds a valid work permit issued under the circumstances described in paragraph 204(a) or (c) or section 205 of the Regulations, the offer is made by an employer who is specified on the work permit and the foreign national works for that employer and has accumulated at least one year of full-time work experience, or the equivalent in part-time work, over a continuous period of work in Canada for that employer;
The type of work permit (open or closed) is not specified in the Ministerial Instructions for the purposes of obtaining 50 or 200 CRS points. Work authorization (work permit) is not a requirement under this subparagraph for the job offer to be valid. The job offer must also meet the other criteria to be valid under the Express Entry program the applicant qualifies for, listed on our website. In both scenarios, the applicants must have a new positive LMIA that approves the specific job offer and names the applicant and their position.
Please be advised that the assessment of an application is based on a case-by-case basis, considering the particular circumstances in conjunction with the supporting documentation available to the officer. The onus is always on the applicant to provide sufficient documentation to satisfy an officer that they meet the requirements.
We trust that this information will assist you.
Sincerely,
Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.answer:
## Hello,
Thank you for your email correspondence to Immigration, Refugee 's Immigration Representatives Mailbox. Please consider the information provided as general program guidance and not a directive for case-specific enquires. Question 1: Can the student attend our institution as a visitor without cancelling his online study permit application, or must the student cancel his online application before applying for an eTA?
Response:
As per R188(1)(c), foreign nationals may enter Canada or remain in Canada without a study permit to attend a course or program of study of 6 months' duration or less. The duration of the course or program of study is often a more important consideration than the number of months the foreign national intends to study. Even if foreign nationals plan to study for 6 months or less, if the course or program is longer than 6 months, they need a study permit. Paragraph R188(1)(c) is not intended to allow a foreign national to complete an entire program without a study permit by taking required program courses one at a time. It is therefore recommended that foreign nationals be encouraged to apply for a study permit for a short-term course or program of study if they intend to apply for another program afterwards. For more information, visit: Find out if you need a study permit Who needs a study permit
Question 2: If the student receives study permit approval while attending our institution, can he flagpole to collect his study permit at the POE and extend his stay for another semester?
Response: If the foreign national followed the instructions to apply for a study permit from outside Canada, they would have filled out the form called Application for Study Permit Made Outside of Canada [IMM 1294]. If their application is approved, they will get an approval letter that says they are allowed to study in Canada. This letter is called the port of entry letter of introduction. Once they have this letter, they must leave and ask to get their study permit on return to Canada. For more information, please visit: Study permit: After you apply-Canada.ca Study permit: Prepare for arrival-Canada.ca We hope this information is helpful.

Good day,
Thank you for the follow up questions on the EMPP.
Please note that the following guidance is subject to change as future versions of EMPP may include updates that require different instructions.
1. Can an applicant reside in Canada while their EMPP application is being processed? This scenario assumes that the individual initially submitted their application from outside of Canada but has since arrived in the country. For the Federal EMPP, yes, an applicant can reside in Canada while their EMPP application is being processed.
2. If residing in Canada during the processing period is permissible, how does the landing process work? The IRCC website indicates that the confirmation of permanent residence is typically sent to the applicant's residence outside of Canada. If the applicant is in Canada when their PR is approved, would they be required to return to their previous country of residence to obtain the PR visa and land at the port of entry? Alternatively, is there a way to confirm PR status from within Canada? If the applicant is in Canada with a legal status when their PR is approved, they do not need to return to their previous country of residence to obtain the PR visa and land at the port of entry. Instead, clients are asked to advise IRCC of any change in circumstance using the web form, including change of address (i.e., country of residence) and contact information and IRCC will connect with them using the email address provided so that they can be landed virtually through our Permanent Resident Portal. Instructions will be sent to the applicant on how to confirm their permanent resident status virtually. Please make sure to update the application with the correct Canadian address to ensure all communication and documentation is sent to the appropriate location. It is important to keep all information current and accurate for smooth processing of your PR status confirmation within Canada.
Thank you!

Hello officer,
Good morning. My name is. I am an Immigration Consultant and my I am sending this email as I have a question regarding how to mention name if client has “hyphen” in the last name. In the family name, his name is written as John-Smith (hyphen and that's the only name he has, no given name and nothing else in the last name, just John-Smith) On his IELTS, his name is John-Smith. On some of his documents his name is John Smith (with space and no hyphen) such as birth certificate, education, even Canadian work permit has John Smith. My question is, when we apply for Canadian PR application, how we write the name for candidate someone like this in immigration forms? I tried best to find it on IRCC websites but couldn't find it. Ruscito, Giovanni (IRCC/IRCC)
threads.answer:
Hello,
Thank you for your inquiry.
IRCC recognizes foundational evidence of identity (EOI) that establishes core identity information such as a given name or given names, surname, date of birth and place of birth. Foundational EOl examples include records of birth, immigration or citizenship from an authority with the necessary jurisdiction. Primary EOl is issued by an authoritative source (for example, a foreign government) and examples include a passport or a travel document.
Since the birth certificate is a foundational evidence of identity in which a passport would be issued, it is recommended that the passport be amended to reflect the birth certificate (without the hyphen). Once the passport has been amended, his PR application can indicate John Smith as his family name without a given name. He can put John-Smith as an alias/also known as (AKA) in the other names section. He must continue to use his name without a hyphen to have his documents issued in a consistent manner for the future.

2. R.75(2)(a)-(c) describes the qualifying work experience for Federal Skilled Worker Class. There is no requirement in this provision for the employment experience to be gained while on valid work authorization, either inside of Canada or from abroad. If the skilled experience was gained in Canada without authorization can the experience still be qualifying for the purpose of FSWP?
Answer:
1. Remote work for an employer outside of the Canadian labour market while residing or studying in Canada may be eligible under the Express Entry for the purposes of Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) points calculation as foreign work experience if it meets all the other requirements. Please note that the system does not currently capture remote work. Please make sure to select the Country/territory of the employer when claiming remote work performed from Canada. When an applicant is invited to apply, please submit an explanation detailing the remote work agreement, and where the employer and employee are physically located.
2. While there is no specific requirement for work authorization for qualifying FSWP work experience, please note that authorization to work, such as a work permit, is part of the evidence required to establish genuine work experience. In the absence of work authorization, for work in Canada or abroad, the declared work experience may be deemed non-genuine and may result in a refusal of an application. In addition, section 75 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations prescribes that membership of the Federal Skilled Worker class is based on the ability of the skilled worker to become economically established in Canada. Circumventing Canadian labour and immigration laws, such as working without authorization, may compromise the applicant's ability to satisfy the officer that they are able to meet this requirement.

In such a case, would this be considered as having met the equivalent of 1 year of full-time work experience, even if the 24 months of part-time work have not been fully completed?

Question: What does “from a Canadian private post-secondary institution that operated under the same rules and regulations as a Canadian public post-secondary institution" refer to under s.30(4)(a)?
(4) For the purpose of this section, an eligible credential is one of the following:
(a) a degree, diploma, certificate or trade or apprenticeship credential from a Canadian public post-secondary institution or from a Canadian private post-secondary institution that operated under the same rules and regulations as a Canadian public post-secondary institution;

threads.subject: Can they study from within Canada without a study permit? – REP-2024-1655 - Due 9-Oct-24
threads.question: The student has used their temporary resident visa (visitor) to enter Canada. They want to pursue a master course, which has three semesters. The first semester is fully online while the second and third are in person. My question is: Can they study for the first semester in Canada without a study permit?
threads.answer:
As per R188(1)(c), foreign nationals may enter Canada or remain in Canada without a study permit to attend a course or program of study of 6 months' duration or less. The duration of the course or program of study is often a more important consideration than the number of months the foreign national intends to study. Even if foreign nationals plan to study for 6 months or less, if the course or program is longer than 6 months, they need a study permit. Paragraph R188(1)(c) was not intended to allow a foreign national to complete an entire program without a study permit by taking required program courses one at a time. It is therefore recommended that foreign nationals be encouraged to apply for a study permit for a short-term course or program of study if they intend to apply for another program afterwards. For more information, visit: Find out if you need a study permit Who needs a study permit We hope this information is helpful.

Thank you for contacting the Immigration Representatives Mailbox. Please note that we cannot respond to case specific questions, therefore the information provided below is focused on general program requirements.
For any job offer being assessed under this category, an officer would need to review all information and circumstances in the application to support a thorough assessment of the eligibility criteria, including genuineness of the job offer, the ability to pay the applicant and the reasonableness of any arrangements on a case-by-case basis.
A job offer must be made by a single employer in Canada that is not a business, this employer is required to have a Canada Revenue Agency business number. It may be acceptable for an employer to have other family members contribute to the caregiver's salary if they have a shared responsibility for the family member's care. In this case, the individual listed on the job offer is solely responsible for issuing pay stubs, establishing employment conditions etc. Relatives residing in other provinces can help fund the caregiver's salary as long as the job listed on the job offer itself isn't taking place in Quebec.
However, the officer will need to be satisfied that the relative who is to co-fund the care will indeed do so. For example, on top of the income and/or savings, an officer may want to know what specific arrangements are being made for the payment of the caregiver wages by the 2 payers, including the means and frequency of contributions. In order to assess the genuineness of the offer, the officer may also look into the reasons why this relative is willing to contribute financially to the care, and a letter of explanation can be provided to that effect. The officer will make a decision based on the information available on the file, or may ask for any additional information or documentation necessary in order to make a decision.
For more information on the job offer assessment, please refer to Genuine and valid job offer.
Please note that the HSW pilot has expired and is now closed to new applications.

Ils peuvent également travailler à temps plein pendant les congés prévus au calendrier d’études.
Si la demande de permis de travail coop est refusée, l’étudiant doit immédiatement quitter son stage coop.

Hello,
Thank you for your question. Please note that we cannot answer case-specific questions but have provided the following information as guidance.
Question:
I am writing to seek clarification on a matter related to the authorized work locations for foreign workers in Canada. Specifically, we would like to understand which document holds greater authority in cases where there is a contradiction between a work permit and either an LMIA (Labour Market Impact Assessment) or an Offer of Employment.
Specifically, if an LMIA was approved listing multiple work locations, but the work permit only lists one, is the employee limited to the one location of work on the work permit or permitted to work at the multiple locations listed on the LMIA.
Alternatively, if an IMU based work permit that was approved based on an Offer of Employment that references multiple locations or advising that the individual will need to be “authorized to work a various employer sites”, but when the work permit is issued it only lists the one primary location with no additional comments, is the work limited to the locations on the work permit or is the worker permitted to work at the other locations based on the declarations in the Offer of Employment.
We ask as we have been struggling to have officers list all work locations on the work permits, and when we submit a request for correction the request is declined and we are advised to submit a new application to add additional work locations, even though the additional work locations were included in the original application. At the recent CBA Immigration Law Conference, it was suggested that the locations on the Offer of Employment or LMIA would take precedence (which would resolve this issue).
Answer:
When the employer has indicated that the foreign worker will be working at multiple job locations, officers should include all locations in the remarks of the work permit. A note must be included in the application in cases where the officer decides to limit the location.
Although multiple work locations are listed on the LMIA and the offer of employment, the employee is limited to working at whichever location is listed on the work permit. Failure to do so could result in the employee being in violation of the conditions of the work permit.

Hello,

Question 2 - Conditions on an LMIA-based work permit When an employee has an LMIA-based work permit and the location of employment is written only under the additional information section, but not under conditions, can an employer send the employee to a different province for a temporary project, as long as the employee works for the same employer and in the same occupation? threads.answer:
Good Day,
Thank you for your email correspondence to 's Immigration Representatives mailbox. We appreciate your patience.
Question 1 - Canadian work experience for the Canadian Experience Class under Express Entry If an employee worked from abroad for one month for a Canadian employer in the middle of their employment, can this one month be counted toward Canadian experience?
Answer: The policy intent of Canadian Experience Class requires that the work performed demonstrates to the Officer that the applicant has entered the Canadian labour market, and a Canadian entity paid the applicant for their work. It must also be evident to the Officer that the work would be considered a business activity that is competitive in the Canadian marketplace, and that this position would normally have been filled by a Canadian citizen or permanent resident. Entry into the Canadian labour market is a necessary element of work experience that demonstrates ones “ability to become economically established in Canada" under R87.1(1) of the IRPR.
Officers would need to review the circumstances and decide if overall they are satisfied the usual place of work duties is in Canada, or elsewhere, AND whether the applicant maintained temporary resident status during the period of work. Factors that might go into that last assessment (TR status) might include whether they had that status, were physically present, and maintained residential ties (habitually resided) at a residence in Canada during the period of work.
While this is largely officer discretion (and there is no calculator available) a cautionary approach to this scenario might be to discount the month residing and working outside Canada, as not meeting the TR status threshold, since the individual would need to be habitually sheltered outside Canada for that month, and accrue 1 additional month in Canada.
Overall, work that compels an employee to reside out of Canada for longer periods of time, and for which they would not require an authorization to work (since it is outside Canada's jurisdiction, in a foreign territory) and where they cannot be considered to have maintained status as a temporary resident, would need to be excluded from counting. That said, an applicant could conceivably satisfy an officer if for instance they remained a factual resident of Canada, etc. Factors that might complicate that could be that the applicant is an independent contractor of the Canadian employer, or employed by the foreign worksite while present, rather than being a wage-earning employee. There isn't a calculator and the officer would need to review to be satisfied the work was ‘in Canada' as a 'temporary resident of Canada'.
Question 2 - Conditions on an LMIA-based work permit When an employee has an LMIA-based work permit and the location of employment is written only under the additional information section, but not under conditions, can an employer send the employee to a different province for a temporary project, as long as the employee works for the same employer and in the same occupation? (valid temporary resident status) during the processing of the application until decision, or may they leave Canada during the processing of the application and still be considered under the conditions? threads.subject: Inquiry Regarding Work Experience Calculation for CEC Applicants-REP-2024-1748 - Due 21-Oct-24
threads.question: I am writing to seek clarification regarding how the IRCC counts work experience for applicants under the Canadian Experience Class (CEC). Specifically, I would like to understand how work hours are assessed when an applicant works a combination of regular full-time and part-time hours in a single job. For instance, if an applicant works 30 hours in certain weeks (full-time) and, in other weeks, works less than 30 hours but more than 15 hours (part-time), or even less than 15 hours, how is this experience counted towards the CEC requirements? For example, If an employee worked part-time for 20 weeks at 20 hours per week, AND 42 weeks full time at 30 hours per week with the same employer, can his part-time work be considered equivalent to 10 full-time weeks of experience, or is there a specific calculation method used to determine equivalency?
threads.answer:
Qualifying work experience may be obtained as a combination of full-time and part-time work. To calculate the hours per week for a period of work experience, the total number of hours worked during that period is divided by the number of weeks in the period. Please note that the system will not count work experience in excess of 30 hours per week. The work hours are calculated only when the applicant performs the duties under their occupation. Periods of leave or rest do not count as hours of performing the duties.
In the proposed scenario, if an applicant worked a mix of part-time and full-time hours, then there are a total of 1660 hours over a period of 62 weeks, or 26 hours per week rounded down.
Alternatively, if an applicant has distinct periods of part-time and full-time work, it would be more accurate to declare those periods as separate work experience entries for the same employer with one period of 20 weeks at 20 hours per week and another period of 42 weeks at 30 hours per week.
Please be advised that it is an obligation to declare all information truthfully and accurately, including accumulated hours of work experience. The assessment of an application is based on a case-by-case basis, considering the particular circumstances in conjunction with the supporting documentation available to the officer. The onus is always on the applicant to provide sufficient documentation to satisfy an officer that they meet the requirements.
We trust that this information will assist you.
Sincerely,
Immigration Representatives Mailbox

Bonjour,
Les clients qui ont été émis une lettre confirmant leurs statut de résidence permanent (RP) durant la pandémie COVID-19 ont été avisé de fournir une copie de cette lettre afin de démontrer leur statut de RP pour appliquer pour des prestations gouvernementales et services dans lesquelles ils étaient éligibles, jusqu’à ce qu’ils reçoivent leur carte RP. La carte RP est un document d’attestation de statut et démontre que le détenteur a le statut de RP au Canada.
Les clients qui n’ont pas reçu un document de la Confirmation de résidence permanente (CRP), peuvent soumettre une demande d'une vérification du Statut (VDS) ou de remplacement d'un document d'immigration. Un document de VDS est un papier ordinaire contenant les renseignements qui apparaissent sur le CRP original. Ce document peut être utilisé lorsque le client doit soumettre une preuve des renseignements historiques d’immigration, tel que la date et le lieu d’entrée au Canada.

threads.question: [...] would a person be able to restore status as a caregiver and obtain an LMlA-based work permit as a caregiver (44100)?
threads.answer:
If a temporary resident has lost their status (section 47 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act [IRPA]) or let their authorization to work or study expire, they may apply to restore that status in accordance with section 182 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR)
It is important to note that since status and authorization are not the same under the IRPA, an applicant can only restore their status to that of a temporary resident and to the authorization that they held immediately prior to the restoration application. As an example, a student who lost their status cannot apply to restore temporary resident status with authorization to work. A visitor cannot restore their status with authorization to work, etc.
- * If the applicant is in Canada and has a valid work permit or study permit and lost their status or let their authorization to work or study permit expire, they may be able to restore their status as a worker or student. The refusal to process does not apply to those applicants. Therefore, they may be eligible to apply for an LMIA-based work permit in NOC 44100 occupation.
- * However, if the applicant is in Canada and has a visitor status only, and lost their status (let their status expire), they may be eligible to restore their status as 'Visitors' if they meet the requirements under section 182 of the regulations. Visitors in Canada (after restoring their TR status) are not eligible to apply for an LMIA-based work permit in NOC 44100 and are subject to the refusal to process if they are destined to work in a province outside Quebec. Those who are destined to work in Quebec may be eligible to apply for an LMiA-based work permit if they meet the requirements under R199(e) of the IRPR.

Temporary residents: Maintained status during processing (previously called implied status) - Canada.ca provides the following information regarding second applications and maintained status:
Second application during processing period
Officers should process both applications and not administratively cancel the outstanding application.
If a second application for extension is submitted before the decision is rendered on the first application, the
decision on the first application affects the applicant's status.
- * If the first application is approved, then the new status and any authorization apply. The decision on the second application may change this.
- * If the first application is rejected for incompleteness, it is returned to the applicant. The first application is considered to have never been received, no extension of authorized stay is granted, and the applicant is in status until the original temporary resident status expires. If the second application is submitted during the period of authorized stay extended by operation of law under R183(5), then their status is maintained by the second application after the decision on the first is finalized until a decision on the second application is made. However, their authorization to work or study may be affected.
- * If the first application is refused, but the original permit was still valid when the second application was received, then the period of authorized stay and the authority to study or work in the original permit is extended until a decision is rendered on the second application.
- * If the first application is refused, and the original permit was expired when the second application was received, then the period of authorized stay is extended but there is no continued authority to study or work.

threads.answer:
Hello,
Please see our response to your question.
Question:
1. 1. Definition of “50% of the program": When determining whether a student has completed at least "50% of their program” in Canada, does this refer to the duration of time (ex. months, day) or the number of credits or courses (ex. 12 credits out of 20)
2. 2. Accelerated Studies: As per the PDI, for students who complete their studies in less time than the normal length of the program, the PGWP should be assessed on the length of the program, not the length of studies. If a student completed 50% of their studies distance learning (online) from within Canada and the remaining 50% in-person, but completed the in-person portion in less time than the online portion, would they still be eligible for PGWP based on the time spent studying in-person? Would the same apply to that student who studied 50% of their program online from outside Canada between September 1, 2022, and August 31, 2024?
3. 3. Exchange, Co-op and Field Research outside Canada: Some students take exchange terms, co-op terms and field research from outside Canada. Would this time spent outside Canada be excluded when calculating the length of their PGWP?
Response:
With regards to your questions:
1. In accordance with the Post-Graduation Work Permit (PGWP) regulations, if over 50% of a study program's courses are completed through distance learning, it is classified as a distance-learning program, making the applicant ineligible for a PGWP. However, if less than 50% of the total courses are completed through distance learning, a PGWP may be granted, with validity based on the program's duration as confirmed by the eligible Designated Learning Institution (DLI), considering credits earned from both in-class and distance-learning courses.
2. The applicant may qualify for PGWP depending on the accelerated program offered by the DLI. It would be up to the applicant to prove that they completed 50% of their accelerated studies distance learning to the officer.
3. Students are eligible for PGWP, but it is only valid for the time spent studying inside Canada. If their study program has an overseas component, they may be eligible for a PGWP as long as they earn a credit from a Canadian school for it. The PGWP will only be valid for the length of the time they studied in Canada. Please visit our websites for more information on Post-graduation work permit (PGWP) [R205(c) - C43] - International Mobility Program-Canada.ca and Work in Canada after you graduate: Who can apply-Canada.ca.

Answer: Yes, an applicant can apply for an LMIA-exempt work permit under CUFTA provided they meet the eligibility of one of the categories (investors, intra-corporate transferees, professionals). threads.answer:
Good Day,
Thank you for your email correspondence to 's Immigration Representatives mailbox.
Question: I am not asking about a specific case. I am asking about a general scenario. Could you clarify what the policy rule would be in the following situation? A Foreign National received a Canadian tourist visa on March 01, 2024, valid until November 30, 2033. However, the individual lost their passport on June 1, 2024, which contained a valid Canadian visa. The individual remains in his country of origin and has since acquired a new passport.
This scenario raises questions regarding the recovery or transfer of the previously approved visa to the new passport and what steps should be taken to retain the travel privileges initially granted.
Key Questions:
1. Visa Recovery/Transfer Process: Is there a formal process to recover or transfer the previously issued tourist visa to her new passport without reapplying for a new visa?
2. Visa Reissuance Request: If a recovery or transfer is possible, what specific documents and steps are required for her to request the reissuance of her tourist visa in her new passport?
3. Application Alternatives: In the event that a visa transfer is not feasible, is the only option to reapply for a new tourist visa? If so, would the previously approved visa status affect her new application, or is she required to undergo the entire process from the beginning?
4. Impact on Future Travel: Could the loss of her passport and the existing visa impact her travel history or future visa applications to Canada, and what measures can be taken to ensure smooth processing?
Approved response:
In the event that a passport is lost or stolen, a foreign national is expected to report the incident and can request a replacement temporary resident visa (TRV) be affixed to their new passport so long as it is still valid. A replacement counterfoil would be issued to the original validity of the lost or stolen document and the replacement fee is $30 as specified in R311(2). If the foreign national would prefer a counterfoil with a longer validity, to match the new passport, they would need to submit a new TRV application and pay the associated fees.
In order to request a replacement counterfoil, foreign nationals can submit a web form request indicating the type of enquiry (Replacement Documents, Amendments to documents and Verification of status documents) and simply provide the supporting rationale and both the residential address and mailing address in the 'Your enquiry' field. Once the appropriate office receives the request, they will send the client instructions on how to pay the replacement fee of $30 and where to
submit their original passport and self-addressed stamped (traceable means only) envelope.
A previously approved TRV application will have no impact on a foreign national's future TRV applications. Keeping in mind, a foreign national will not be able to travel to Canada until they are issued a replacement (or new) counterfoil in their new passport. However, it is recommended that the foreign national, upon applying for a TRV, provide an explanation of their situation and proof that their previous passport that contained a valid Canadian TRV was lost or stolen (i.e. police report). Please note that failure to present this information could cause delays in the processing of the application.
We trust that this information will assist you.
Sincerely,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.answer:
Good day,
Israeli nationals are eligible to submit an application for an open work permit from within Canada under these special measures if they meet the following conditions:
they hold a passport or travel document issued by Israel or the Palestinian Authority; or are a foreign national family member-per the definition of subsection 1(3) of the Regulations— of a Canadian citizen or permanent resident who left Israel or the Palestinian Territories on or after October 7, 2023; and they have valid temporary resident status in Canada.
A study permit confers temporary resident status. Therefore, Israeli nationals who are in Canada on a valid study permit would be eligible to apply under the facilitative measures to support Israeli and Palestinian nationals in Canada to extend or change the conditions of their temporary stay as worker, student or visitor as long as they are physically present in Canada and hold valid temporary resident status, regardless of the date of their arrival. The public policy allows eligible temporary residents in Canada to submit an application for an open work permit, free of charge, while remaining in Canada.
Instructions on how to apply can be found here: Measures for Israeli nationals, Palestinian passport holders and family members in Canada-Canada.ca.
Please note that clients may hold a work permit and study permit at the same time; however, all standard eligibility and inadmissibility requirements must be met. If they intend to apply for an additional permit, they must be eligible for both permits and must show the officer that they can study and work at the same time, if they intend to do so.
Thank you,

Bonjour, Merci de contacter la boîte aux lettres des représentants de l'immigration. Veuillez noter que nous ne répondons pas aux demandes spécifiques à un cas particulier.
Question: J'aimerais savoir si cet enfant (non biologique, non adopté, mais sous tutelle légale) peut être ajouté à la demande de résidence permanente du Programme régulier des travailleurs qualifiés du Québec. Y a-t-il d'autres documents, en plus de la tutelle, qui doivent être ajoutés à la demande ?
Answer: Un enfant à charge est reconnu par IRCC suivant les Règlements sur l'immigration et la protection des réfugiés comme étant l'enfant qui :
- a) d’une part, par rapport à l’un de ses parents : o (i) soit en est l’enfant biologique et n’a pas été adopté par une personne autre que son époux ou conjoint de fait, (ii) soit en est l’enfant adoptif;
- b) d’autre part, remplit l’une des condítions suivantes :
(i) il est âgé de moins de vingt-deux ans et n’est pas un époux ou conjoint de fait, (ii) il est âgé de vingt-deux ans ou plus et n’a pas cessé de dépendre, pour l’essentiel, du soutien financier de l’un ou l’autre de ses parents depuis le moment où il a atteint l’âge de vingt-deux ans, et ne peut subvenir à ses besoins du fait de son état physique ou mental. (dependent child)
Une tutelle légale ne créé pas de filiation juridique entre l’enfant et les tuteurs, au Canada. Comme une tutelle légale ne correspond pas à la définition de l’adoption en vertu du R3(2), un enfant sous une tutelle légale n’est pas considéré comme un « enfant à charge » tel que défini au R2 du Règlement sur l’immigration et la protection des réfugiés (RIPR).
Pour inclure cet enfant dans sa demande de résidence permanente au Canada, sous le programme de travailleurs qualifiés du Québec, le demandeur principal devra soumettre une preuve d’adoption plénière légale qui est valide aux fins de l’immigration.
Cordialement, La boîte aux lettres des représentants de l'immigration

Question: Je travaille au Cégep de Lévis et j’aimerais clarifier quelques points avec vous concernant le permis de travail stage coop pour les étudiants internationaux.
Si un étudiant possédait un permis d’études et un permis de travail stage coop valides, et qu’il a soumis une demande de renouvellement pour ces deux permis avant leur expiration, est-ce qu'il conserve les mêmes autorisations en ce qui concerne le permis de stage ? Autrement dit, peut-il continuer à travailler à temps plein dans le cadre d'un stage obligatoire de son programme coopératif en attendant la réponse d’IRCC par rapport à leur demande de permis de travail stage coop et de permis d’études ?
Réponse:
Tous les résidents temporaires se voient automatiquement imposer l’obligation de quitter le Canada à la fin de leur période de séjour autorisée. Toutefois, en vertu de l'article R181, un résident temporaire peut demander à faire prolonger sa période de séjour autorisée avant qu’elle ne prenne fin. Si tel est le cas, sa période de séjour autorisée à titre de résident temporaire est prolongée par effet de la loi jusqu'à ce qu’une décision soit prise [R183(5)]. Cette personne est alors réputée avoir le statut légal de résident temporaire au cours de la période de traitement de sa demande.
Remarque : Le stage coop ou le stage professionnel ne peut représenter plus de 50 % de la durée totale du programme d'études.
Veuillez consulter [https://www.canada.ca/fr/immigration-refugies-citoyennete/organisation/publications-](https://www.canada.ca/fr/immigration-refugies-citoyennete/organisation/publications-) guides/bulletins-guides-operationnels/residents-temporaires/visiteurs/statut-implicite-prolongation-sejour.html pour plus d’informations.
Cordialement,

threads.question:
Dear Sir/Madam,
, member in good standing with the CICC
This is. I have a question about Sponsoring
Common-Law Partner in Canada Class.
If the sponsor is living in Canada with their Common-Law Partner and the partner has valid temporary status, do they have to have been living at least 12 months with each other at the time of making the application?
Kind Regards,
threads.answer:
Good day,
Thank you for contacting the Immigration Representatives Mailbox
Please note that this mailbox is intended for general guidance and does not provide responses to case-specific inquiries. If you have case specific questions about a file, you are encouraged to submit a Webform at: [http://www.ircc.canada.ca/english/contacts/web-form.asp](http://www.ircc.canada.ca/english/contacts/web-form.asp)
A common-law partner is defined as a person who has been living in a conjugal relationship with another person continuously for at least one year. A conjugal relationship exists when there is a significant degree of commitment between two people. This can include sharing the same home; supporting each other financially and emotionally; having children together (if applicable); presenting themselves in public as a couple, etc.
It should be noted that a common-law relationship is defined by continuous cohabitation for at least one year, which is not the same as intermittent cohabitation adding up to one year. That being said, from time to time, one or the other partner may have to leave home for reasons such as work or business travel, family obligations etc. We cannot provide a specific timeframe or frequency of time spent apart that would or would not be acceptable as this is assessed on a case-by-case basis based on individual circumstances and is up to the discretion of the processing officer; however generally speaking, the separation must be temporary and short.
Furthermore, if the applicant is applying under the Spouse and Common-law Partner in Canada class (SCLPC), there is also the requirement under R124(a) of the IRPR that a foreign national cohabits with their sponsor in Canada:
124 A foreign national is a member of the spouse or common-law partner in Canada class if they
(a) are the spouse or common-law partner of a sponsor and cohabit with that sponsor in Canada; This requirement applies from the date the application is locked-in until the applicant becomes a Permanent Resident. IRCC Officers must continue to be satisfied that the partners are in a bona fide (genuine) relationship and will assess each case individually based on the specific circumstances of the applicant and evidence provided in order to determine whether an applicant is a member of the class under which they have applied and that they meet the eligibility requirements, including the criteria mentioned above. The onus is on the applicant to prove that they have been living common-law for at least one year before an application is received by IRCC and to include relevant details and evidence regarding their particular circumstances. There is no guarantee that a case will be approved. We hope you find this information useful.
Thank you,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.answer:
Hello,
Thank you for your email correspondence to 's Immigration Representatives mailbox. We appreciate your patience.
Note that this service provides guidance and not case-specific advice.
Please find the answers to your questions below:
1. 1. When providing data relating to reciprocal employment volumes, is it acceptable to omit TFWs employed in Canada on the basis of non-C20 based work permits (open work permit holders, TFWP-based WPs)?
Reciprocal employment volumes are based on temporary foreign workers coming under lRCC's lnternational Mobility Program (i.e., exempted from a labour market impact assessment, under C-20). Those coming under the ESDC-led Temporary Foreign Worker Program do not count in the calculation of reciprocal employment volumes.
2. 2. Does the visa/work authorization category of Canadians working abroad affect the assessment of reciprocity?
In assessing reciprocity, officers can consider not only the number ofindividuals working in Canada and abroad, but also employment duration and job level. Work authorization category is not taken into consideration when assessing reciprocity. Reciprocity could be shown by supplying an exchange agreement between the Canadian and foreign parties, a letter from the recelving Canadian institution, the work contract (if it provides evidence of reciprocity). or any other documentation that can showreciprocalopportunities.
For more information, please consult the following webpages:
International Mobility Program (IMP): Canadian interests-Reciprocal employment general guidelines R205(b), C20 - Canada.ca
We hope this information is of assistance. Do not hesitate to reach out again if you required further clarification.

threads.answer:

Though nothing is stopping an applicant from submitting an application for citizenship with a stay of proceedings, the recommendation is to wait until the one-year time period after the stay of proceedings has passed before applying for citizenship, to ensure that enough time has passed (in the event that the application gets processed faster than expected) or that no further action was taken or that no new charges were filed against the applicant (which maylead to a refusal).

No, the spouse of an lEC work permit holder is not automatically eligible for a spousal open work permit based solely on their partner holding an lEC work permit. However, your spouse or common-law partner has the following options:
Option 1: Apply for International Experience Canada
Your spouse or common-law partner can submit a profile to the International Experience Canada program. They must meet the requirements and follow the application steps if they are invited to apply for a work permit.
Option 2: Apply for a work permit outside the International Experience Canada program
In some cases, your spouse or common-law partner may be able to apply for an open work permit, which would allow them to accept a job from any employer.
Starting January 30, 2023, family members of most foreign workers can apply for an open work permit. Find out more about these changes. In other cases, they must apply for an employer-specific work permit. The employer may have to get a Labour Market Impact Assessment (LMIA). An LMIA allows an employer to hire someone for a specific job. Find out if your spouse or common-law partner's employer needs an LMIA to hire them.
How we assess their application
For both options, your spouse or common-law partner's work permit application will be assessed separately from yours.
If your spouse or common-law partner is not eligible for a work permit, they may be able to come to Canada as a visitor.
See also Can my spouse or common-law partner and dependent children come with me to Canada?
We hope this information is of assistance.

threads.answer:
regarding online courses --REP-2024-0938-- DUE 03 JUL 2024
Hello,
Thank you for your email correspondence to 's Immigration Representatives mailbox.
We appreciate your patience. Please find the answers to your questions below:
Question: When we calculate the online courses, should we calculate by number of courses or credits? I assume we should calculate by credits.
Response: Generally, the 50% requirement is calculated in terms of credits earned. It is up to the DLl to determine if their program is eligible for a post-graduation work permit (PGWP). The onus is on the student to confirm this with the DLI.
Question: For a 2-year program, can one of the four semesters be fully online distance learning in Canada if the total online distance courses are less than 50% of the program?
Response: Yes. As long as less than 50% of the program of study's total courses are completed inside Canada by distance learning, the student may be eligible for a PGWP. Please refer to our website for additional detail: Work in Canada after you graduate: Who can apply-Canada.ca
Question: A student has received an ECE certificate from the province by doing an international credential assessment [https://www.workbc.ca/career-profiles/early-childhood-educators-and-assistants](https://www.workbc.ca/career-profiles/early-childhood-educators-and-assistants), (She actually first got the ECE certificate assessment from the province of Saskatchewan, then transferred the ECE certificate with BC) and we recognize this BC provincial ECE certificate equal to our first year of the Early Childhood Education program. So, she only needs second year courses with us to receive the 2-year program diploma. However, the student has finished two minimum fulltime studies (9 credits each semester) with us when she receives this provincial credential assessment. Can she combine those study time (two semesters) before receives the confirmation for first year credits transfer with her second year to get a 3-year PGWP?
Response: If an international student received their educational credential from an eligible Canadian DLl, only the time they studied in Canada would factor into their eligibility for a PGWP.
In cases where more than one program from an eligible DLl was completed, the work permit may be issued for the combined length of the 2 programs up to 3 years. Please note that both programs must be completed within 2 years, each program of study must meet all PGWP eligibility requirements and be at least 8 months in length. Please refer to our website for additional detail: Post-graduation work permit (PGWP) [R205(c) - C43] -International Mobility Program-Canada.ca

Lorsqu'un résident temporaire soumet une demande de prorogation de son statut avant l'expiration de sa période de séjour autorisée, conformément à l’article R181, il peut bénéficier du statut conservé en vertu de l'article [R183(5)]. “officers can assess whether the employer is financially able to pay the caregiver the salary described in the job offer or if there is a genuine need for a caregiver by examining
- financial information provided by the employer
- the caregiver's salary"
Information provided in the job offer, may be also used by an officer to assess whether the job offer is valid and genuine. The assessment can vary on a case-by-case basis, but officers may use the LICO (Low income cut-offs) to inform their decision and request additional documentation from the employer.
Acceptable forms of proof include but are not limited to:
- Notice of Assessment (NOA) from Canada Revenue Agency or T4/T1 for the most recent tax year,
- Employment Insurance stubs
- Employment letter including salary and date of hiring
- Pay stubs
- Bank statements

threads.question:
Can you please clarify if it is possible to claim CRS points in Express Entry in the following situation:
A person is inside Canada with a valid work permit and is working full time in a skilled occupation, at the same time this person is working remotely full time in a skilled position in their home country.
1. 1. Can this person claim transferability factor points simultaneously for work experience inside and outside of Canada?
2. 2. Or, if the person can only claim transferability factor points for one experience, chose which one to claim points for? If not, how does Express Entry allocate these points?
Can a person holding a valid work permit and residing in Canada who is not working for a Canadian employer, but is working for a company remotely in their home country, claim transferability factor points in Express Entry?
threads.answer:
Remote work for a foreign employer while residing in Canada may be eligible as foreign work experience both towards minimum program requirements and Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) score under the skill transferability points if it meets all the requirements.
The applicant may claim concurrent work experience for two full-time jobs: one in Canada and one performed remotely outside Canada. Depending on the applicant's gualifications the system may grant them CRS skill transferability points for foreign work experience and CRS core points for Canadian work experience at the same time.
The system will not grant additional Federal Skilled Worker program selection criteria points for work experience in excess of 30 hours per week.
Please note that the system does not currently capture remote work. Please make sure to select the Country/territory of the employer when claiming remote work performed from Canada. When the applicant is invited to apply, please submit an explanation detailing the remote work agreement, and where the employer and employee are physically located.
The assessment of an application is based on a case-by-case basis, considering the particular circumstances in conjunction with the supporting documentation available to the officer. The onus is on thē applicant to provide sufficient documentation

Foreign nationals who are in Canada as temporary residents and are seeking to extend their temporary resident status or their authorization to work or study must apply by electronic means only, unless otherwise specified. On June 4, 2019, the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR) were amended to make an electronic application mandatory for most temporary residence applications made from within Canada. Specifically, section R9.2 provides that the following applications must be made by the electronic means made available or specified by the Minister for that purpose:
- an application for an extension of an authorization to remain in Canada as a temporary resident
- an application that is made in Canada for a work or study permit or for renewal of such a permit
- an application for the restoration of temporary resident status
- an application that is made pursuant to a youth mobility arrangement entered into by Canada
Therefore, the study permit extension application must be submitted online in advance of the expiry date on the current study permit for maintained status to begin while the extension application processes. Maintained status is an extension of the period of authorized stay as a temporary resident if they have applied to extend their period of authorized stay before it ends. As indicated in our operational instructions and guidelines, the date and time of receipt are important for determining if status is maintained under subsection R183(5). For electronic applications, the department uses Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) around the world to ensure that time is equal for all. Therefore, receipt dates and times do not depend on time zones; all applications must be submitted before midnight UTC on the date the applicant's status expires. If the application was received after midnight UTC on the date of expiry, the applicant does not maintain their status under subsection R183(5).
This means that to benefit from maintained status, an electronic application must be received in the system, regardless of the system used.

Response: They must be a full-time student both before and after a regularly scheduled break to work full-time during the break. In this situation they can only work up to 20 hours per week during the break. If the spring/summer period is not a regularly scheduled break, then students authorized to work off-campus can only do so up to 20 hours per week.
2. 2. If a deferral is approved by the school and they issued a new letter of acceptance, can the student come to Canada with their previous IRCC letter of introduction which is still valid? Response: To enter Canada, they must have a valid port of entry letter of introduction from IRCC and the original and updated letter of acceptance from the same DLI. As long as they will be attending the same DLl, they do not need to reapply for a study permit. If a student changes their program of study to a different DLl after their visa is issued, they need to submit a new study permit application to IRCC. Students should immediately submit their new LOA to IRCC using the online web form if they made any changes to their program of study within the same DLl or to a different DLI while their study permit application is still in process.

If they have a new passport, they do not need to change their study permit until it expires.
4. 4. Given it is a new application for IRCC portal application instead of study permit extension, do they have maintained status? Response: Regardless of the system used, if IRCC received a complete application before the expiry date of their previous document, they would have maintained status until a decision is made on the new application. On this page [https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-manuals/temporary-residents/study-permits/making-application.htmi](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-manuals/temporary-residents/study-permits/making-application.htmi), it is written: "Students participating in exchange programs are only eligible to work off campus if they hold a study permit. The processing officer must include the appropriate work authorization conditions when issuing a study permit to exchange students." This clearly stipulate that an exchange student holding a study permit is allowed to work off campus, even if the exchange is less then 6 months.
However, to my knowledge, this authorization to work off campus is not mentioned anywhere else on IRCC websites. Therefore, I would like to have a confirmation if exchange student holding a study permit are allowed to work off campus. If yes, I would like to know if it's mention anywhere else on IRCC websites.
threads.answer:
Exchange students are students who have been admitted to an institution as visiting students. However, they are not subject to any tuition fees from their host institution, as these fees are covered by an exchange agreement between the host and home institutions. In most cases, exchange students do not require a study permit, since their length of stay is usually less than 6 months. However, they may still apply for a study permit. For programs of 6 months or longer in duration, exchange students must apply for a study permit. Students participating in exchange programs are eligible to work off campus only if they hold a study permit. The processing officer must include the appropriate work authorization conditions when issuing a study permit to exchange students.
While a study permit is not required for short-term courses, an officer must accept and process an application for a study permit, even when the duration of the course or program of study is 6 months or less [R188(2)].
For more information, please visit our website <[https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-manuals/temporary-residents/study-permits/making-application.html](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-manuals/temporary-residents/study-permits/making-application.html)>.

If the dependent (Person B) of a principal applicant (Person A) under the Canadian Experience Class (CEC) is married to someone else (Person C), and C is living outside of Canada.
