threads.answer:
A person, who is married to a third party, may be considered a common-law partner (dependent) of a principal applicant, if they meet certain conditions. Persons who are married to third parties may be considered common-law partners provided their marriage has broken down and they have lived separate and apart from their spouse for at least one year, during which time they must have cohabited in a conjugal relationship with the common-law partner. Cohabitation with a common-law partner can only be considered to have stārted once a physical separation from the spouse has occurred. A common-law relationship cannot be legally established if one or both parties continue to maintain a conjugal relationship with a person to whom they remain legally married.
Please be advised that the assessment of an application is based on a case-by-case basis, considering the particular circumstances in conjunction with the supporting documentation available to the officer. The onus is always on the applicant to provide sufficient documentation to satisfy an officer that they meet the requirements.

threads.answer:
Dear Fran,
Thank you for your correspondence on October 15, 2024.
In general, IRCC cannot issue status documents beyond the validity of a client's passport or travel document, or if their passport or travel document has expired. With that in mind, IRCC is aware of the difficulty and delays Ukrainian clients are experiencing in regard to renewing their passports.
The Embassy of Ukraine to Canada (Ottawa, ON) and Consulates General of Ukraine (Toronto, ON; Edmonton, AB) continue to provide consular support and services to Ukrainian nationals living in Canada, including passport extension services. Ukrainian nationals may extend the validity of their passports by up to 5 years beyond the original expiry date via an ink stamp. Such passports remain valid for applications for temporary residence extension, permanent residence, and travel to Canada. For more information, please visit Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Ukraine website MFA-E-Cherha.
Generally, all foreign nationals applying for permanent or temporary residency in Canada are required to provide a valid passport or travel document as per Section 52 the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR). However, if
applicants cannot meet these requirements due to compelling and exceptional circumstances, the Minister and delegated
decision-makers may consider their situations on a case-by-case basis. The onus would be on the applicant to provide an explanation or evidence relating to their situation to support why they are unable to provide a valid passport or travel document. Officers may consider issuing a temporary resident permit if the Ukrainian national does not meet the requirement under section R52 to hold a valid passport or travel document.
Foreign nationals with legal temporary resident status in Canada are responsible for adhering to the conditions of their entry, including timely application for status extension or restoration, and compliance with entry conditions. If clients apply before the expiry date of their temporary resident status in Canada, they can continue working or studying with maintained status until IRCC makes a decision on their application.
If a temporary resident has lost their status or let their authorization to work or study expire, they may apply to restore that status in accordance with Section 182 of IRPR. Foreign nationals have 90 days from the date they lose their temporary resident status to apply for restoration of temporary resident status. To apply to restore their status, they must meet the requirements outlined under Section 182 of IRPR. If they do not meet the above requirements, clients may wish to consult IRCC website, including this guide for information on applying to remain in Canada as a temporary resident permit holder.
For more information, please visit Immigration measures and support for Ukrainians and their families and Ukraine immigration measures: Contact us
Sincerely, Immigration Representatives Mailbox

Question Pour les permis de travail dans la catégorie Professionnelle sous l'Accord de libre-échange Canada-Colombie (ALECC), comment IRCC évalue si le demandeur possède les permis d’exercice d’une profession au Canada? Comment IRCC détermine si la personne possède un permis d’exercice pour une profession dans le cadre des demandes de permis de travail professionnel sous l’ALECC? Est-ce que cette même exemption s’applique pour les permis de travail professionnel sous l'ALECC?
Réponse
Professions réglementées
Pour être éligible à un emploi dans la catégorie professionnelle de l'ALECC, les attentes suivantes seront revues :
Les employeurs qui embauchent un travailleur étranger pour une profession réglementée au Canada doivent s’assurer que des dispositions sont prises auprès de l’organisme de réglementation approprié pour la certification ou l'inscription du travailleur étranger ou l’octroi d’un permis à ce dernier. Une profession réglementée est une profession pour laquelle un organisme professionnel ou de réglementation a l’autorité d’établir des exigences d’entrée et des normes de pratique menant à la certification l’inscription ou l’octroi d’un permis (par exemple, les métiers spécialisés à qualification obligatoire).
Il est de la responsabilité de l’employeur et du travailleur d’obtenir les documents nécessaires pour
Infomt
inon pratiquer au Canada. Aux fins de la délivrance d’un permis de travail, (IRCC) doit être convaincu que le travailleur qualifié est capable de faire le travail qui lui est offert. IRCC vérifiera si le travailleur qualifié détient l’accréditation ou le permis requis pour exercer une profession réglementée au Canada. Si le demandeur n’a pas d’accréditation ou de permis, IRCC évaluera s’il sera vraisemblablement admissible à une accréditation une fois au Canada avant de délivrer un permis de travail.
Lorsqu’il évalue une offre d’emploi aux fins de la délivrance d'un visa de résident permanent, IRCC doit être convaincu que les travailleurs qualifiés sont aptes à exercer les fonctions du poste offert, et qu’ils vont probablement accepter et occuper ce poste. (source)
Nous espérons que ces informations vous seront utiles.
Cordialement,

Par exemple pour la CNP 11110 – Vérificateur et Comptable, on exige que la personne possède l'accréditation d'une organisation provinciale ou régionale (CPA, CG, CMA, etc.).

Il revient à l'employeur au Canada et au professionnel de s’assurer avant le début de la période d’emploi que les exigences à cet égard sont respectées.
Est-ce que cette même exemption s’applique pour les permis de travail professionnel sous l'ALECC?

threads.subject: The need to apply for restoration of status while applying for the PGWP 90 days after graduation-REP-2024- 1921 -Due 7-Nov-24
threads.answer:
Hello,
Thank you for your email correspondence to 's Immigration Representatives mailbox. We appreciate your patience. Note that this service provides guidance and not case-specific advice.
Please find the answers to your questions below:
Questions
1. 1. Do applicants need to apply for restoration of status if they apply for the PGWP 90 days after graduation because their study permit becomes invalid 90 days after completing the studies?
2. 2. Applying for a PĠWP 90 days after graduation with an invalid study permit renders the applicant unable to work in Canada while awaiting a decision on their PGWP application. What are the other implications of having an invalid study permit?
Responses
1. 1. IRPR does indicate that under R222(1) a Study Permit becomesinvalid 90 days after completing the study program or on the day it expires or is cancelled, whichever comes first', however, it is important to note that the FN retains their status and authority to study for the full duration of this document even though the original program of study may have been completed. For example, despite having completed their original program of study, the FN could decide to continue studying in a different program or even at a different school, on the merits of their original document all the while submitting an updated study permit application for consideration. They also remain eligible to submit their Post Grad Work Permit application on the merits of their SP as long as at time of application the document was not expired. In this scenario, they do not require restoration.
2. 2. If the FN submits their PGWP application before the document expires then they meet the expectations of R199 and are entitled to continue working as per R186(w) until a decision is made on the PGWP application. The following eligibility requirements for a WP are highlighted below: In Canada – study permit is valid
Information disclosed under theAcessto InformationAct Study permits are generally issued for 90 days longer than the expected end date of the program. However, international students are provided 180 days from the completion of their studies to apply for a PGWP. Applicants must maintain their status in Canada and their ability to apply from within Canada under section R199.
Applicants may apply for a PGWP from within Canada if their study permit is still valid (not expired) or if they meet one of the other requirements of section R199 at the time they submit their application.
Applicants who apply for their work permit while their study permit remains valid may be authorized to work without a permit pending a decision on the work permit application under paragraph R186(w). (source)
For more information, please consult the following webpages:
Post-graduation work permit (PGWP) [R205(c) - C43] — International Mobility Program-Canada.ca
We hope this information is of assistance. Do not hesitate to reach out again if you required further clarification.
Sincerely,
Immigration Representatives Mailbox
De : Envoyé : 9 octobre 2024 16:29 À: Objet : RE: The need to apply for restoration of status while applying for the PGWP 90 days after graduation
As per R222(1), a study permit becomes invalid 90 days after completing the study program or on the day it expires or is cancelled, whichever comes first.
Students have up to 180 days after graduation to apply for a Post-Graduation Work Permit (PGWP).
A study permit must be valid (not expired) when graduates submit their applications to be eligible to work in Canada while awaiting a decision on their PGWP application.
Applying for a PGWP 90 days after graduation makes the study permit invalid, which means the applicant cannot work in Canada while awaiting a decision on their PGWP application.
My understanding is that PGWP applicants must apply for restoration of status only if their study permit has expired. However, there is no need to apply for restoration of status if applying for the PGWP while the study permit has become invalid but not expired.

threads.answer:
Attachments:
Hello,
Thank you for your email correspondence to Immigration, Refugee 's Immigration Representatives Mailbox.
QUESTION: I'm an authorized representative as per A91(2) and would like to seek clarification regarding IRPR Subsection 220.1(1), which outlines the conditions for holders of study permits in Canada. Specifically, I'm interested in understanding the implications of a situation where a student, after receiving a study permit from a Designated Learning Institution (DLl), is unable to begin their program as planned due to delays in the permit issuance. If a student needs to delay the start of their program by more than six months from the permit issuance date but the study permit remains valid for another two years, would they be required to apply for a new study permit to pursue a new course of study, or can they proceed with the current permit? For additional context, the student either holds a valid work permit during this period or has left Canada to return to their home country and plans to re-enter before the new program start date.
RESPONSE: Thank you for your enquiry. Please consider the information provided as general program guidance and not a directive for case-specific enquires. In exceptional circumstances, a student may be required to defer their program's start date to the next semester. If the student defers their program start date, it should be formally approved by the DLI. In some cases, the deferral is imposed by the DLI.
If the study permit holder is in Canada at the time of deferral, and they wish to remain in Canada, they must begin their studies the following semester or within 150 days from the date the deferred enrolment is confirmed, whichever comes
first. Otherwise, they should do either of the following:
* change their status (to visitor status or worker status)
- * leave Canada
Note: In all deferral cases, students should obtain an updated letter of acceptance from the DLI.
If they change their status or leave Canada, they are considered compliant with their study permit conditions.
- * If the student changes their status to visitor or worker, they may resume their studies, using their previous study permit, as long as the study permit is valid.
- * If they leave Canada, they may be able to re-enter Canada as an international student if they have a valid study permit and can demonstrate to the border services officer at the Port of Entry that they meet all the requirements. •* Please see international students travelling outside Canada and then re-entering for more information.
and Cizenship Canedaot Citoyenneté Canada
If they do not change their status or leave Canada, they are considered non-compliant with their study permit
conditions, which may result in:
* a removal order (exclusion order) issued for non-compliance, per subparagraph R228(1)(c)(v), or
- * impacts to the outcome of any future applications.
Please visit our website for additional information on Deferred enrolment and Your conditions as a study permit holder in Canada-Canada.ca
We hope that this information will assist you.

threads.answer:
Good day
Thank you for reaching out to IRCC.
Under the Temporary public policy for nationals of Israel and the Palestinian Territories who are in Canada as temporary residents, Israeli nationals and Palestinian passport holders with valid temporary resident status who are currently in Canada are eligible to apply for a fee-exempt open work permit (new or extension), study permit (new or extension), or visitor record (to extend status as a visitor). Whether or not they hold additional citizenship does not affect their eligibility under this temporary public policy; however, the must apply using their travel document issued by Israel or the Palestinian authorities to be eligible for these measures. By applying for a new study permit or open work permit, it is understood that clients are applying for an extension of their authorization to remain in Canada as a temporary resident under section 181 of the Regulations.
Clients should ensure to upload a copy of their proof of Israeli or Palestinian passport when completing an application. Dual citizens may also provide a copy of their non-Israeli or non-Palestinian passport that is associated to their valid temporary resident status document, if applicable. As per the instructions found at Measures for Israeli nationals, Palestinian passport holders and family members in Canada, clients must upload the photo or identification page of their passport or travel document and a letter that states “I am exempt from paying application fees under the ISR/PSE2023 special measures."
Please bear in mind that foreign nationals eligible under this public policy are subject to all other legislative obligations and admissibility and selection requirements not exempted under this, or another, public policy.

Response:
As a study permit holder, you must:
•* be enrolled at a designated learning institution (DLl), unless you're exempt
- * show you're actively pursuing your studies, unless you're exempt, by o * being enrolled full-time or part-time during each academic semester (excluding regularly scheduled breaks) o * making progress towards completing your program's courses, and o * not taking authorized leaves longer than 150 days from your study program
* tell us any time you change post-secondary schools

- * leave Canada when your permit expires
Scheduled breaks are not considered leave from studies. To be considered a regularly scheduled break, the break must be part of the DLl's academic calendar (for instance, winter and summer holidays, Reading Week). Any leave taken outside of a scheduled break from a program of study in Canada should not exceed 150 days from the date the leave commenced and must be authorized by their Designated Learning Institution. If a student does not resume their studies within 150 days, they are considered non-compliant with their study permit conditions.
If a student does not meet their conditions as a study permit holder in Canada, they must:
* change their status (to visitor status or worker status)
- * leave Canada
If they change their status or leave Canada, they are consider compliant with their study permit conditions.
For PGWP eligibility requirements including taking leave from your studies, please see our website: PGWP eligibility criteria
Assessment of an application is based on a case-by-case basis, considering the particular circumstances in conjunction with the supporting documentation available to the officer. The onus is always on the applicant to provide sufficient documentation to satisfy an officer that they meet the requirements.

Hello
Thank you for your email correspondence to Immigration, Refugee 's Immigration Representatives Mailbox. Please consider the information provided as general program guidance and not a directive for case-specific enquires.
Foreign nationals with legal temporary resident status in Canada are responsible for adhering to the conditions of their entry, including timely application for status extension or restoration, and compliance with entry conditions. If a temporary resident applies for a status extension before the expiry date of their temporary resident status in Canada, they can continue working or studying with maintained status until IRCC makes a decision on their application.
Generally, all foreign nationals applying for permanent or temporary residency in Canada are required to provide a valid passport or travel document as per Section 52 the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR). However, if
applicants cannot meet these requirements due to compelling and exceptional circumstances, the Minister and delegated
decision-makers may consider their situations on a case-by-case basis. The onus would be on the applicant to provide an explanation or evidence relating to their situation to support why they are unable to provide a valid passport or travel document.
If a temporary resident has lost their status or let their authorization to work or study expire, they may apply to restore that status in accordance with Section 182 of IRPR. Foreign nationals have 90 days from the date they lose their temporary resident status to apply for restoration of temporary resident status. To apply to restore their status, they must meet the requirements outlined under Section 182 of IRPR.
If they do not meet the above requirements, clients may wish to consult IRCC website, including this guide for information on applying to remain in Canada as a temporary resident permit holder. Officers may consider issuing a temporary resident permit (TRP) if a foreign national does not meet the requirement under section R52 to hold a valid passport or travel document.
Per section A24, the issuance of a TRP document confers temporary resident status to the holder. As such, a TRP cannot be issued to a foreign national with a valid status. Therefore, the foreign national must be out of status to be eligible for a TRP.
Foreign nationals who have been issued a TRP for a validity period of at least 6 months can apply in Canada for a work permit. Please see the following link for more information: Temporary resident permits (TRPs): Eligibility and assessment-Canada.ca
Further information about the Immigration measures and support for Ukrainians and their families is available on the IRCC website.

threads.question:
Dear ImmRep,
I am writing to confirm IRCC's definition of affiliate with respect to establishing whether two entities are affiliated for the purposes of an intra-company transferee work permit.
As you know, one of IRCC's definitions of affiliate is: one of two legal entities, owned and controlled by the same group of individuals, each individual owning and controlling approximately the same share or proportion of each company.
In my client's case, the foreign company (XYZ Foreign Inc) has two shareholders (Person A and Person B) with the shares split 50/50. On the other hand, the Canadian company (XYZ Canada Inc) has two shareholders (Person A and different individual, Person C) with a 95/5 split in favour of Person A, who owns 50% of XYZ Foreign Inc. Person A controls and directs both XYZ Foreign Inc and XYZ Canada Inc.
Since IRCC defines affiliate companies as those " ...owned and controlled by the same group of individuals....[with]
each individual owning and controlling approximately the same share or proportion of each company," would the above-mentioned share structure satisfy the affiliate requirements or must the share breakdown be approximately the same in each company?
Put differently, are three individuals (Person A, B, And C) required to hold shares in both XYZ Foreign Inc. and XYZ Canada Inc. with approximately the same proportion of shares. Or does an affiliate relationship exist so long as one individual has a controlling interest (e.g., Person A has a controlling interest in both XYZ Foreign Inc and XYZ Canada Inc) notwithstanding the fact that the two entities have a different mix of shareholders (I.e., Person A & B in Foreign Company vs Person A and C in Canadian company).
Thank you. Get Outlook for Android
threads.answer:
Hello,
Thank you for your question. Please note that we cannot answer case-specific questions but have provided the following
information as guidance.
Question
I am writing to confirm IRCC's definition of affiliate with respect to establishing whether two entities are affiliated for the
purposes of an intra-company transferee work permit.
As you know, one of IRCC's definitions of affiliate is: one of two legal entities, owned and controlled by the same group of
individuals, each individual owning and controlling approximately the same share or proportion of each company.
In my client's case, the foreign company (XYZ Foreign Inc) has two shareholders (Person A and Person B) with the shares split 50/50. On the other hand, the Canadian company (XYZ Canada Inc) has two shareholders (Person A and different individual, Person C) with a 95/5 split in favour of Person A, who owns 50% of XYZ Foreign Inc. Person A controls and directs both XYZ
Foreign Inc and XYZ Canada Inc.
Since IRCC defines affiliate companies as those " ...owned and controlled by the same group of individuals.[with] each individual owning and controlling approximately the same share or proportion of each company," would the above- mentioned share structure satisfy the affiliate requirements or must the share breakdown be approximately the same in each company? Put differently, are three individuals (Person A, B, And C) required to hold shares in both XYZ Foreign Inc. and XYZ Canada Inc. with approximately the same proportion of shares. Or does an affiliate relationship exist so long as one individual has a controlling interest (e.g., Person A has a controlling interest in both XYZ Foreign Inc and XYZ Canada Inc) notwithstanding the fact that the two entities have a different mix of shareholders (I.e., Person A & B in Foreign Company vs Person A and C in Canadian company).
Proposed Response
As you have correctly noted, for IRCC, one of the definitions of affiliate is "one of two legal entities, owned and controlled by the same group of individuals, each individual owning and controlling approximately the same share or proportion of each company."
As per the publicly available instructions for officers on intra-company transferees, "ownership" means the right of possession with full power and authority to control, and "control” means the right and authority to direct management and operations of the enterprise.
In the case you have described, any of the three individuals (Person A, B, And C) who exert ownership or control of XYZ Foreign Inc. must also exert ownership or control of XYZ Canada Inc. The individuals who own and control these 2 companies are required to hold shares in both XYZ Foreign Inc. and XYZ Canada Inc. with approximately the same proportion of shares in order for it to qualify an “affiliate”.
For more information, please consult Intra-company transferees (ICT) -[R205(a) - C61, C62, C63] - Canadian interests-International Mobility Program
Citoyenneté Canada
Thank you. The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

From # Bonjour,
Une société étrangère a transféré un employé au Canada en vertu d’une offre d’emploi soumise sur le portail de l’employeur. La durée de l’emploi requise est de 3 ans. Toutefois, le permis de travail a été émis pour une période plus courte, vu l’expiration prochaine du passeport du travailleur. Le travailleur a reçu son nouveau passeport valide pour 10 ans. Est-ce que nous pouvons demander la prorogation du permis de travail du travailleur en nous basant sur la même offre d’emploi? Dans la négative, autrement dit, au cas où nous devons soumettre une nouvelle offre d’emploi, est-ce que nous pouvons avoir le fondement juridique car l’information ne semble pas être disponible en ligne.
Je vous remercie d’avance pour votre assistance et je reste à votre disposition pour toute information ou clarification.
Cordialement,
and Citizenship Caneda
threads.answer:
Bonjour,
Merci de contacter la boîte électronique des représentants de l'immigration.
Ces renseignements sont fournis à titre d'orientation générale et ne constituent pas une directive pour des dossiers individuels. Pour des demandes de renseignements sur des cas spécifiques, les demandeurs peuvent contacter le Ministère en soumettant le Formulaire Web d'IRCC.
Question: Une société étrangère a transféré un employé au Canada en vertu d’une offre d’emploi soumise sur le portail de l’employeur. La durée de l’emploi requise est de 3 ans. Toutefois, le permis de travail a été émis pour une période plus courte, vu l’expiration prochaine du passeport du travailleur. Le travailleur a reçu son nouveau passeport valide pour 10 ans. Est-ce que nous pouvons demander la prorogation du permis de travail du travailleur en nous basant sur la même offre d’emploi? Dans la négative, autrement dit, au cas où nous devons soumettre une nouvelle offre d’emploi, est-ce que nous pouvons avoir le fondement juridique car l’information ne semble pas être disponible en ligne.
Je vous remercie d’avance pour votre assistance et je reste à votre disposition pour toute information ou clarification
Réponse : Une nouvelle offre d’emploi et des frais de conformité de l’employeur sont exigés. Le paragraphe 52(1) du Règlement sur l’immigration et la protection des réfugiés (RIPR) exige que « En plus de remplir les autres exigences réglementaires, l’étranger qui cherche à devenir résident temporaire doit détenir l’un des documents suivants, valide pour la période de séjour autorisée : a) un passeport »
Les étrangers doivent avoir un passeport valide qui couvre toute la durée de leur séjour. Un permis de travail ne peut être délivré pour une période supérieure à la validité du passeport, quelle que soit la durée de l’offre d’emploi. Lorsque le permis de travail est délivré, les conditions imposées à l’employeur ne sont en vigueur que pour la durée du permis de travail.
Pour délivrer ou prolonger un permis de travail en vertu du R200(1)(c)(ii.1), il doit y avoir une « offre ». L’offre initiale a été utilisée lors de la délivrance du premier permis de travail –le fait que la durée totale de l’offre n’ait pas été indiquée dans le permis de travail n’a aucune incidence sur le fait que l’offre a été utilisée. Conformément au R200(3)(f.1), un agent ne peut pas délivrer un permis de travail à un ressortissant étranger qui présente une demande en vertu du R200(1)(c)(ii.1) si les frais de conformité de l’employeur n’ont pas été payés ou si l’offre d’emploi n’a pas été soumise avant que l’étranger ne présente une demande de permis de travail. Par conséquent, une nouvelle offre est requise sur la base de la prolongation du permis de travail.
Conformément à l’article 303.1 du RIPR (plus précisément les exceptions 303.1(4.1) et 303.1(5)), un permis de travail qui n’est pas délivré pour la durée demandée n’est pas l’une des raisons pour lesquelles une exception aux frais peut s’appliquer. Le R303.1(1)(c) exige spécifiquement que les frais soient payés si l’offre est faite à un ressortissant étranger qui présente une demande de renouvellement de permis de travail (concernant le travail décrit au R204 ou R205). L’employeur devra soumettre une nouvelle offre d’emploi et le paiement des frais de conformité de l’employeur pour la demande de prolongation du client.
and Citizenshi Canada et Ciloyeneé Canada
Cordialement, Adresse électronique des représentants de l'immigration

With regards to your question, if a visitor applies for an initial (first-ever) work permit using an “outside-of-Canada" application from inside Canada, they will not be issued a TRV from inside Canada by CPC-O. permit, and TRV (as required).

The VAC for that country can confirm with certainty and may request specific information (for ex., the client may be required to state clearly on their application why they have not applied in their normal country of residence).

threads.question:
We are writing to seek clarification on R188(1)(c) which provides the authority for foreign nationals to attend a course or program of study without a study permit. Questions/Clarifications Required:
- * How is course defined?
- * Would general English classes to learn more vocabulary, grammar, and practice speaking with 20 hours per week of attendance with no definite time frame or duration (register whenever convenient) be considered as a course?
- * Because such classes do not have a set duration, it is unclear to us how the 6 months are calculated if the foreign national has an authorized stay of more than 6 months.
threads.answer:
- * The course of study may be part-time or full-time and should be completed within the period authorized upon entry (that is, up to 6 months).
- * English Second Language (ESL) courses, even those for self-improvement purposes, can be considered as courses under the study permit exemption, provided they meet the duration requirements.
- * The duration of the course or program of study is often a more important consideration than the number of months the foreign national intends to study. With the exception of exchange programs, if the course or program itself is longer than 6 months, a study permit is required, even if the foreign national plans to study for 6 months or less.
For more information on the activities that are not considered studies and do not require a study permit visit our webpage: Study permits: Who needs a study permit
We hope that this information is helpful to you.
Thank you,

threads.subject: Query re new ICT guidelines on requiring physical commercial premises-REP-2024-1927 - Due 8-Nov-24
threads.question: Under the update October 3 guidelines for ICTs under 205(a), the guidelines set out that, to use this ICT category, the Canadian entity must have “physical commercial premises.” The new FTA ICT guidelines do NOT include that language. There is no reference in the FTA ICT guidelines that the Canadian related entity needs to have “physical commercial premises” in Canada. Can you confirm that. Does this mean that the Canadian operation could be a remote operation e.g have no physical office space?I understand that this would still have to be justified e.g. if it is a remote model, why does the TFW need to be in Canada.
threads.answer:
Under the expectations of R204(a), the enterprise in Canada does not need to have ‘physical commercial premises' in order to qualify for a work permit under the ICT category. As you noted, the Canadian operation could be a remote operation, but the test would be from one operation to another – if there is no physical presence in Canada, there may not be a need for an ICT. The onus is on the applicant to demonstrate that a work permit is required for them to complete their duties in Canada on behalf of the enterprise.
The FTAs provisions recognize that an enterprise could be incorporated with revenue and income generating within Canada without having a brick and mortar' presence.
We hope this information is of assistance. Do not hesitate to reach out again if you required further clarification.
Sincerely,

Bonjour,
Question : D'une manière générale, si une personne remplit les conditions pour être admissible à la politique d'intérêt public permettant à certains titulaires de permis de travail d'étudier sans permis d'études, mais vient à demander un nouveau permis de travail pour prolonger son séjour, la personne peut-elle continuer d'étudier sans permis d'études jusqu'à l'expiration de son permis de travail actuel (malgré la demande de prolongation du permis de travail en cours)?
Réponse : Une personne visée par cette politique d’intérêt public peut étudier sans permis d'études en fonction de son permis de travail initial ou de la prolongation de permis de travail qui a été soumise le ou avant le 7 juin 2023. Ces personnes ont la première des trois dates suivante pour étudier :
- la date d'expiration de leur permis de travail approuvé ou de la prolongation du permis de travail;
- la date à laquelle nous refusons leur demande de prolongation de permis de travail; ou
- le 27 juin 2026 (date d’expiration de cette politique d’intérêt public).
Il s'agit d'une mesure temporaire et unique qui ne s'appliquerait pas aux personnes qui demandent une prolongation de permis de travail après la date du 7 juin 2023.
Si ces clients souhaitent continuer à étudier après l'expiration de leur permis de travail, ils doivent demander un permis d'études.

threads.subject: Clarification on 6-Month Work Experience Requirement for Express Entry Occupation-Based Selection-REP- 2024-2080 - Due 26-Nov-24
threads.question:
I am writing to seek clarification on the 6-month work experience requirement for the occupation-based selection under the Express Entry program.
The eligibility criteria specify that applicants must have accumulated, within the past three years, a minimum of six months of continuous, full-time work experience (or an equivalent amount of part-time work) in a single occupation listed in the table, either in Canada or abroad.
My specific question pertains to the interpretation of this requirement for work experience gained in Canada, particularly whether experience acquired under a Co-op work permit is considered valid or not.
I understand that for the Canadian Experience Class, Canadian work experience gained while on a Co-op work permit is not eligible. However, under the Federal Skilled Workers Program, Co-op work experience is recognized if it is paid, as indicated here:([https://www.ircc.canada.ca/english/helpcentre/answer.asp?qnum=394&top=29](https://www.ircc.canada.ca/english/helpcentre/answer.asp?qnum=394&top=29)).
According to the guidelines here: [https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-) manuals/operational-bulletins-manuals/permanent-residence/express-entry/assessing-electronic-application-on-section- a11-2.html#decision, it seems that the same definitions applied in the FSW are used to assess the 6-month work experience requirement under occupation-based selection. However, I would like to confirm whether compasated Co-op work experience is also considered eligible here.
threads.answer:
Please be advised that each round of invitation under the Category Based Selection (CBS) has it's own set of Ministerial Instructions attached to it. These instructions define who is eligible to be invited in a particular round.
At the moment, selection criteria for CBS rounds does not disqualify work experience obtained while being a full-time student, meaning that work experience gained as a full-time student in Canada may be eligible under CBS if all the other requirements are met.
However, to make a successful application for Permanent Residence under the Category Based Selection, the applicant must also meet the minimum criteria for Express Entry, including being eligible for 1 of the 3immigration programs it covers and meet all of the requirements in the instructions for that round of CBS.
For example, to qualify under the Canadian Experience Class minimum entry criteria described under Section 87.1 of Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR) has to be met.
Subsection 87.1(3) specifically describes work experience obtained while being a full-time student or working as self- employed as ineligible. Thus, even though experience obtained while being a ull-time student in Canada may count towards CBS, the same experience will not be eligible under the Canadian Experience Class.
Please be advised that the assessment of an application is based on a case-by-case basis, considering the particular circumstances in conjunction with the supporting documentation available to the officer. The onus is always on the applicant to provide sufficient documentation to satisfy an officer that they meet the requirements.
We trust that this information will assist you.
Sincerely,
Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.subject: for approval please-FW: Clarification on SUV refusals due to CC submission by DEs-REP-2024-1813 - Due 28-Oct-24
threads.answer:
Hello,
Thank you for your email correspondence to 's Immigration Representatives mailbox. We apologize for the delay and appreciate your patience.
Please see our response to your enquiry, below:
IRCC's current operational practice, informed by its interpretation of R98.04(1), requires that the CC be received by IRCC from the DE as part of the application process, particularly at the time the PR application is being assessed. You will find our Program Delivery Instructions (PDI) relating to this here: Economic classes: Procedures at the Centralized Intake Office for applications (non-Express Entry) - Canada.ca
While R98.04(1) mandates that the commitment must be made by a person authorized to bind the DE, the requirement for when and how the CC must be received stems from IRCC's operational guidance, the PDI, rather than the regulatory text itself. According to this guidance, it is essential that the CC is submitted by the DE directly to IRCC as part of the completeness check for the SUV PR application, prior to or at the time ofthe PR application submission.
Regarding the past practice of issuing Procedural Fairness Letters (PFLs) and allowing DEs to resend the CC in response to these letters, IRCC’s policy and procedures have been refined to enhance the completeness and transparency of the process. If the CC is not received by IRCC in a timely manner, the PR application may be deemed incomplete, resulting in a possible reje ction. The interpretation that the DE must provide the CC directly and in a timely fashion aligns with IRCC's overall goal of ensuring the integrity and accountability of the SUV program
While the regulation itself does not specify a clear timeframe, IRCC's operational guidelines fill that gap by establishing that the CC must be available at the time the application is being reviewed for completeness. It is this procedural requirement, rather than the strict wording of R98.04(1), that forms the basis for refusals when CCs are not received in time.
We understand that this may cause some concern among applicants, particularly in cases where CCs have been present in response to PFLs, but applications were still refused. It is recommended that applicants ensure the DE submits the CC directly to IRCC in advance or concurrently with the PR application to avoid such outcomes.
Please be advised that the assessment of an application is based on a case-by-case basis, considering the particular circumstances in conjunction with the supporting documentation available to the officer. The onus is always on the applicant to provide sufficient documentation to satisfy an officer that they meet the requirements.
Kind regards,

De : Envoye : 26 septembre 2024 16:43 À : Objet : Clarification on SUV refusals due to CC submission by DEs
Hello,
We have observed an increasing number ofStart-up Visa (SUV) application refusals based on the ground that Commitment Certificates (CCs) were not received by IRCC from the Designated Entities (DEs) at the time of application submission. These refusals frequently cite R98.04(1) as the legal basis. For your convenience, this section states:
\fi720Form of commitment
\fi72098.04 (1) A commitment must be in a written or electronic form that is acceptable to the Minister and must be provided by a person who has the authority to bind the designated entity.
This provision does not explicitly require the CC to be submitted by the DE directly to IRCC, nor does it specify a timeline for when the CC must be provided in relation to the PR application. The regulation only requires that the commitment be made by a person authorized to bind the DE, without defining to whom or by when the CC must be submitted.
Even assuming an interpretation that the DE must submit the CC to IRCC, R98.04(1) does not establish a specific deadline, such as requiring the CC to be received at the time ofthe PR application submission.
In past practice, we have seen IRCC issue PFLs requesting proof that the CC was submitted by the DE. However, in several instances where applicants had requested the DE to resend the CC directly to IRCC in response to the PFL, their applications were still refused. This is concerning, as R98.04(1) does not prescribe a specific timeframe for the submission of the CC, even under the interpretation that it must be sent directly to IRCC by the DE.
Could you please clarify the basis for these refusals and confirm the source ofthe specific timeframe for submission of the CC by the DE?
Kindest,

threads.answer:
Good day,
Here is information on on/off campus work and CO-OP, for more information please see the links provided.
- On Campus-Eligible students may use on campus work authorization under their study permit conditions. There is no limit on work hours for on-campus work. Study permits: Working on campus-Canada.ca
- Off campus-Students can work off campus without a work permit [R186(y)]. They can work part time (up to 20 hours a week) during a regular academic session and full time during regularly scheduled breaks between academic sessions. Students who have maintained full-time status for the duration of their program of study, and who only require a part-time course load in their final academic session in order to complete their program of study, are allowed to work full-time during the regularly scheduled break before their last semester and are allowed to work off campus up to 20 hours per week during their final academic session. Study permits: Off-campus work-Canada.ca
- Off Campus & CO-OP-If the DLI considers a co-op student with a co-op work permit to have full-time status during the “work experience" portion of their program, and if the student continues to comply with the eligibility requirements under the co-op work permit program, the student may be eligible to work off campus, pursuant to paragraph R186(y), on top of their co-op work hours. Study permits: Of-campus work-Canada.ca
- CO-OP-Students who intend to perform work that is an essential part of a post-secondary academic, vocational or professional training program offered by a designated learning institution (DLI) in Canada. The work cannot form more than 50% of the total program of study. o Students who are already in Canada and have applied for a co-op work permit may begin their co-op placement using their on-campus and off-campus work authorization, provided they meet all the eligibility requirements. There is no limit on work hours for on-campus work. A student may accept employment on the campus of the university or college at which they are a full-time student under paragraph 186(f) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR). For off-campus work authorization, as per paragraph R186(v), students can work a total of 20 hours per week during an academic term or semester while they are waiting for their co-op work permit; however, the 20 hours must include both the hours worked at their co-op job and those worked at their regular paid job (if they have one). They can work full-time during the regularly scheduled breaks. If the co-op work permit application is refused, they must stop their co-op work immediately. Work related to a research, educational or training progran- exeimption codes C31, C32 and C33 (International Mobility Program) - Canada.ca
NOTE: Students may not work until they have commenced their program of study. They must actually commence studies in Canada at a DLI before being eligible to work. Non-compliance with study permit conditions or the act of working without authorization may result in enforcement action. It may also negatively affect future applications made under the Immigration and
Lon Refugee Protection Act and the IRPR. For example, a subsequent study permit or work permit may not be issued.

Immigraton Representatives / Représentants immigration (IRCC)
Hello,
Please see our response to your question.
QUESTIONS:
- Is there a residency requirement associated with this open work permit category?
- Will IRCC accept an application under this stream if an applicant meets all of the requirements AND does not reside in Canada or Hong Kong? Please confirm whether the Open Work Permit can be submitted by a Hong Kong citizen regardless of their place of residence (ie. they can be resident of a third country other than Canada and Hong Kong).
- Can an applicant who has never resided in Hong Kong apply (as long as they meet all other requirements)?
- Does it matter if an applicant is a dual citizen?
- If non-residents of either Canada and Hong Kong can apply and are eligible (assuming all other criteria are met), are there any additional documents that should be submitted regarding the last time they resided in Hong Kong?
RESPONSE:
Under the Temporary Public Policy to exempt certain Hong Kong residents from work permit requirements, Hong Kong nationals applying for this type of work permit may apply from either inside of Canada or overseas. This public policy took effect on February 9, 2023, and will expire on February 7, 2025. It replaces a previous public policy that was in effect from February 1, 2021, until February 7, 2023.
When a Hong Kong national is applying overseas, they do not have to be resident in Hong Kong in order to do so, nor do they need to have ever resided in Hong Kong. They can be a resident of a third country. Proof of residence is not a requirement to apply under this stream. Our client-facing instructions clearing indicate this (please see here: Public policy: Open work permits for Hong Kong recent graduates-Canada.ca). Eligibility under this stream is limited to someone who holds a valid passport issued by the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region or the United Kingdom to a British National Overseas.
We hope this helps.

threads.question: “ What is the acceptable distance from one another for sponsors under the private sponsorship of refugees-Group of 5?; In the guides, it says that sponsors must "live in the same community where the refugee is expected to settle" but there is no mention of the distance."
threads.answer:
Per paragraph 153(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR), a sponsor must reside or have representatives in the refugee’s expected community of settlement [https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-manuals/refugee-protection/terms-definitions-related-refugee-protection.html#community-settlement](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-manuals/refugee-protection/terms-definitions-related-refugee-protection.html#community-settlement).
In assessing compliance with this regulation, officers will consider the sponsor's ability to provide adequate in-person support to the sponsored refugee. This assessment will take into account the Settlement Plan and any other documentation provided, as well as the vulnerability of the sponsored refugee. There is no maximum or minimum distance defining “community of settlement" as situations vary and there may be situations in which the sponsor does not live directly in the same village, town or city but could be considered to reside in the same general community.
The aim of this assessment is to ensure refugees arriving in Canada have adequate support from their sponsors.
Thank you kindly,

threads.subject: Clarification on Status Following Approvals of Work Permit and Visitor Record-REP-2024-1988 - Due 14- Nov-24
threads.question:
I am seeking clarification regarding the status of a foreign national in Canada under the following circumstances:
If a foreign national applies for a work permit extension while previous work permit was valid, and later apply a visitor record during the maintained status, and their work permit gets approved first, followed by the approval of the visitor record, what would be their status in Canada?
In this scenario, can the foreign national continue working under the newly approved work permit, or does the approval of the visitor record void the new work permit?
threads.answer:
In this scenario, the foreign worker can continue working under the new approved work permit. The visitor record doesn’t override the work permit. Foreign Worker can hold two status at the same tine.
The work permit and visitor record are not connected. The work permit grants the client authorization to work in Canada, this authorization expires on the expiry date listed on the work permit. The visitor record grants the client visitor status, this status expires on the expiry date listed on the visitor record. Before their status expires, applicants should make sure they have applied for a visitor or work permit extension if they wish to continue staying and working in Canada.

threads.subject: Clarification on PGWP Eligibility Requirements for Specific Study Permit Scenarios-REP-2024-2147 - Due 3- Dec-24
threads.answer:
Hello,
Please see our response to your question.
QUESTION:
We are seeking clarification on recent changes to PGWP eligibility, particularly concerning study permit extensions and cases involving program stacking. Your guidance on the following scenarios will help us advise students accurately to ensure compliance with the updated requirements.
Could you clarify the interpretation of“study permit application"” under the new field of study requirements? Specifically, does this term refer only to the initial study permit application, or do extensions submitted after November 1, 2024, also fall under this requirement? Here are the scenarios where additional guidance would be valuable:
1. Study Permit Extensions Submitted After November 1, 2024: If a student extends their study permit after November 1, 2024, for a program not listed in the eligible fields of study, would they be affected by the new PGWP eligibility requirements, even if their initial study permit was submitted before this date?
2. Enrollment in a Second Program Outside Eligible Fields: If a student initially applied for a study permit before November 1, 2024, but later enrolls in a second program (starting in 2025) that does not align with the eligible fields, will their PGWP eligibility remain unaffected due to the original submission date, or could this impact their eligibility?
3. Re-entry Following Withdrawal and Study Permit Extension After November 1, 2024: If a student withdrew from their program, re-entered their studies after November 1, 2024, and then applied for a study permit extension, would this re-entry and extension impact their PGWP eligibility under the updated regulations?
RESPONSE:
All PGWP applications (except those from flight school graduates) submitted on or after November 1, 2024 must comply with the new language requirements, regardless of when the student applied for their study permit or when they started their program of study.
If the student applies for a study permit extension under the same program of study as the study permit they applied for before November 1, 2024, then they do not need to meet the field of study requirement. If the student applies for a study permit extension under a different program of study than the study permit they applied for before November 1, 2024, then their study permit extension application must meet the field of study requirements applicable to their study program to be eligible for a PGWP.

Regularly scheduled break: To be considered a regularly scheduled break, the break must be part of the DLI's academic calendar (for instance, winter and summer holidays, Reading Week). However, if the client receives their e-CoPR while abroad, they must apply for a permanent resident travel document (PRTD) to return to Canada on a commercial carrier (i.e., airplane, boat, train or bus.).

threads.answer:
Good day,
\cbpat2The link that you provided contains information specific to co-op work permits for post-secondary students. A co-op work permit for post-secondary students is not the same as a regular open work permit. Yes, students in co-op placement may work at any employer approved by the DLI for the co-op placement; however, that co-op work must be an essential part of the program that all participants enrolled in that program are required to complete in order to receive their degree, diploma or certificate (and cannot form more than 50% of the total program of study). \cbpat2 \cbpat2The co-op work permit must be linked to the Designated Learning Institution (DLI) where the student is completing their program of studies. However, holders of a valid study permits who have applied for a co-op work permit may begin their co-op placement using their on-campus and off-campus work authorization, provided they meet all the eligibility requirements. \cbpat2 \cbpat2There is no limit on work hours for on-campus work. A student may accept employment on the campus of the university or college at which they are a ful-time student. Under current instructions, for off-campus work, students can work a total of 20 hours per week during an academic term or semester while they are waiting for their co-op work permit; however, the 20 hours must include both the hours worked at their co-op job and those worked at their regular paid job (if they have one). They can work full-time during the regularly scheduled breaks between academic sessions. \cbpat2 \cbpat2Please note: IRCC recently pre-published proposed regulatory amendments which would require, among other conditions, students to obtain a new study permit if they change DLIs. Additionally, these regulations would also increase the maximum number of off-campus work hours to 24 hours. However, these regulations are not yet finalized. \cbpat2
For more information, please refer to: Work related to a research, educational or training program- exemption codes C31, C32 and C33 (International Mobility Program) - Canada.ca and; Work as a co-op student or intern-Canada.ca
We hope this clarifies.

The Super Visa is a multiple-entry temporary resident visa (TRV), issued with a validity ofup to 10 years. The period of authorized stay is 5 years for each entry. If they are/were granted entry into Canada by a BSO, after June 22, 2023, then the foreign national is/was authorized to stay in Canada for 5 years.
As a super visa holder, you should have a valid health insurance policy while in Canada. If your health insurance will expire before you leave Canada, you may need to renew or maintain your health insurance during your stay. Hello,
Thank you for your email correspondence to Immigration, Refugee ’s Immigration Representatives Mailbox.
Please consider the information provided as general program guidance and not a directive for case-specific enquires.
\cbpat2As a study permit holder, you must:
- be enrolled at a designated learning institution (DLI), unless you're exempt
- show you’re actively pursuing your studies, unless you’re exempt, by o being enrolled full-time or part-time during each academic semester (excluding regularly scheduled breaks) o making progress towards completing your program's courses, and o not taking authorized leaves longer than 150 days from your study program
- tell us any time you change post-secondary schools
- end your studies if you no longer meet the requirements of being a student, and
- leave Canada when your permit expires
\cbpat2Scheduled breaks are not considered leave from studies.
\cbpat2To be considered a regularly scheduled break, the break must be part of the DLI's academic calendar (for instance, winter and summer holidays, Reading Week).
Any leave taken outside of a scheduled break from a program of study in Canada should not exceed 150 days from the date the leave commenced and must be authorized by their Designated Learning Institution. If a student does not resume their studies within 150 days, they are considered non-compliant with their study permit conditions.
For more information, please see: Your conditions as a study permit holder in Canada-Canada.ca
We hope this information is helpful.
Thank you kindly,

QUESTION: I am reaching out to clarify the PGWP eligibility requirements for students who changed programs after arriving in Canada but before November 1, 2024, and will apply for a SP extension soon. If a student changed their program before November 1, 2024, and they need a Study Permit extension after November 1, 2024, are they eligible for PGWP based on the old rules?
Example:
A student applied for a Study Permit for Computer Programming Diploma starting on Fall 2023. In Winter 2024 this student changed his program to Early Learning and Child Care Diploma.
He needs to apply for a Study Permit extension soon.
Is this student eligible for PGWP based on the old rules, as Early Learning and Child Care Diploma is not included on the High Demand Occupations list? RESPONSE:
All PGWP applications (except those from flight school graduates) submitted on or after November 1, 2024 must comply with the new language requirements, regardless of when the student applied for their study permit or when they started their program of study.
If the student applies for a study permit extension under the same program of study as the study permit they applied for before November 1, 2024, then they do not need to meet the field of study requirement. If the student applies for a study permit extension under a different program of study than the study permit they applied for before November 1, 2024, then their study permit extension application must meet the field of study requirements applicable to their study program to be eligible for a PGWP.
We have recently updated our website to provide clients with further details on the new PGWP eligibility requirements at the following link: Work in Canada after you graduate: Who can apply-Canada.ca

threads.answer:
Hello,
Please see our response to your question.
QUESTION:
The government of Canada recently announced that the essential members of a Canadian start up who have already submitted their PR applications can now apply for open work permits. I request for your clarification and guidance on the following points:
1. Would such essential members need a valid Letter of Support (LOS) from the Designated Organization to apply for O WP or even could they apply with a LOS which has passed the validity of 6 months?
2. What will be the process to apply for the OWP for the founders who have already secured closed work permits but the closed work permits are still valid for another year or two?

RESPONSE:
With the new SUV open work permit, applicants do not need to have a valid Letter of Support (LOS) when applying, as was the case with the former employer-specific (closed) SUV work permit. As long as the LOS was submitted before it expired when the applicant submitted their permanent resident application, this now suffices for the SUV open work permit (O WP).
If someone currently holds an SUV employer-specific (closed) work permit and they want to apply for the new SUV OWP, they are eligible to apply.
Finally, for your final question, as each application is based on its own merit, if someone were to have their SUV O WP refused, it would not invalidate the client's existing SUV employer-specific (closed) work permit.

threads.subject: Question regarding the validity of visitor records-REP-2024-2158 - Due 4-Dec-24
threads.answer:
Hello,
Thank you for your email correspondence to Immigration, Refugee ’s Immigration Representatives Mailbox.
Question:
We have a question if the visitor record remains valid in this scenario:
The minor child of a Ukrainian national with a 3-year work permit under CUAET holds a visitor record under CUAET measures.
If the minor child exited Canada for s short period of time and returned to Canada, will their visitor record remain valid, and they will be allowed to stay until the expiry date?
Or is it invalidated once the child exited Canada and once, they return they have only a visitor stay of 6 months if no other visitor record is issued or other determination of the CBSA officer?
Approved response:
A foreign national's temporary resident status ends when they leave Canada or when the Visitor Record (VR) expires. Further, as per R183(4)(a) temporary resident status ends the day on which the foreign national leaves Canada, meaning the VR or the stamp in the passport (whether there is a date written under it or not) is irrelevant once they leave. Should the foreign national return to Canada, the Border Services Officer (BSO) will complete an examination and determine the new authorized period of stay. If there is no stamp or handwritten date in the foreign national's passport, their authorized period of stay is 6 months from the date of entry, or the date indicated by the BSO. If the foreign national wishes to remain in Canada beyond the authorized period of stay, they will need to extend their stay.
Please be advised that a foreign national's entry into Canada, is at the discretion of a BSO at a Canadian POE and they have the authority to determine the length of stay that a temporary resident may remain in Canada.
We trust that this information will assist you.
Sincerely,
Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.question:
I would like to obtain advisement from IRCC regarding ability to engage in consulting work remotely for a US-based business while my client is also physically located in Canada and currently has work under a CUSMA closed work permit in Canada.
My client is ancurrently residing in Canada as a foreign worker and employed full-time (30+ hours per week) for a Canadian business. This client has a CUSMA professional work permit with the stipulation that they are not authorized to work for any other employer than the one stated on the work permit.
However, the IRCC website ([https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-)
manuals/operational-bulletins-manuals/temporary-residents/foreign-workers/what-is-work.html) notes that temporary foreign
workers may engage in remote work for other employers outside of Canada (if also remunerated from outside Canada), see screenshot below.
My client has an opportunity to provide some part-time consulting work remotely for a US-based business (this US-based business does not conduct any business in Canada) and her payment would be through ar n the United States.
My client would like to pursue this opportunity, if possible, while also still maintaining the full-time employment in Canada under their work permit. From the IRCC website, it appears that this is allowed. However, my client consulted with their international CPA to see what the potential tax implications would be for this type of arrangement, and my client was advised that any remote work for a US-based business would still be considered “sourced’ in Canada (since it would be conducted remotely from Canada, consulting via internet to the US).
The CPA advised that this consulting income therefore would need to be reported on a Canadian tax return, thus appearing to be Canadian income from another entity other than the sponsor of the work permit (though the consulting work would be US income).
This has caused some confusion as from an Immigration standpoint, she is not working with a Canadian client, not be paid by this part time client, while at the same time she is not entering the labor market in Canada with this client.
Can IRCC please advise if this type of scenario is allowed and would not violate any terms of my client's CUSMA professional work permit?
Thank you in advance for your assistance and any clarification you can provide is appreciated.
threads.answer:
As indicated in the PDI you linked (Temporary Foreign Worker and International Mobility Programs: What is work? - Canada.ca), work done in Canada for an employer who is located outside of Canada and which is remunerated from outside of Canada is not considered work and so no work permit is required. The condition “Not authorized to work for any other employer" is added for clarity to employer-specific work permits and does not apply to activities which IRCC does not consider to be work for the purposes of work permit issuance.
Sincerely,

threads.subject: Work after submitting PGWP -REP-2024-1932 - Due 8-Nov-24
threads.question:
From IRCC website, a student can work full-time while waiting for a decision on their PGWP application if they:
- Had a valid study permit at the time of submitting the application
- Completed their study program
- Were eligible to work off-campus without a work permit during their studies and did not exceed the permitted work hours
Is this "study program" refer to the program that they apply for PGWP? For example, student graduate from program B in Fall 2024 and from program A in Winter 2025. Student does not meet the requirements to apply for PGWP with program A, so they apply for PGWP with program B after Winter 2025. In this case, can student work full-time while waiting for IRCC's decision, provided that they have valid study permit and were eligible to work off campus before?
threads.answer:
Applicants who submit a work permit application after completing their program of study and before their study permit expires may be eligible to work full time under R186(w) until a decision is made on their application. The program of study is whichever program they were authorized to enroll in by their study permit. Note that PGWP eligibility of the program is not a consideration for eligibility under R186(w), only that they met the requirements of R186(v) (i.e. they were eligible to work off-campus) during their studies.
Thank you kindly,

threads.subject: using 186(j) for an employer-specific work permit holder-REP-2024-1968 - Due 13-Nov-24
threads.question:
Can a temporary foreign worker who is in Canada on an employer-specific work permit take advantage of Regulation 186(j) to accept an invitation to act as a guest speaker for a different institution? I.e. they would be paid for the guest speaking engagement of less than 5 days by an institution not listed on their work permit, in a different Canadian location.
I could not find a clear answer to this question upon reviewing the available guidance: [https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-manuals/temporary-residents/foreign-workers/work-without-permit/authorization-work-without-work-permit-public-speakers.html](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-manuals/temporary-residents/foreign-workers/work-without-permit/authorization-work-without-work-permit-public-speakers.html)
threads.answer:
The foreign worker is subject to the conditions on their work permit which could limit the people they can work for and the type of jobs they can work. They may be eligible to work under R186(j) provided they are not in violation of the conditions of their work permit by doing so and they have the appropriate authorization to work.
This tool can help determine if a separate work permit will be required: Find out if you need a work permit-Canada.ca
Furthermore, if the foreign worker is being sent there by their employer and will be paid by their employer, then it would still count as work under their current work permit.
Hope this helps.

Bonjour,
Merci de contacter la boîte électronique des représentants de l'immigration.
Ces renseignements sont fournis à titre d'orientation générale et ne constituent pas une directive pour des dossiers individuels. Pour des demandes de renseignements sur des cas spécifiques, les demandeurs peuvent contacter le Ministère en soumettant le Formulaire Web d'IRCC. Veuillez trouver les réponses à vos questions ci-dessous :
Questions
1. Autrement dit, un travailleur étranger temporaire peut-il appliquer pour le permis de son choix ou si les nouvelles instructions du 3 octobre 2024 ont complètement remplacé le permis de travail fermé de type A77 ?
2. Ensuite, nous aimerions savoir s'il est toujours possible pour un travailleur étranger temporaire, dans le cadre de l'exemption d'EIMT C62 transfert intra-compagnie, de venir travailler au Canada sous une base intermittente ? C'est-à- dire que durant la période de validité de son permis de travail, il peut être appelé à faire des aller-retours entre le Canada et son pays d'origine, afin de pouvoir administrer à la fois l'entreprise canadienne et l'entreprise étrangère. Le cas échéant, est-ce que le travailleur est tout de même sujet à l'exigence de respecter le salaire médian, considérant qu'il peut être rémunéré par l'entreprise étrangère dans le cadre de son emploi au Canada et que sa rémunération, lorsqu’'il travaille à l'étranger, pourrait être différente de celle qui reçoit au Canada ?
Réponse
1. Le nouveau permis de travail ouvert pour le Programme de visa pour démarrage d’entreprise, valable jusqu’à 3 ans, qui a été annoncé le 3 octobre, remplace le précédent permis de travail lié à un employeur donné, valable jusqu’à un an. Les candidats qui sollicitent ce type de permis de travail n’ont désormais plus que l’option du permis de travail ouvert.
2. Les étrangers mutés à titre de cadres n’ont pas nécessairement besoin de s’installer à temps plein au Canada pour gérer l’entreprise canadienne. Cependant, ils doivent occuper un poste au sein de l’entreprise canadienne et avoir une relation employeur-employé évidente avec l’entreprise canadienne. Le cadre doit diriger l’entreprise canadienne au quotidien. (source) Il n’est pas obligatoire que l’étranger soit rémunéré par l’entreprise canadienne ou en dollars canadiens et lorsqu’il travaille à l’étranger, son salaire peut être différent de celui qu’il reçoit au Canada.
Nous espérons que ces informations vous seront utiles.
Pour plus d’informations, veuillez consulter la page Web suivante :

Si le permis de travail n’est accessible que si tardivement pour les candidats au programme SUV, le programme devient moins attrayant pour les entrepreneurs désirant rapidement développer leur entreprise au Canada.
Ainsi, on m’a demandé si vos services accepteront une preuve de dépôt de demande de résidence permanente (courriel d’IRCC attestant du dépôt + reçu des frais IRCC) telle que précédemment exigée? Ou est-il prévu d’émettre les accusés réception plus rapidement après le dépôt d’une demande?
Auriez-vous l’amabilité de clarifier cette exigence afin que nous puissions informer nos candidats adéquatement.
Merci et bonne journée,

threads.question:
Subje et: Clarification regarding Measures for Israeli nationals, Palestinian passport holders and family members in Canada
Good day, I am seeking clarification regarding the Measures for Israeli nationals, Palestinian passport holders and family members in Canada My client is an who is does not have an Passport.
Does the special measures extend to the spouse allowing the spouse also to apply for the Open Work Permit?
Thank you
Regards,
mmigration, Refugees
threads.answer:
Good day and thank you for your enquiry.
Under the Temporary public policy for nationals of Israel and the Palestinian Territories who are in Canada as temporary residents, clients who meet the following conditions may be eligible to apply for a fee-exempt study permit or open work permit, or to extend or change the conditions of their temporary stay:
- Is an Israeli national or Palestinian passport holder in Canada (if the client does not have an Israeli passport but has Israeli citizenship, they must provide proof of Israeli citizenship along with a valid passport from another country)
- and has valid temporary resident status in Canada
Under the Temporary public policy for foreign nationals who are family members of Canadian citizens and permanent residents who left Israel or the Palestinian Territories on or after October 7, 2023, clients who meet the following conditions may be eligible to apply for a fee-exempt study permit or open work permit, or to extend or change the conditions of their temporary stay:
- Foreign nationals: o who are family members —per the definition of subsection 1(3) of the Regulations—of a Canadian citizen or permanent resident of Canada who left Israel or the Palestinian Territories on or after October 7, 2023; OR, o who were issued a temporary resident visa following facilitation under the Temporary public policy to facilitate temporary resident visas for certain extended family affected by the crisis in Gaza; OR, o who were issued a temporary resident visa based on exemptions from the Act or Regulations granted by a delegated officer on humanitarian and compassionate grounds between January 9 and June 30, 2024, and are a family member—per the definition of subsection 1(3) of the Regulations—of a foreign national who holds a passport or other document issued by the Palestinian authority; OR, o who were issued a temporary resident permit by a designated officer between January 9 and June 30, 2024, and are a family member—per the definition of subsection 1(3) of the Regulations—of a foreign national who holds a passport or other document issued by the Palestinian authority,
- and has valid temporary resident status in Canada
Please note that the Temporary public policy for foreign nationals who are family members of Canadian citizens and permanent residents who left Israel or the Palestinian Territories on or after October 7, 2023, would not extend to the spouse in question by way of being a family member as per subsection 1(3) of the Regulations, as the Israeli spouse in Canada is a temporary resident. These measures only apply to immediate family members ofCanadian citizens or permanent residents only.
To further determine eligibility, we invite you to visit: Measures for Israeli nationals, Palestinian passport holders and family members in Canada-Canada.ca
and Citizenshi Canada et Ciloyeneé Canada
