threads.subject: Auditeur libre en rétablissement de statut / Statut conservé travailleurs autorisés à étudier sans PÉ-REP-2024- 2130 - Due 2-Dec-24
threads.answer:
Bonjour,
Merci de contacter la boîte électronique des représentants de l'immigration.
Ces renseignements sont fournis à titre d'orientation générale et ne constituent pas une directive pour des dossiers individuels. Pour des demandes de renseignements sur des cas spécifiques, les demandeurs peuvent contacter le Ministère en soumettant le Formulaire Web d'IRCC.
1. Si le statut de l'étudiant étranger a expiré, il y a infraction à la Loi sur l'immigration et la protection des réfugiés (LIPR). L’étudiant étranger présentant une demande de rétablissement a perdu son statut ainsi que l’autorisation d’étudier. Il ne peut done pas continuer d’aller à l’école avant que son statut et son autorisation aient été rétablis et qu’un nouveau permis d’études ait été délivré. Dans la même logique, un étranger en période de rétablissement de son statut ne peut suivre des cours à titre d’auditeur libre puisque cela est un privilège donné aux étrangers détenteurs d’un statut de résident temporaire valide au Canada. Pour plus d’information sur le rétablissement de statut, veuillez consulter : Rétablissement du statut de résident temporaire-Canada.ca
2. La Politique d’intérêt public permettant à certains titulaires de permis de travail d’étudier sans permis d’études permet à certaines travailleurs étrangers temporaires d’étudier dans un programme d’études qui a une durée de plus de 6 mois sans avoir à demander un permis d’études. Pour être admissible, la personne doit être autorisée à travailler au Canada soit avec un permis de travail (PT) valide et la demande associée à ce PT a été reçue par IRCC le ou avant le 7 juin 2023; ou après avoir présenté une demande de prolongation d’un PT le ou avant le 7 juin 2023 et être autorisée à travailler en vertu de l’alinéa R186u) en attendant qu'IRCC traite la demande de prolongation du PT.
3. En effet, il ne s’agit pas d’une erreur, la page a été modifiée avec les instructions mises à jour suivante : Permis d’études : Présenter une demande-Canada.ca. Le résident temporaire a un statut conservé pendant le traitement de sa nouvelle demande, à condition que celle-ci ait été déposée avant la date d'expiration du permis initial. Il peut poursuivre ses études, son emploi ou sa visite, et ce, aux mêmes conditions que sur son permis initial, en attendant que sa demande soit finalisée (p. ex., il continue de ne pas être autorisé à étudier, s'il ne l'était pas auparavant). Pour plus d’information sur les permis d’études pour les enfants mineurs, veuillez consulter : Permis d’études : Lignes directrices sur les enfants mineurs-Canada.ca
Nous espérons que ceci clarifie vos questions.
Cordialement,
Adresse électronique des représentants de l'immigration
and Citizenship Caneda
De : Envoyé : 1 novembre 2024 17:47 À : Objet : Auditeur libre en rétablissement de statut / Statut conservé travailleurs autorisés à étudier sans PÉ
Bonjour, je suis consultante en immigration, membre en règle du CCIC
Je suis conseillère auprès de la t nous rencontrons certains cas pour lesquels nous avons de la difficulté à trouver des réponses; je fais donc appel à vous.
1. Les cours suivis à titre d’auditeur libre, soit des cours qui ne seront pas crédités, sont une activité qui n’exige pas que l’étranger soit titulaire d’un permis d’études valide. Je me questionne quant à l’étudiant qui a été titulaire d’un permis d’études expiré, qui a demandé le rétablissement de statut dans les 90 jours de l’échéance de son permis d’études. Est-ce que cette personne, en état de rétablissement de statut serait autorisée à étudier à titre d’auditeur libre qui ne recevra jamais de crédit pour lesdits cours? Je comprends que cet étranger n’a pas de statut légal mais il est toujours autorisé à séjourner au Canada jusqu’à ce qu’une décision soit rendue. Est-ce que cette autorisation de séjour en fait un candidat éligible à être un auditeur libre?
2. Ma deuxième question concerne les TET autorisés à étudier sans permis d’études en vertu de la politique d’intérêt public temporaire visant à permettre aux étrangers titulaires d’un permis de travail valide d’étudier sans permis d’études. Les TET visés par cette politique sont-ils autorisés à débuter un programme d’études en vertu du statut conservé s’ils soumettent une demande de permis d’études avant l’échéance de leur permis de travail qui avaient été émis avant le 7 juin 2023?
3. threads.subject: R216 and R219- REP-2024-2061 -Due 25-Nov-24
threads.question:
Hello,
Two provisions ofIRPR (216 and 219) seem to refer to the same requirement – having an admission from a DLI before being granted a Study Permit. However, provision 219 has an exception, but 216 does not.
Can you confirm if the exception of R219 also applies to R216?
And if not, does it mean that the exception of R219 does not exist in practice, as the requirement of R216(e) still must be met?
For reference:
Study permits
- 216 (1) Subject to subsections (2) and (3), an officer shall issue a study permit to a foreign national if, following an examination, it is established that the foreign national
- (a) applied for it in accordance with this Part;
- (b) will leave Canada by the end of the period authorized for their stay under Division 2 of Part 9;
- (c) meets the requirements of this Part;
- (d) meets the requirements of subsections 30(2) and (3), if they must submit to a medical examination under paragraph 16(2)(b) of the Act; and
- (e) has been accepted to undertake a program of study at a designated learning institution.
Acceptance letter
- 219 (1) A study permit shall not be issued to a foreign national unless they have written documentation from the designated learning institution where they intend to study that states that they have been accepted to study there.
- Exception
(2) Subsection (1) does not apply to
- (a) a family member of a foreign national whose application for a work permit or a study permit is approved in writing
before the foreign national enters Canada.
Thank you for your support, it is greatly appreciated.
threads.answer:
R216 and R219 do have some overlapping requirements concerning the admission to a DLI for study permits. R216 outlines the basic requirements for a study permit, while R219 specifies circumstances under which the admission requirement can be waived. The exception in R219 does exist, but it only applies to situations explicitly described in that provision. Applicants who do not meet the admission requirement of R216 may still have the possibility of being considered under the exceptions provided by R219. However, if they do not qualify for those exceptions, they must fulfill the admission requirement of R216(e). In practice, this means that while R219 allows some flexibility, R216 maintains a strict requirement for a DLI admission unless one qualifies for the exceptions laid out in R219.
Sincerely, Immigration Representatives Mailbox

The Super Visa is a multiple-entry temporary resident visa (TRV), issued with a validity of up to 10 years. As per changes to the Immigration and Refugees Protection Act on June 22, 2023, the period of authorized stay is 5 years for each entry. At the port of entry, a Border Services Officer (BSO) will examine the foreign national as per R180. If they are/were granted entry into Canada by a BSO after June 22, 2023, the foreign national is/was authorized to stay in Canada for 5 years from the date of entry.

threads.subject: Working for a Canadian company abroad-REP-2024-2247 - Due 09-Dec-24
threads.answer:
Good afternoon,
Thank you for your question. Please note that we cannot answer case-specific questions but have provided the following information as guidance.
In accordance with A28(2)(i), any time a client spends outside Canada and is not employed full-time by a Canadian Business or in the federal public administration or the public service of a province, does not count towards time spent in Canada. This requirement is outlined in Guide IMM 5445.
In addition, IRCC’s terms and definitions webpage builds upon this requirement and states:
The Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR) enables permanent residents to comply with the residency obligation while working abroad, provided they (all must apply):
- Are under contract to or are full-time employees of a Canadian business or public service, where the assignment is controlled from the head office located in Canada
- Are assigned on a full-time basis as a term of their employment outside of Canada or contract to a position outside of Canada with o The business where they are employed An affiliated enterprise 。 A client
- Maintain a connection to a Canadian business
- Are assigned on a temporary basis to the work assignment
- Will continue working for the employer, in Canada, after the assignment."
However, if a permanent resident (PR) of Canada is working for a Canadian company but that PR has chosen to work remotely for that company in the USA and their Canadian employer has approved this arrangement, this PR is not working for a branch of that Canadian company that itself is outside of Canada – this is strictly remote working, and they have not been assigned to work abroad temporarily. The situation therefore will not meet the criteria of being assigned’ to work abroad full-time, temporarily, and will not count towards a PR's residency obligation. This information can be found here Permanent resident status determination-Canada.ca.
We hope this information is helpful.
Thank you,

threads.subject: GATS Intra Corporate Transferees-REP-2024-1969 - Due 13-Nov-24
threads.question:
Can Global Affairs Canada confirm whether the scope of Canada's obligations in the WTO Implementation Act and the GATS includes intra corporate transferees, and confirm that there ought to (continue to) be a procedure that allows the temporary entry of intracompany transferees according to the terms of the GATS?

Can IRCC please provide Guidelines on how to apply for a GATS intra corporate transfer?
threads.answer:
Thank you for your inquiry regarding Canada's updated guidelines for intra corporate transferees (ICTs) and their relationship to Canada's commitments under the World Trade Organization General Agreement on Trade in Services (GATS).
Canada remains firmly committed to its obligations under the WTO GATS, which include provisions for the temporary entry of eligible intra-corporate transferees. These commitments remain unchanged and are embedded in Canada's domestic framework, as implemented through the WTO Agreement Implementation Act and the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR). The procedures facilitating the temporary entry of these transferees continue to be in place, as outlined further in

.

Canada’s commitments under the WTO GATS with respect to temporary entry of intra-company transfers (ICTs) are specified under administrative codes C62 and C63, which replaced C12 in December 2022. Detailed information on this program can be found at the following link:
Intra-company transferees (ICT) — [R205(a) – C61. C62, C63] – Canadian interests — International Mobility Program-Canada.ca
For clarity :
- A Multinational Corporation (MNC) is a company that has revenue generating business operations in at least one country other than its home country that generates revenue beyond its borders.
- The ICT provisions under C61 do not allow an enterprise to become an MNC by establishing their first international enterprise in Canada.
- However, the ICT provisions under C62 and C63 permit the issuance ofICT work permits if one of the exis ting business operations is already established in Canada, therefore meeting the definition of an MNC.
We recognize that recent updates to the guidance may have raised questions, and further revisions are in progress to provide additional clarification regarding this matter.
We hope this information is helpful. Please do not hesitate to reach out if further clarification is required.
Sincerely,
Immigration Representatives Mailbox
De :
Envoyé : 15 octobre 2024 16:33 À : consultations@international.gc.ca Representantsirnmigration.IRCC@cic.gc.ca>; Objet : GATS Intra Corporate Transferees
ATTN: WTO Team, Trade Policy and Negotiations Division (TCW), Global Affairs Canada
Counsel/Representatives Liaison Team, Policy Branch, IRCC
Dear Sir/Madam:
Issue summary: IRCC’s new October 3, 2024 Guidelines (C61-63) outlining the eligibility criteria for intra-company transferees for Canadian work permits are more restrictive than its commitments allow in the GATS. Thus, the new Guidelines, if implemented without a separate Guideline publication for GATS Intra corporate transferees, could violate Canadian law and its international legal commitments.
Questions:
1. Can Global Affairs Canada confirm whether the scope of Canada's obligations in the WTO Implementation Act and the GATS includes intra corporate transferees, and confirm that there ought to (continue to) be a procedure that allows the temporary entry of intracompany transferees according to the terms of the GATS?
2. Can IRCC please provide Guidelines on how to apply for a GATS intra corporate transfer?
Background: For the past couple of decades, up until October 3, 2024, Canada's immigration department extended Canada's commitments under the General Agreement on Trade and Services (GATS) concerning intra corporate transferees to all natural and juridical persons, irrespective of WTO membership. This was done under the authority of s. 205(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (Regulations) and code C12 of the Temporary Foreign Worker Guidelines (Guidelines). This authority allowed any one foreign national who worked for any one business outside of Canada for 1 year in the past 3-year period to be authorized to work in Canada for a related business.
Citoyenneté Canada Guideline C12 thus liberalized Canadian law, extending Canada’s GATS commitments beyond the (current) 164 WTO Member States to all foreign nationals and business, anywhere.
On October 3, 2024, Canada’s immigration department appears to have deleted its C12 Guidelines. It also published new guidelines for interpreting s. 205(a) of the Regulations as they concern intra corporate transferees, and added new program codes C61, C62 and C63 to its Guidelines. These C61-63 Guidelines require that a foreign national be employed by a “multinational corporation” to qualify as an intra corporate transferee. “Multinational corporation” is defined as requiring there to be two businesses in two separate countries outside of Canada: the foreign country in which the foreign national works plus one other country other than Canada.
In other words, the new Guidelines increased the threshold from one foreign business to two foreign businesses.
As a corollary issue, before a foreign national may apply for a LMIA-exempt work permit (i.e., exempt from an economic need test), the Regulations require a Canadian to employer submit a form to IRCC specifying the terms and conditions of employment. This form, called the “Offer of Employment to a Foreign National Exempt from a LMIA" form, contains a drop-down menu for selecting the applicable Guideline program code. However, not only has IRCC deleted C12 Guidelines from its manuals, but it also removed code C12 from the form, and has not published a replacement code.
Thus, there is no clear procedure for applying for a GATS intra corporate transfer work permit.
The Law: The determination with respect to the entry of natural persons into Canada is made by IRCC or CBSA under their delegated authorities under the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA) and its Regulations made thereunder.
Section 204(a) of the Regulations provides the legal authority for the issuance of a work permit to a foreign national under an international agreement.
The GATS is one such agreement.
The WTO Agreement Implementation Act, SC 1994 c.47 (WTO Act) came into force January 1, 1995. The WTO Act makes Annex 1B, the GATS, law in Canada.
According to the GATS:
Natural persons of another Member who have been employed by juridical persons of another Member for a period of not less than one year and who seek temporary entry in order to render services to (i) the same juridical person which is engaged in substantive business operations in Canada or (ii) a juridical person constituted in Canada and engaged in substantive business operations in Canada which is owned by or controlled by or affiliated with the aforementioned juridical person
In the language of immigration law, “natural person” means “foreign national”, “another Member" means any WTO member state, and “employed by juridical persons” means employed by a foreign entity (sole proprietor, partnership or a corporation).
Put another way, the GATS commits Canada to admit for work, under the authority of s. 204(a) of the Regulations,:
1. A foreign national who is a citizen of any WTO Member state who,
2. Has been employed by a foreign entity (i.e., sole proprietor, partnership or corporation) located in any WTO Member state for at least 1 year, and
3. Who seeks temporary entry into Canada to render services to either:
a. A branch operation of the foreign entity, or
b. A Canadian subsidiary or Canadian affiliate of the foreign entity.

Despite this, IRCC has not (yet) published new Guidelines with respect to GATS intra corporate transferees.

threads.answer:
Hello,
Thank you for your question. Please note that we cannot answer case-specific questions but have provided the following information as guidance.
To be eligible to apply for Stream A(In-Canada Graduates) the following requirements are:
Education require ments
Applicants must have graduated from a designated learning institution in Canada in the 3 years before they apply with one of the following:
- a post-secondary degree (for example, associate, bachelor’s, master's, doctoral)
- a post-secondary diploma (not graduate or post-graduate) for a program that is at least 2 years in length
- a graduate or post-graduate credential for a program that is at least 1 year in length and o the program required them to have a post-secondary degree or diploma (from Canada or from abroad) as a prerequisite and o they graduated from the post-secondary degree or diploma no more than 5 years before the start of the graduate or post-graduate program
The program of study can be completed in any field of study, with at least 50% of the program of study completed while physically present in Canada, either in class or online.
Then, the applicant must show that they have been physically in Canada for at least 50% of the total school days of their program of study.
Lastly, the principal applicant must be physically present in Canada when they apply and when permanent residence is granted.
The principal applicant must provide proof of being physically present in Canada at the time of their application. This can include
- a copy of a lease or rental agreement
- a letter from a landlord or property owner attesting to residence and specifying dates
- utility bills or any other bills that contain the applicant's residential address

Dear IMMREP,
I am writing to bring to your attention a recent regulatory change that may have unintended consequences for thousands of students in Canada. While I understand this matter may fall outside the scope ofIMMREP, I would greatly appreciate it if you could raise this issue with the relevant policy section. If you have other recommendations or contacts, please let me know.
In brief, the new regulations on study permit applications for changing Designated Learning Institutions (DLIs) will unexpectedly impact thousands of students. According to the regulations published in the Canada Gazette yesterday, R189.1 prohibits new study permit applicants from studying at their new DLI while their applications are being processed. While there are some exceptions, they are very limited.
This is contrary to the information provided during the public consultation, which explicitly stated that students could continue their studies while awaiting decisions on new study permit applications:
"An increase in the volume of study permit applications submitted may increase processing times for this line of business. However, the impact of longer processing times would be mitigated as students who have applied to change
Cioyenneté Canada
L'nmndion the DLI would be allowed to attend the new DLI as long as the study permit application has been submitted."
This situation is further exacerbated by the following factors:
1. Processing Delays: With public consultation timelines set at 120 days, the current processing time for study permit extensions from within Canada is approximately 15 weeks, and for new study permit applications, it's 22 weeks. Therefore, no student will be issued a new study permit in time for the January 2025 term.
2. Impact on Students: Thousands of students who have completed a program or were planning to transfer to a new DLI under the previous rules will now need to take a leave of absence and will be unable to continue their studies. While we are assisting students in managing their compliance, this raises questions about working off-campus, leaves of absence, and other related issues.
Additionally, I have a few key concerns:
- Lack of Anticipation: These changes were not anticipated. The public consultation explicitly stated that students could continue their studies while awaiting decisions on new study permit applications.
- Retroactive Implementation: The retroactive application of these changes to November 8 did not provide sufficient time for students to submit their applications under the previous rules.
- Widespread Disruption: Thousands of students will now be forced to defer their studies due to these changes.
I believe a solution that could be implemented quickly is to add a code in the study permit applications to prioritize them, ensuring their study permits are decided in time for the January 2025 intake. This would be a temporary measure to address the immediate concerns.
I understand that IRCC is meeting with CBIE tomorrow to discuss these issues. I hope this matter will be given due consideration, as it has significant implications for students and educational institutions across Canada.
Thank you for your attention to this matter.
Best regards,

threads.subject: Definition of "studies" and definition of "courses of general interest or self-improvement" - REP-2024-1830- Due 30-Oct-24
threads.question:
Could you please specify what definition of the concept “studies" is currently being used by your department to determine whether an specific educational activity is considered “studies" for the purpose of IRPA?
-

Would you please specify the definition of“courses of general interest or self-improvement’
-
threads.answer:
IRCC does not have a definition of“studies", in either the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act or Regulations, that is used to determine whether a specific educational activity requires a study permit. Further information regarding when a study permit may be required, please consult the following Program Delivery Instructions entitled “Study permits: Who needs a study permit". Foreign nationals are required to obtain a study permit for engaging in academic, professional, vocational or other education or training that is more than 6 months in duration at a designated learning institution (DLI) in Canada.

IRCC does not have a specific definition of“courses of general interest or self-improvement". However, these courses are typically non-degree programs designed for personal enrichment rather than academic credit or professional certification. These courses often focus on hobbies, recreational activities, or personal development and do not result in formal qualifications or credentials. Typically, these are courses with a duration of 6 months or less.
We hope this information is helpful.
Regards,

threads.question: I am seeking your clarification with regards to the new PGWP eligibility for students who applied for study permit extensions under a different program of study than the study permit they applied before Nov. 1, 2024, apart from the new language requirement, do they have to meet the field of study requirements applicable for their study programs to be eligible for PGWP eligibility?
threads.answer:
In determining whether a program is PGWP-eligible:
the language requirement is applicable to all PGWP applications (except those from flight school graduates) submitted on or after November 1, 2024, regardless of when the student applied for their study permit or when they started their program of study.
the field of study requirement is applicable depending on the level of study and when a student applies tor their student permit.
If the student applies for a study permit extension under the same program of study as the study permit they applied for before November 1, 2024, then they do not need to meet the field of study requirement.
If the student applies for a study permit extension under a different program of study than the study permit they applied for before November 1, 2024, then their study permit extension application must meet the field of study requirements applicable to their study program to be eligible for a PGWP.

threads.question: I am reaching out to seek clarification regarding the full-time course load requirements for international students. Specifically, I would like to understand whether the definition of a full-time course load is determined by the institution or if the IRCC has its own set of guidelines for what constitutes full-time or part-time status for international students. For example, if an international student is enrolled in three courses, each worth 3 credits, would that be considered a full-time course load or part-time? Additionally, I would like to confirm whether international students are required to maintain full-time status in order to comply with the conditions of their study permit
threads.answer:
Full time course load is determined by the designated learning institution (DLI). From an IRCC perspective, at a minimum, students must have part-time status with their institution to be considered to be actively pursuing their studies.
The province of Quebec requires students to maintain full-time status with their institution to be considered to be actively pursuing their studies. See more details on requirements for students in Quebec.
For more information on full-time and part-time studies, see Study permits: Other considerations.

threads.subject: Inquiry Regarding Distance Learning and Express Entry Points on Post-Graduation Work Permit-REP-2024- 2204 - Due 9-Dec-24
threads.question:
I am writing to inquire about the eligibility of a candidate holding a Post-Graduation Work Permit (PGWP) in Canada to pursue a distance (online) degree program from an institution in India. Specifically, I would like to know if such a candidate can later claim points for this foreign education in the Express Entry system, provided the Educational Credential Assessment (ECA) has been completed through WES.
I would appreciate your guidance on whether the completion of an online program while on a PGWP in Canada can be used to earn points for education under the Express Entry Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS).
threads.answer:
As per the Ministerial Instructions, for a candidate to be awarded Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) points for their education they must meet the requirements listed under MI1 1(3):
Educational credentials
1 73(3) In order for a foreign national to be assigned points under subsection (1),
- (a) their educational credentials must be Canadian educational credentials; or
- (b) they must have an educational credential equivalency assessment in respect of their foreign educational credentials issued by an organization or institution designated under subsection 75(4) of the Regulations.
Please be advised that the assessment of an application is based on a case-by-case basis; each application will be considered on its own merits, with a final decision based on a review of all the information available to the officer at the time of decision. The onus is always on the applicant to provide sufficient documentation to satisfy an officer that they meet the requirements.

Réponse
Pour pouvoir travailler en attendant une décision concernant son PTPD, un ressortissant étranger doit répondre aux critères d'éligibilité suivants :

Vous avez l’autorisation de travailler jusqu’à ce qu’une décision soit prise à l’égard de votre demande de permis de travail, même si la date de validité de 120 jours est expirée. Si vous avez besoin d’une preuve d’autorisation pour continuer à travailler, vous pouvez la demander au moyen de notre formulaire Web. (source)

threads.subject: Seeking clarity on Canadian Experience Class and Canadian work experience points. - REP-2024-2014 -Due 19-Nov-24
threads.question:
Can a foreign worker who is in Canada as the holder of an open work permit claim points for Canadian work experience if they are employed by a company overseas? The employment is full time, paid, employer has no operations in Canada, employee works remotely for the job, remuneration is paid in their bank account in that country.
In other words, in order for an applicant to claim Canadian Experience Class eligibility or points for Canadian Experience on Express Entry is there a requirement for their employer to be a Canadian Business, have operations in Canada or the remuneration for the employee to be received in Canada or any other such requirement? Please confirm any employer requirements if applicable to the Canadian experience class.
threads.answer:
The policy intent for Canadian work experience requires that the work performed demonstrates to the Officer that the applicant has entered the Canadian labour market, and a Canadian entity paid the applicant for their work. It must also be evident to the Officer that the work would be considered a business activity that is competitive in the Canadian labour market, and that this position would normally have been filled by a Canadian citizen or permanent resident. Entry into the Canadian labour market is also a necessary element of work experience under the Canadian Experience Class that demonstrates ones “ability to become economically established in Canada" under R87.1(1) of the IRPR.
Remote work for a foreign employer while residing in Canada may be eligible under the Express Entry as foreign work experience if it meets all the other requirements. Work outside of the Canadian labour market is not eligible as Canadian work experience.
Please note that the system does not currently capture remote work. When an applicant is invited to apply, please submit an explanation, detailing the remote work agreement, and where the employer and employee are physically located.
Please be advised that the assessment of an application is based on a case-by-case basis, considering the particular circumstances in conjunction with the supporting documentation available to the officer. The onus is always on the applicant to provide sufficient documentation to satisfy an officer that they meet the requirements.
We trust that this information will assist you.

threads.subject: Clarification Request Regarding FSW Minimum Work Experience Requirement-REP-2024-2234 - Due 10- Dec-24
threads.question:
As stated in paragraph 75(2)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR), applicants must, within ten years prior to the date of their permanent resident application, accumulate at least one year of continuous full-time work experience (or the equivalent in part-time) in their primary occupation, excluding restricted occupations, as listed in NOC TEER categories 0, 1, 2, or 3.
The IRCC website (link: [https://www.canada.ca/en/inmigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-](https://www.canada.ca/en/inmigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-) entry/eligibility/federal-skilled-workers.html) provides examples of acceptable work experience combinations for this requirement:
Full-time at one job: 30 hours per week for 12 months, totaling 1,560 hours
- Equivalent part-tie work: e.g., 15 hours per week for 24 months, totaling 1,560 hours (allowing multiple part-time jobs if needed)
- Full-time at more than one job: 30 hours per week across jobs for 12 months, totaling 1,560 hours
My question is whether a combination of part-time and full-time work experience (with no gap in between), acquired within the last 10 years, all in the primary occupation with no employer change and totaling at least 1,560 hours over a continuous period of at least 12 months, would also meet the one-year continuous work requirement.
threads.answer:
Yes, a combination of part-time and full-time work experience (with no gap in between), acquired within the last 10 years, all in the primary occupation with no employer change and totaling at least 1,560 hours over a continuous period of at least 12 months, would also meet the one-year continuous work requirement (provided it meets all other requirements). Work experience must be acquired over a period of at least 1 year; work in excess of 30 hours per week over a shorter period cannot compensate for any shorter overall period of experience.
Please be advised that the assessment of an application is based on a case-by-case basis; each application will be considered on its own merits, with a final decision based on a review of all the information available to the officer at the time of decision. The onus is always on the applicant to provide sufficient documentation to satisfy an officer that they meet the requirements.
We trust that this information will assist you.
Sincerely,
Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.subject: Calculating Education under Express Entry-REP-2024-2088- Due 27-Nov-24
threads.question:
I have a client who obtained a joint double degree (Bachelor ofMath from University of Waterloo) and Bachelor of Business Admin (Wilfred Laurier University) within 5 years in Canada. She received a degree from each institution and attended a convocation separately at each institution.
Under Express Entry, what is her highest level of education?
- “Two or more certificates, diplomas or degrees. One must be for a program of three or more years"
OR
- Bachelor's degree (three or more year program at university, college, trade or technical school or other institute"
threads.answer:
A candidate will be awarded education points under the Comprehensive Ranking System for having ‘two or more post-secondary program credentials’ if the education credentials represent separate certificates, diplomas or degrees. If one credential is used as a component of the second credential, then it is not two separate credentials even though their might be two separate certificates. To get points for having two or more post-secondary credentials, at least one of the credentials must be for three years or more.
Please be advised that the assessment of an application is based on a case-by-case basis; each application will be considered on its own merits, with a final decision based on a review of all the information available to the officer at the time of decision. The onus is always on the applicant to provide sufficient documentation to satisfy an officer that they meet the requirements.
We trust that this information will assist you.

Do secondary students have 90 days after completing their studies per R222? This is unclear based on the new rules, which are not updated thoroughly on IRCC's websites.
Background
1. The concerning language about a possible out-of-status/restoration was found here, which implies that a study permit goes into expiry on completion. This is on the new posted instructions on the front-end of IRCC's website: You need to apply for a new study permit to attend a post-secondary school. Important information: If you finish your secondary school studies early, your study permit will no longer be valid 90 days after you complete your studies, regardless of the date that is shown on your study permit.
Source: [https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/study-canada/change-schools.html](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/study-canada/change-schools.html) (found under If
you're moving from secondary to post-secondary levels
2. That inference does not match the language of the proposed regulations. When piecing together the regulations using current and proposed language, it suggests they do have 90 days. 222 (1) A study permit becomes invalid upon the first to occur of the following days:
(a) the day that is 90 days after the day on which the permit holder completes their studies, (a.1) the day on which the permit holder is no longer enrolled at the designated learning institution that is named in the permit, other than as a result of completing their studies;
(b) the day on which the permit is cancelled under section 243.2; or
(c) the day on which the permit expires.
Current regs: [https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/regulations/SOR-2002-227/section-222.html](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/regulations/SOR-2002-227/section-222.html)
Proposed reg for 222(1)(a.1): [https://www.gazette.gc.ca/rp-pr/p1/2024/2024-06-29/html/reg1-eng.html](https://www.gazette.gc.ca/rp-pr/p1/2024/2024-06-29/html/reg1-eng.html) (see point 8 under 'Regulations Amending the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (Designated Learning Institutions)")
Thank you for any assistance that can be provided,

of the Access to Information Act de la Loi sur l'acces a l'information
mmigration, Réfugiés
Information disclosed under the Access to Information Ac
threads.answer:
As per 222 (1) A study permit becomes invalid upon the first to occur of the following days:
(a) the day that is 90 days after the day on which the permit holder completes their studies, (a.1) the day on which the permit holder is no longer enrolled at the designated learning institution that is named in the permit, other than as a result of completing their studies;
(b) the day on which the permit is cancelled under section 243.2; or
(c) the day on which the permit expires.
If a student finishes (completes) their studies before their study permit expires, their study permit will stop being valid 90 days after they complete their studies, no matter what day is printed on the study permit.
A study permit holder studies are officially completed on the date their school first notifies them by any of the following:
- completion letter
- transcript
- degree or diploma

threads.question:
I am seeking clarification regarding the current policies related to the admission of TRV-exempt foreign nationals who have lost their maintained status in Canada as a worker due to brief travel to the United States.
My understanding is that, upon departure from Canada, the TRV-exempt foreign national loses their maintained status as a worker. Therefore, they must either wait for the new work permit to be approved before re-entering Canada as a worker or apply for a new
work permit at the border.
My client has recently encountered a situation where a CBSA officer stated that proof of having submitted a work permit extension application with IRCC is sufficient for re-admission to Canada as a worker in the absence of a valid work permit, and that maintained status as a worker continues upon re-entry to Canada and that they may resume work in Canada until their work
permit renewal application has been granted.
Contrary to these instructions from the CBSA officer, my understanding was that maintained status ceases to exist once the foreign national departs Canada. Please see the following IRCC's instructions-also copied below: [https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-manuals/temporary-residents/visitors/implied-status-](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-manuals/temporary-residents/visitors/implied-status-) extending-stay.html
“Re-enter Canada as a temporary resident
Applicants may be allowed to re-enter Canada as a temporary resident pending a decision on the extension of their study permit or work permit in Canada, provided they are temporary resident visa (TRV) exempt as per section R190 or hold a valid multiple-entry visa. The border services officer will set the period of authorized stay on entry.
Temporary residents from TRV-required countries whose period of authorized stay has been extended under subsection R183(5) and who are seeking re-entry to Canada following a visit solely to the United States or St. Pierre and Miquelon are considered to be TRV exempt, as per subparagraph R190(3)(f)(ii). This interpretation of the legislation is consistent with paragraph 30 of the Federal Court decision De Brito v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Imanigration). 2003 FC
1379. If a TRV-required national has travelled anywhere other than the United States or St. Pierre and Miquelon, regardless of whether their period of authorized stay was extended under subsection R183(5), they are not TRV exempt. Regardless of the De Brito decision, the authorization to work and study without a permit under paragraph R186(u) or section R189 while pending a decision on an application ends on departure from Canada. If the new study or work permit has not been issued prior to the applicant's return, they may not resume work or study in Canada until their application for renewal has been granted. Those not able to resume work must satisfy the border services officer that they have

Could you please provide current guidance on this matter? I want to ensure that I am advising accurately on the implications of temporary foreign workers' short-term travel to the United States while on maintained status.
threads.answer:
Your understanding is correct- a TRV-exempt foreign national is allowed to re-enter Canada but they lost their authorization to work under R186(u) upon departure from Canada. Upon re-entry they are not authorized to resume working in Canda until their application for work permit extension is approved or unless they applied at the port of entry for a new work permit and re-entered as a worker provided they meet the requirements of section R198. Proof of having submitted an extension is not sufficient for authorization to resume working in Canada.

threads.question:
As per the updated eligibility criteria based on the field of study program (outlined at: https//www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/study-canada/work/after-graduation/eligibility.html ), applicants who have graduated from a university program that does not result in a bachelor's, master's, or doctoral degree, or from a college or other non-university program, must have graduated in an eligible field of study. The exception to this requirement applies only to applicants who submitted their study permit application before November 1, 2024.
I would like to inquire whether an international student who initially submitted their study permit application before November 1, 2024, but was required to apply for an extension of their study permit on or after November 1, 2024, in order to complete their studies, would still be exempt from the field of study requirement when applying for a PGWP. Or does the fact that the study permit extension was applied for on or after November 1, 2024, make the applicant subject to the field of study eligibility requirement?
threads.answer:
All PGWP applications (except those from flight school graduates) submitted on or after November 1, 2024 must comply with the new language requirements, regardless of when the student applied for their study permit or when they started their program of study.
If the student applies for a study permit extension under the same program of study as the study permit they applied for before November 1, 2024, then they do not need to meet the field of study requirement. If the student applies for a study permit extension under a different program of study than the study permit they applied for before November 1, 2024, then their study permit extension application must meet the field of study requirements applicable to their study program to be eligible for a PGWP.
We have recently updated our website to provide clients with further details on the new PGWP eligibility requirements at the following link: Work in Canada after you graduate: Who can apply-Canada.ca

As per the Home Child Care Provider and Home Support Worker pilot guide, common-law refers to a person who is living in a conjugal relationship with another person (any gender), and has done so continuously for a period of at least one year. A conjugal relationship exists when there is a significant degree of commitment between two people.
his can be shown with evidence that the couple share the same home, support each other financially and emotionally, have children together, or present themselves in public as a couple.

If the applicant does not inform IRCC of these types of changes, it could delay processing or may result in the refusal of the application or the exclusion of a family member.

threads.subject: LMIA exempt job offer and change of working conditions-REP-2024-2095- Due 27-Nov-24
threads.question: Does the TFW need to apply for a change of condition as a worker with a new LMIA-exempt offer of enployment if the wage is around 12 % higher than what was indicated in the initial LMIA-exempt offer of employment ? In other words, is it necessary to submit another offer of employment and reapply for a work permit if the TF W only receives more favorable work conditions (wage, benefits, vacations, etc)?
threads.answer:
Under the International Mobility Program (IMP), all employers, apart from those exempted from the employer compliance regime, who make an offer of employment to a foreign national referred to in subparagraph 200(1 )(c)(ji.1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR) must comply with the conditions imposed under sections R209.2 and R209.4. An employer may be inspected and must ensure they have met these conditions.
Per IRPR 209.2.(1).An employer who has made an offer of employment to a foreign national referred to in subparagraph 200(1)
(c)(ii. 1) must comply with the following conditions:
- “(a) during the period of enployment for which the work permit is issued to the foreign national... (iii) subject to subparagraph (vii), the employer must provide the foreign national with employment in the same occupation as that set out in the foreign national's offer of employment and with wages and working conditions that are substantially the same as — but not less favourable than— those set out in that offer..."
“Substantially the same, but not less favourable, wages" means the following:
- wages paid cannot be less than those outlined in the offer of employment provided as per section R209.1 1(e)(i)(A).
- any unusual deductions (such as transportation costs) should be stated in the offer of employment.
In case of wage increase, proactive notification to IRCC is not required under the IMP, however employers may be inspected on the conditions listed above; therefore, they will have to provide proof at the time of inspection that they met these conditions or provide a justification for why they did not. As per the "Wages" section on the Enployer Compliance webpage, an increase in wages under the IMP may not lead to a finding of non-compliance with respect to providing substantially the same wages under subparagraph R209.2(1)(a)(iii). However, wages paid that are higher than those stated in the offer of employment may indicate a change in duties, which could mean a different occupation than that offered. An increase in wages may also result in a finding
and Citizenshi Canada et Ciloyeneé Canada
that the employer did not provide “substantially the same" wages if the increase would have affected the ability of the foreign national to qualify for the Labour Market Impact Assessment (LMIA) exemption.
Employers who have concerns that they are not meeting conditions of the offer of employment can use the voluntary disclosure process. For more information, please visit the public instructions here: Employer compliance inspections-Canada.ca

threads.subject: Requirement for a COOP work permit-REP-2024-2260 - Due 12-Dec-24
threads.answer:
Good day,
Thank you for your inquiry. Please see the response below:
Work is defined in the Regulations as an activity for which wages are paid or commission is earned, or that competes directly with activities of Canadian citizens or permanent residents in the Canadian labour market. This includes unpaid employment undertaken for the purpose of obtaining work experience, such as an internship or practicum normally done by a student.
Temporary Foreign Worker and International Mobility Programs: What is work? - Canada.ca.
As such, if an unpaid internship or other activity for work experience is required to obtain the credits needed for graduation, an international student is required to apply and obtain a co-op work permit. The work cannot form more than 50% of the total program of study.
Students who are already in Canada and have applied for a co-op work permit may begin their co-op placement using their on-campus and off-campus work authorization, provided they meet all the eligibility requirements.
There is no limit on work hours for on-campus work. A student may accept employment on the campus of the university or college at which they are a full-time student under paragraph 186(f).
For off-campus work authorization, as per paragraph R186(y), students can work a total of 24 hours per week during an academic term or semester while they are waiting for their co-op work permit; however, the 24 hours must include both the hours worked at their co-op job and those worked at their regular paid job (if they have one). They can work full-time during the regularly scheduled breaks.
If the co-op work permit application is refused, they must stop their co-op work immediately.
Please note that the increase from 20 to 24 hours of work off campus while classes are in session took effect on November 8th, 2024. Our websites will be updated shortly.
\cbpat3For more information, please see: Work related to a research, educational or training program– exemption codes C31. C32 and C33 (International Mobility Program) - Canada.ca
We hope this information was helpful.
Thank you kindly,

If a student is suspended from their designated learning institution (DLI) due to academic performance or policy violations, they are considered not enrolled during the suspension period. However, IRCC provides guidelines for leaves from study:

If a student falls out of status and does not extend their study permit (SP), they must leave Canada. However, in the scenario above, the student has changed their status to a visitor. As a visitor in Canada, they can apply for a study permit through one of two ways:
1. Apply for a study permit as though they are outside Canada, provided their visitor status remains valid during the processing period. Once the new study permit is approved, they can resume their studies.
2. Apply for a study permit after completing a prerequisite program.

QUESTION: On the issue of program stacking where a previous credential is completed on a study permit issued prior to November 1, 2024 AND a new credential is completed on a study permit issued on/afterNovember 1, 2024:
- Must BOTH study program CIPs match the new field of study requirements to be PGWP eligible/receive the maximum PGWP length?
- OR is only the new program of study required to meet the field of study requirements to be PGWP eligible/receive the maximum PGWP length?
Please note that the program manual instructions have not been updated since August 15, 2024 to reflect guidance on this issue: [https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-) manuals/temporary-residents/study-permits/post-graduation-work-perimit-prograi.html Response: If the student applies for a study permit extension under the same program of study as the study permit they applied for before November 1, 2024, then they do not need to meet the field of study requirement. If the student applies for a study permit extension under a different program of study than the study permit they applied for before November 1, 2024, then their study permit extension application must meet the field of study requirements applicable to their study program to be eligible for a PGWP. We are in the process of updating the program manual instructions, in the meantime we have recently updated our website to provide clients with further details on the new PGWP eligibility requirements at the following link: Work in Canada after you graduate: Who can apply-Canada.ca

threads.subject: Refugee Status Determination Document-Pakistan-REP-2024-2213 - Due 10-Dec-24
threads.answer:
Hello,
Please note that we do not respond to case specific questions, as each case is assessed by an independent officer considering the particular circumstances in conjunction with the supporting documentation available to them. The onus is always on the applicant to provide sufficient documentation to satisfy an officer that they meet the requirements of the program they are applying under.
However, as per EMPP public policies, we are able to provide the following guidance:
In order to be eligible under the EMPP, the foreign national must possess one of the following documents:
· a positive Refugee Status Determination (RSD) from the UN Refugee Agency or a refugee-hosting state
· proof you’re registered or recorded as a person of concern by the UN Refugee Agency
· a refugee certificate from the United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine in the Near East (UNRWA)
· proof of being registered or recorded as a person of concern with UNRWA
· a Trusted Partner Referral Letter
Please note, proof of being registered or recorded as a person of concern documents are only deemed eligible under the EMPP when issued by the UN Refugee Agency or UNRWA.
The foreign national who does not have one of the above documents, may still be eligible under the EMPP if they have:
· Proof of having Temporary Protected Status issued by the hosting state where the foreign national is residing at the time of their application for permanent residence
This document must be accompanied by a completed durable solution information form (IMM 0195), for an officer to assess.
For the purposes of the Group of Five, the information we currently have indicates that this document is only issued to refugees. Therefore it would likely be considered a valid refugee status document for the purposes of the Group of Five private sponsorship program.
Regards,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.answer:
Hello,
Thank you for your email correspondence to ’s Immigration Representatives mailbox.
This information is provided as general policy guidance and is not a directive for individual case files. For case-specific enquiries, applicants can contact the Department by submitting the IRCC Web form.
Applicants can use the IRCC Portal to submit their application. However, as per the Ministerial Instructions for super visas, a foreign national must apply for a super visa from outside Canada. Iftheir application is approved, and they receive a super visa in their passport, then they may travel to Canada. At the port of entry, a Border Services Officer (BSO) will examine the foreign national as per R180. If the BSO grants entry, then the foreign national is authorized to stay in Canada for 5 years.
A temporary resident visa-including a super visa—does not guarantee entry to Canada, nor does it grant temporary resident status in Canada. It is the BSO who authorizes temporary resident status in Canada. See Temporary resident visa versus temporary resident status for more information.
\sb1 73Please note that it is important for Super Visa holders to ensure that their passport as well as their health insurance remain valid for the duration of their stay in Canada.
We trust that this information will be of assistance.
Sincerely,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

Thank you all again for your ongoing cooperation as we work to implement regulatory changes to the International Student Program, which came into effect on November 8, 2024. As part of the new regulations, students wishing to change designated learning institutions (DLIs) need to apply for a new study permit extension – and most students changing DLIs may only begin
nmigration, Réfugiés studying at the new DLI after the application is approved.
Since the pre-publication of the draft regulations in the Canada Gazette in June 2024, IRCC has been notifying its partners and stakeholders ofthe regulatory changes and that they were expected to come into in the fall. Since the regulations came into force on November 8, 2024, we heard your concerns regarding the impact that it will have on students who intend to change DLIs in January 2025.
As such, the following policy clarification has been issued to provide a grace period for students affected by the timing of this regulation. To be eligible, students must:
- Have been accepted to a DLI for the Winter/ Spring 2025 semester;
- Have applied for a new study permit;
- Have a study permit that remains valid and that doesn't have the DLI name printed on it, and
- Meet all their existing study permit conditions.
International students that meet these conditions may start attending the new DLI they were intending to transfer to while their study permit is being processed.
These regulations are key in providing greater oversight to protect international students, and ensuring that DLIs are meeting their reporting obligations – ultimately strengthening the integrity of the International Student Program.
An updated web notice will be published shortly. In the meantime, please share this information with your members.
Thank you for your attention to this important matter. Should you have any questions or need further clarification, please don't hesitate to contact the following inbox: IRCC.StudentStakeholder-PartiesPrenantesdesetudiants.IRCC@cic.gc.ca.

threads.subject: Study Permit Extensions-New Rule-REP-2024-1997 - Due 18-Nov-24
threads.question: If a student applies for a study permit before November 1, 2024 (currently pursuing one year program this Fall), and later needs to apply for an extension in April 2025 to continue their studies at the same DLI in a new one-year program, will the extended permit be subject to the new "field of study rule" or the current rules in place before November 1 st?
threads.answer:
If the student applies for a study permit extension under the same program of study as the study permit they applied for before November 1, 2024, then they do not need to meet the field of study requirement. If the student applies for a study permit extension under a different program of study than the study permit they applied for before November 1, 2024, then their study permit extension application must meet the field of study requirements applicable to their study program to be eligible for a PGWP.

threads.subject: Second Generation-Citizenship-REP-2024-2152 - Due 3-Dec-24
threads.answer:
Good day,
The Citizenship Act continues to include a first-generation limit to citizenship by descent. This limit generally means someone isn't automatically a Canadian citizen if they were born outside Canada to a Canadian parent, and their Canadian parent was also born outside Canada to a Canadian parent.
In December 2023, the Ontario Superior Court of Justice declared that the first-generation limit (FGL) for many individuals is unconstitutional. However, the Court has suspended the declaration until December 19, 2024. This means that the current rules stil apply until further notice.
Changes to the FGL is also expected to arise from Bill C-71, An Act to amend the Citizenship Act (2024), which was introduced in the House of Commons on May 23, 2024. Bill C-71 and updates on the parliamentary progression of the Bill can be found here: C- 71 (44-1) - LEGISinfo-Parliament of Canada_ This legislation extends citizenship by descent beyond the first generation in a way that is inclusive and protects the value of Canadian citizenship.
At this time, applicants who are subject to the FGL are encouraged to consult the online tool found here: Changes to the first generation limit on citizenship-Canada.ca. Interim measures are in place for applicants affected by the current FGL rules and may submit an application for citizenship certificate along with an urgent processing request. Once submitted, an officer determines if the application qualifies for urgent processing. If the officer finds that the application qualifies for urgent processing the applicant will be offered the option to ask for a discretionary grant of citizenship (meaning they may become a Canadian citizen at the Minister's discretion) as well as the instructions to apply for the grant.
IRCC will continue to update the website information on the changes to the first-generation limit on citizenship here: Canadian citizenship-Canada.ca. Please check back periodically to obtain the most up to date information.
Thank you kindly,

Below is IRCC's guidance with respect to “implied status":
It should be noted that “status” and “authorization" are separate in the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA). A foreign national who submits the “Application to change conditions or extend my stay in Canada – Worker" application form [IMM 5710] is in effect submitting two applications in one. The foreign national is applying under section R181 for an “extension of status” and under section R201 of to “renew the work permit". If submitted before the expiry of their present work permit, this combined application has 3 effects:
1. Should a decision not be made on the “application" under section R181 before the expiration of their present status, the foreign national will be allowed to remain by operation of law (implied status) under subsection R183(5).
2. The application for renewal under section R201 triggers the ability for the foreign national to “work without a permit" under paragraph R1 86(u), unless they leave Canada.
3. Any conditions imposed on the initial work permit carry over into the implied status period under subsection R183(6). For example, if a person held an open work permit, they may continue working for any employer until the new work permit is issued or the application is refused.
Temporary residents authorized to work without a permit
Temporary residents authorized to work in Canada without a permit either pursuant to section R186 or under the Public policy facilitating entry into Canada for short-term work do not hold a work permit and therefore are not applying for a renewal under subsection R201(1).
The authorization to work without a permit under paragraph R186(u) applies only if the temporary resident has applied for a renewal of a valid work permit under section R201.
In addition, those working pursuant to the Public policy facilitating entry into Canada for short-term work are not listed under section R199 and therefore may not apply for a work permit after entry to Canada.
Authorized to work without a permit under section R186 or exempt from the requirement to obtain a work permit pursuant to the Public policy facilitating entry into Canada for short-term work
If the applicant is applying for a new work permit, paragraph R186(u) does not apply.
Open work permit holder

renew an open work permit, paragraph R186(u) applies, and the open work permit conditions continue to apply while the application is being processed o renew the work permit as an employer-specific work permit, paragraph R186(u) applies, and the open work permit conditions continue to apply while the application is being processed change to a study permit or visitor record, paragraph R186(u) does not apply
While R186(u) only specified that an application needs to be made under subsection 201(1), IRCC guidance said that R186(u) only applies if they have applied for a renewal of a valid work permit. Since the work permit request was for a new work permit and not a renewal of a valid work permit, it appears that the claimant would not be able to benefit from R186(u) without applying to extend their existing work permit. However as it is not clearly stated in R186(u), it can also be interpreted that the claimant can benefit from R186(u).

threads.subject: [Request for clarification] International student working hours during scheduled breaks at a DLI-REP-2024-2252
threads.answer:
- Due 11-Dec-24 Hello, Thank you for your inquiry. We can confirm that the responses received on October 23rd, 2023, and January 15th, 2024, are accurate and are the same responses worded differently. The response from December 4th, 2023, would not apply. We sincerely apologize for the confusion.
- By definition, for a break to be considered a regularly scheduled break, it must be part of the DLI's academic calendar (for instance, winter and summer holidays, Reading Week). Each regularly scheduled break should not be longer than 150 days. The max imum cumulative duration of scheduled breaks is 180 days per calendar year. Therefore, if a break is considered a regularly scheduled break based on the DLI's academic calendar, it is also considered to be a scheduled break for the students. However, in order to work off campus without a work permit under paragraph R186(v), students must hold full-time status during the academic session before and after their regularly scheduled break (with the exception of a part-time course load in their final academic session). A student may, on their own, decide to undertake a course load during their scheduled break. This does not change the nature of the DLI designated academic break.
- Additionally, a regularly scheduled break must be for a duration of at least seven consecutive days for eligible students to work off campus on a full-time basis. For example, if an academic break is for a week (including weekends); the student is allowed to work full time for those seven consecutive days.
- Statutory holidays such as labour day, for example, would not on their own constitute a regularly scheduled break, regardless of whether they come before or after a weekend. As a result, on that date, students cannot work on a full-time basis. However, if a statutory holiday falls within an existing scheduled break, for instance, if labour day falls within a reading week break (with 7 consecutive days) slated in the academic calendar, it falls within a regularly scheduled break and the full-time work rules would apply.
We hope that you find this response helpful.
Sincerely,

threads.answer:
Bonjour,
Merci de contacter la boîte électronique pour les représentants en immigration.
Ces renseignements sont fournis à titre d'orientation générale et ne constituent pas une directive pour des dossiers individuels. Pour des demandes de renseignements sur des cas spécifiques, les demandeurs peuvent contacter le Ministère en soumettant le Formulaire Web d'IRCC. Question: Bonjour, J’ai une question par rapport aux nouvelles mesures relatives au changement d’établissement. Nous devions accueillir certains nouveaux étudiants en provenance d’autres EED de même niveau (collégial) à la rentrée de janvier. Nous avons aussi des étudiants qui devaient passer à l’université en janvier. Ils ont tous entrepris leurs démarches dans le contexte où leur permis d’études valide permettait un changement d’établissement facile. Cependant, la nouvelle mesure demandant d’obtenir un nouveau permis d’études lié au nouvel EED avant d’entreprendre les études dans le nouvel EED rend leur projet irréaliste en raison des longs délais de traitement. Y a-t-il une exception d’application de cette mesure pour ce type de candidats qui avaient entamé leurs démarches de changement d’établissement sous les anciennes mesures et pour qui le nom de l’EED n’apparait pas sur le permis d’études encore en cours de validité? (On y voit Établissement d’enseignement désigné sur la ligne de l’institution). Réponse: Les étudiants dont le nom d'EED ne figure pas sur leur permis d'études valide peuvent participer à un nouveau EED s'ils en ont informé IRCC par le portail IRCC avant le 8 novembre 2024. Ceci s'applique également aux étudiants qui ont suivi les instructions fournies par IRCC en utilisant le formulaire web pour changer d'EED entre le 1er novembre 2024 et le 15 novembre
2024. Il est essentiel que ces étudiants s'assurent que leur permis d'études actuel ne comporte aucune condition les empêchant de participer à un autre EED. Les étudiants qui n'ont pas soumis de changement d’EED par leur compte sécurisé IRCC ou le formulaire web pour les dates mentionnées ci-dessus, devront soumettre une demande d'extension de permis d'études pour changer d'EED. Toutefois, veuillez noter que l’IRCC a annoncé un délai additionnel pour les étudiants affectés par le calendrier des nouveaux changements réglementaires, en particulier pour ceux qui ont été acceptés dans un nouvel EED pour la session d’hiver/printemps 2025. Pour plus de renseignements, veuillez consulter le site Web de l'IRCC. Cordialement, Boîte électronique pour les représentants en immigration

threads.subject: Requesting clarification for the new IRCC policy on DLI change-REP-2024-2398 - Due 24-Dec-24
threads.question:
ear IRCC Team, I would like to seek clarification on the new DLI change process. According to the new DLI change process, starting Nov. 8th, 2024 students must be enrolled in the DLI named on their study permit. It states on the page that students can no longer change DLIs by letting IRCC know through their IRCC account. To change DLIs, now students must apply for a new study permit. Reference: [https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/study-canada/change-schools.html](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/study-canada/change-schools.html)
If a student applied to change their DLI using their IRCC secure account or via Webform prior to November 8th but have not received a confirmation from IRCC that their DLI has been changed yet, can they start at the new DLI without submitting a new study permit? Also, students who submitted a study permit extension before Nov. 8th and wanted to change their DLI so they submitted the new Letter of Acceptance with their study permit application, can they start studying at the new DLI until a decision is made on their study permit extension application?
threads.answer:
Good day, The following students do not need to apply for a new study permit:
- Students who have informed IRCC of the change in their Designated Learning institutions (DLI) using their IRCC account prior to November 8, 2024.
- Students who followed the instructions provided by IRCC using the webform to change DLIs between November 1, 2024 and November 15, 2024.
These students must ensure that there are no conditions are imposed on their current study permit that prevents them from attending another DLI. Students after November 8, 2024, who have not submitted a DLI change through their IRCC secure account or web-form will need to apply for a new study permit extension if they are changing DLIs. Please note that IRCC has announced a grace period for students impacted by the timing of the new regulations, specifically for those accepted to a new DLI for the winter/spring semester of 2025. For more information, please refer to the IRCC website.
Sincerely,

threads.answer:
Good afternoon,
We are happy to provide a response to your questions. Please note that we cannot answer case-specific questions but have provided the following information as guidance.
The former Immigration Act came into force in 1978. Under the former Immigration Act, permanent residents (PRs) had to have the “intention" to live in Canada. Pursuant to paragraph 24(1)(a) of the Immigration Act, a person ceases to be a PR when that person leaves or remains outside of Canada with the intention of abandoning Canada as that person’s place of permanent residence." For further clarification, residence was deemed abandoned “where a PR is outside of Canada for more than one hundred and eighty-three days in any twelve month period, that person shall be deemed to have abandoned Canada as his place of permanent residence unless that person satisfies an immigration officer or an adjudicator, as the case may be, that he did not intend to abandon Canada as his place of permanent residence." Under the Immigration Act, intent to abandon was the test for retaining permanent resident status. The residency obligations as we know it today were not introduced until the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act came into force in 2001.
An archived copy of the Immigration Act can be found here.
We hope you find this information helpful.

threads.answer:
Hello,
Thank you for your inquiry.
- By definition, for a break to be considered a regularly scheduled break, it must be part of the DLI's academic calendar (for instance, winter and summer holidays, Reading Week). Each regularly scheduled break should not be longer than 150 days. The maximum cumulative duration of scheduled breaks is 180 days per calendar year. Therefore, if a break is considered a regularly scheduled break based on the DLI's academic calendar, it is also considered to be a scheduled break for the students. However, in order to work off campus without a work permit under paragraph R186(v), students must hold full-time status during the academic session before and after their regularly scheduled break (with the exception of a part-time course load in their final academic session). Les critères des domaines d’études s’appliquent donc à tous nos programmes sauf au Baccalauréat. Le tourisme, l’hôtellerie et la restauration étant malheureusement exclus de domaines admissibles, nous avons plusieurs questions pour nos étudiants actuels qui doivent renouveler leur permis d’études. J’ai 3 cas de figure où j’aimerais des précisions :
- J’ai plusieurs étudiants dans des programmes qui doivent renouveler leur permis d’études après le 1er novembre, car la lettre d’introduction avait été émise trop tard et leurs rentrées ont dû être repoussées. Ex. : Étudiants au DEP (programme de 18 mois/1 890h), admis pour l’aout 2023, lettre d’introduction reçue par l’étudiant en septembre ou octobre, donc rentrée reporté à janvier 2024. Le programme devait se terminer en décembre 2024, mais suite au report se terminera en mai 2025. Le permis demandé avant le 1er novembre 2024 est valide jusqu’à la fin mars 2025. Ces étudiants doivent donc maintenant renouveler leur permis (après le 1er novembre) pour pouvoir terminer leur programme. Quelle date de demande de permis sera prise en compte l’initial ou la demande de renouvellement afin de savoir s’ils doivent se conformer au domaine d’études admissible?
- Deuxième cas de figure, suite à un DEP en cuisine (18 mois) par exemple, des étudiants aimeraient poursuivre vers un programme de poursuite une ASP toujours en cuisine (9 mois). Ces étudiants devraient demander une prolongation de leur permis d’étude afin de poursuivre leurs études dans notre établissement ? Le permis initial a été demandé avant le 1er novembre 2024, mais la demande de prolongation se fera après le 1 er novembre 2024. Quelle date de demande de permis sera prise en compte l’initial ou la demande de renouvellement afin de savoir s’ils doivent se conformer au domaine d’études admissible?
- Finalement, 3e cas de figure, des étudiants avaient été admis dans un programme différent avec un permis demandé avant le 1 er novembre, ils ont changé de programme et ont débuté leurs études chez nous. Leur programme se termine après la date d’expiration de leur permis qui avait été délivré pour un autre EED et un autre domaine d’études (sans mention sur le PE). Ces étudiants qui demanderont une prolongation de leur Permis d’études après le 1 er novembre 2024 ? Comment sera traitée leur demande de PTPD ? Quelle date de demande de permis sera prise en compte l’initial ou la demande de renouvellement afin de savoir s’ils doivent se conformer au domaine d’études admissible?
En résumé, en cas de renouvellement, quelle date de demande de permis sera prise en compte l’initial ou la demande de renouvellement afin de savoir s’ils doivent se conformer au domaine d’études admissible? Et y a-t-il des différences s’il s’agit d’un renouvellement pour poursuivre un même programme (report d’admission ou échéance du passeport ou du CAQ avant la fin du programme ou prolongation du programme suite à des échecs, un congé de maladie autorisé ou autre), une poursuite d’études dans le même EED au même niveau d’enseignement ou encore un renouvellement de permis d’études suite à un changement de programme et de EED ?

Students who have already changed DLIs before November 8 and who have already started their programs at the new DLI should have submitted their DLI transfer information in their online account as per the instructions in effect before the regulation changes. Additionally, can they begin their studies in January 2025 while their study permit application is still pending? Answer Since November 8, 2024, students who wish to change DLIs will need to apply for a new study permit extension. However, the following students do not need to apply for a new study permit:
- Students who have informed IRCC of the change in their Designated Learning institutions (DLI) using their IRCC account prior to November 8, 2024.

threads.subject: Post Graduate Work Permit updates-REP-2024-2052- Due 22-Nov-24
threads.question: f0I wanted to get some clarification about new PGWP changes coming to effect as of Nov 1, 2024. On website it says, if you submit your study permit application on or after Nov 1, 2024, applicants must meet the new requirements of language and field of study requirements. I wanted to check if an initial study permit was submitted before Nov 1, 2024 and student submitted study permit extension after nov 1, 2024; would the same rules will apply to study permit extensions as well.
threads.answer:
All PGWP applications (except those from flight school graduates) submitted on or after November 1, 2024 must comply with the new language requirements, regardless of when the student applied for their study permit or when they started their program of study. If the student applied for a study permit extension under the same program of study as the study permit they applied for before November 1, 2024, then they do not need to meet the field of study requirement. If the student applied for a study permit extension under a different program of study than the study permit they applied for before November 1, 2024, then their study permit extension application must meet the field of study requirements applicable to their study program to be eligible for a PGWP. We have recently updated our website to provide clients with further details on the new PGWP eligibility requirements at the following link: Work in Canada after you graduate: Who can apply-Canada.ca We hope this information is of assistance.
