threads.answer:
Bonjour,
Veuillez noter que la boîte aux lettres des représentants en immigration ne peut répondre qu’aux demandes générales relatives aux programmes ou aux politiques d'immigration et qu'aucune réponse spécifique à un cas ne peut être fournie.
Un permis de travail coop est un permis de travail ouvert et peut être utiliser pour travailler dans le programme coop pour lequel le permis a été demandé, si l’étudiant demeure éligible à l’utiliser. Les détenteurs d’un permis de travail coop doivent également s’assurer de respecter les conditions indiqués sur leur permis.
Veuillez prendre note qu’un agent peut recommander l'imposition de conditions lors de la délivrance d'un permis à l’égard d’un résident temporaire conformément à l'article Rl85. À ce titre, s’il y a un lieu de travail indiqué sur un permis de travail, le détenteur de ce permis n'est autorisé à travailler que dans le lieu de travail qui y in indiqué. Que la déclaration soit rédigée dans les sections des conditions ou des remarques, elle sert les mêmes objectifs et ne fait aucune différence. Les étudiants sont liés par les deux de manière égale.
Si une condition figurant sur le permis d'un étudiant ne s'applique pas à l'étudiant ou s'il pense que la condition a été introduite par erreur, le titulaire du permis d'études et du permis coop peut demander une modification de ses conditions.
Nous espérons que ces informations vous seront utiles.

threads.subject: Seeking clarification on recent amendments to IRPR R189.1 and R217.1 - REP-2024-2367 - Due 20-Dec-24
threads.answer:
Good day,
Thank you for contacting the Immigration Represe ntatives Mailbox
Please note that this mailbox is intended for general guidance and does not provide responses to case-specific inquiries. Ifyou have case specific questions about a file, you are encouraged to submit a Webform at: http//www.ircc.canada.ca/english/contacts/web-form.asp
I am writing to seek clarification regarding the recent amendments to sections 189.1 and 217.1 IRPR, as outlined in the Canada Gazette. Specifically, I would like to inquire about the following scenarios:
- New study permit application
- 189.1 A foreign national who has submitted an application for a new study permit in accordance with section 217.1 is authorized to study at the designated learning institution, as defined in section 211.1, that is named in that application until a decision is made on the application if ...
- Change of designated learning institution
- 217.1 If the holder of a study permit in Canada whose permit names a designated learning institution is accepted to undertake a course or program of study at a different designated learning institution and intends to attend that new institution, they must submit an application for a new study permit that name the new designated learning institution.
In the case that the DLI's name was not explicated named on client's study permit, for example, the Institution Name on study permit was mark as “DESIGNATED LEARNING INST-ON”, and there is not DLI's name in the condition section, would the client still be required to submit new study permit and wait for the approval if they wish to change DLI? Or in this case, they should follow the previous process by submit a webform to inform IRCC and can commerce their study at any new DLI (including other province) imminently?
A1: Students who have informed IRCC of the change in their Designated Learning institutions (DLI) using their IRCC account prior to November 8, 2024, and students who followed the instructions provided by IRCC using the webform to change DLIs between November 1, 2024 and November 15, 2024, do not need to submit a new study permit application to change DLIs. These students must ensure that there are no conditions are imposed on their current study permit that prevents them from attending another DLI.
Students after November 8, 2024, who have not submitted a DLI change through their IRCC secure account or web-form wil need to apply for a new study permit extension if they are changing DLIs.
Please note that IRCC has issued a grace period for students impacted by the timing of the new regulations, specifically for those accepted to a new DLI for the winter/spring semester of 2025. For more information, please refer to the IRCC website.
Cioyenneté Canada
Lnmn Q2: In the case of section 217.1 of the IRPR applies and the client holds a study permit specifying a named DLI, could you please clarify the following situation:
If the client submits an application for a new study permit, and their previous permit expires while awaiting the decision, with their studies at the previous DLI already completed, would maintained status still apply in this case, allowing the client to legally remain in Canada? Alternatively, would the client also need to apply for a visitor record to maintain legal status?
A2: Students that apply for a new study permit prior to the expiration of their current study permit continue to maintain their status. Please note, students may be required or may wish to take leave from their studies while in Canada. For the purpose of assessing if a student is actively pursuing their studies, any leave taken from a program of studies in Canada should not exceed 150 days from the date the leave commenced and must be authorized by their DLI.
For more information, please see the following link: Your conditions as a study permit holder in Canada-Canada.ca
Sincerely,

Please note the Temporary public policy to exempt certain in-Canada foreign nationals from the inmigration medical examination requirement has been extended until October 5, 2029. If a client currently resides in Canada and has completed an IME within the last 5 years, they may be exempt from the requirement to complete an additional medical exam. Please note that the foreign national must meet the following conditions to be exempt from a subsequent IME:
0. Has submitted an application to become a permanent resident or for a permanent residence visa and is physically present in Canada;
1. Has submitted to an Immigration Medical Examination within five years prior to the coming into effect of this temporary public policy;
2. The Department has a record of that Immigration Medical Examination, and the most recent examination submitted to was assessed and coded as:
a. M1: indicating they pose no danger to public health and public safety;
b. M3 (except where they have been assessed and coded as “TR only" or “EDE only’): indicating they have a health condition present but are not expected to place an excessive demand on health or sócial services; or
c. M2 or M2/3 (except where they have been assessed and coded as “TR only” or “EDE only’): indicating they are a potential risk to public health, but they have complied with their requirement to report to provincial/territorial health authorities for medical surveillance; and
3. Has not resided or stayed for a total period in excess of six months in an area that the Minister determines has a higher incidence of serious communicable disease than Canada (i.e., identified on IRCC's tuberculosis designated country and territory list) within the year prior to the coming into effect of this temporary public policy.

The date and time of receipt are important for determining if status is maintained under subsection R183(5). For electronic applications, the department uses Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) around the world to ensure that time is equal for all. Therefore, receipt dates and times do not depend on time zones; all applications must be submitted before midnight UTC on the date the applicant's status expires. If the application was received after midnight UTC on the date of expiry, the applicant does not maintain their status under subsection R183(5).

If a student completes two consecutive programs that are PGWP-eligible within two years of completion of the first program when applying for a PGWP, both programs could be considered for the purpose of determining the length of the PGWP.
\sb240To qualify for program stacking in relation to PGWP duration, both PGWP-eligible programs must be:
- a minimum of 8 months in duration; and
- completed at a PGWP-eligible DLI within 2 years of the completion of the first program

According to the new PGWP requirements, it indicates CLB 7/NCLC 7 is required for graduates from a "university" bachelor's, master's or doctoral degree, and CLB 5/NCLC 5 is required for graduates from college program or any other prograns not listed above. Could you please clarify the language requirements for graduates who completed a bachelor's degree from a college?
RESPONSE:
Graduates that acquire a college credential, including those pursuing bachelor's degree programs, will be required to demonstrate minimun language proficiency CLB/NCLC 5 when applying for a PGWP on or after November 1, 2024.
QUESTION 2:
Also, as per the current PGWP validity criteria, students would qualify for 3-year PGWP by completing 2 one-year programs if the total duration of their study is 2 years or longer. Would it still apply after the new PGWP requirements come into effect on Nov 1, 2024 if both programs are related to a field of study?
RESPONSE:
On or after November 1, 2024, if a student completes two consecutive programs that are PGWP-eligible within two years of completion of the first program when applying for a PGWP, both prograns could be considered for the purpose of determining the length of the PGWP (referred to as "program stacking"). If the combined length of the eligible programs is 2 years or longer, the PGWP may be valid for up to 3 years.
To qualify for program stacking in relation to PGWP duration, both PGWP-eligible programs must be:
- a minimum of 8 months in duration; and
- completed at a PGWP-eligible DLI within 2 years of the completion of the first program.
In determining whether a program is PGWP-eligible:
- the language requirement is applicable to all PGWP applications (except those from flight school graduates) submitted on or after November 1, 2024, regardless of when the student applied for their study permit or when they started their program of study.
- the field of study requirement is applicable depending on the level of study and when a student applies for their student permit. o If the student applies for a study permit extension under the same program of study as the study permit they applied for before November 1, 2024, then they do not need to meet the field of study requirement. o If the student applies for a study permit extension under a different program of study than the study permit they applied for before November 1, 2024, then their study permit extension application must meet the field of study requirements applicable to their study program to be eligible for a PGWP.

Students who are changing DLI but remaining in the same program-will they be able to maintain PGWP eligibility if they will not be able to start in Winter 2025? Our understanding is they will not be able to start studying on their secondary study permit as they were allowed before. They will need a new study permit to start the program, correct?
threads.answer:
We understand the challenges posed by these changes for students attending a new DLI in the winter 2025 semester. We encourage students to regularly check the IRCC website as we make further updates to it. PGWP applicants must meet all applicable requirements to be eligible for a PGWP. This includes maintaining full-time status as a student in Canada at a PGWP-eligible DLI during each semester of their study program, although an exception to this requirement includes students who have taken an approved leave from their studies. For more information on the PGWP eligibility requirements, please see: Work in Canada after you graduate: Who can apply-Canada.ca For more information on what counts as an authorized leave from studies, please see: Your conditions as a study permit holder in Canada-Canada.ca Please note that new PGWP requirements came into effect on November 1, 2024.
- If a student applies for a study permit extension on or after November 1, 2024, under the same program for which they have study authorization via the study permit they applied for before November 1, 2024, then they do not need to meet the new field of study requirement.
- If a student applies for a study permit extension under a different program from the one they were granted study authorization via the study permit they applied for before November 1, 2024, then their study permit extension application must meet the new field of study requirements applicable to their program to be eligible for a PGWP.
- All PGWP applications (except those from flight school graduates) submitted on or after November 1, 2024 must comply with the new language requirements, regardless of when the student applied for their study permit or when they started their program of study.

The following students do not need to apply for a new study permit:
- Students who have informed IRCC of the change in their Designated Learning institutions (DLI) using their IRCC account prior to November 8, 2024.
- Students who followed the instructions provided by IRCC using the webform to change DLIs between November 1, 2024 and November 15, 2024.
These students must ensure that there are no conditions are imposed on their current study permit that prevents them from attending another DLI. Students after November 8, 2024, who have not submitted a DLI change through their IRCC secure account or web-form will need to apply for a new study permit if they are changing DLIs.

Students that submitted a study permit extension application before November 8, 2024 and has been approved for a new program starting in Winter/Spring 2025 do not need to apply for a new study permit. However, if they decide to change DLIs they will need to submit a new study permit extension application.

Secondary school students need to apply for a new study permit to attend a post-secondary school. If a student finishes their secondary school studies early, their study permit will no longer be valid 90 days after they complete their studies, regardless of the date that is shown on their study permit.
\sb160For more information, please visit the IRCC Website.
Thank you kindly,

When a foreign national applies for a new or subsequent TRP, they are not applying under R181 as they do not meet the requirements listed in R179. Therefore, when a TRP applicant applies for a TRP, they are not applying for an extension of their authorization to remain in Canada, they are making an application for a TRP under A24(1). As a result, TRP applicants, either for a new or subsequent TRP, do not meet R181(2) and do not benefit from maintained status as outlined in R183(5). As per R186(u), a FN may only be able to renew their work permit and be authorized to work without a permit under maintained status if they meet R201(1). A FN that requires a TRP to remain in Canada will not have met R201(1)(b). Thus, they are not eligible to renew their work permit and work without a valid work permit as they do not hold maintained status.

Ifyou have case specific questions about a file, you are encouraged to submit a Webform at: [http://www.ircc.canada.ca/english/contacts/web-form.asp](http://www.ircc.canada.ca/english/contacts/web-form.asp)
QUESTION:
In cases where students are program stacking with a 1-year program completed before 1 November 2024 and another 1-year program completed after 1 November 2024, does the first program get grandfathered in under the old rules? Or does the field of study requirement now apply retroactively (to both periods of study)?
- In order words, if the program completed before 1 November 2024 fails to satisfy the field of study criterion, does that mean the Applicant only gets a 1-year (provided that the program completed after 1 November 2024 meets the progran of study requirement)? Or do they get a 3-year work permit?
RESPONSE:
The field of study requirement is applicable to an individual program depending on when the applicant applies for the study permit associated to the program. Please note that the field of study requirement is applicable based on the applicant's level of study and the date they applied for their study permit (rather than when they completed the program of study).
For the first program, since they would have applied for the associated study permit before November 1, 2024, the field of study
requirement would not apply to that program for the purposes of PGWP eligibility.
For the second program, the field of study requirement only applies if the applicant applied for the associated study permit on or after November 1, 2024. If the student applied for their study permit to pursue the second program on or after November 1, 2024, then they must meet the field of study requirement for the program to be considered PGWP-eligible.
Assuming the student applied for their study permit for the second program on or after November 1, 2024, only the second program would need to meet the field of study requirement, since this requirement would not be applicable to the first one. If the student's second program meets the field of study requirement, and both non-university programs were 1-year in duration, then the student may be eligible for a 3-year PGWP, noting that all other PGWP eligibility requirements must be met.
We hope this information is of assistance.
Thank you kindly.

Students who have maintained full-time status for the duration of their program of study, and who only require a part-time course load in their final academic session in order to complete their program of study, are allowed to work full-time during the regularly scheduled break before their last semester and are allowed to work off campus up to 20 hours per week during their final academic session. Response: Students who intend to perform work that is an essential part of a post-secondary academic, vocational or professional training program offered by a designated learning institution (DLI) in Canada. The work cannot form more than 50% of the total program of study.
- Students who are already in Canada and have applied for a co-op work permit may begin their co-op placement using their on-campus and off-campus work authorization, provided they meet all the eligibility requirements. There is no limit on work hours for on-campus work. A student may accept employment on the campus of the university or college at which they are a full-time student under paragraph 186(f) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR). For off-campus work authorization, as per paragraph R186(v), students can work a total of 20 hours per week during an academic term or semester while they are waiting for their co-op work permit; however, the 20 hours must include both the hours worked at their co-op job and those worked at their regular paid job (if they have one). threads.question:
I have a question regarding the on-campus work authorization for international students enrolled in two DLIs at the same time. If a student has enrolled FT at both institutions (at one DLI they are registered FT in a degree program; at another DLI, they are FT registered as a non-degree student) and they can only indicate one DLI to the IRCC, which one is considered as a main DLI and hence on-campus work authorization applies.
Our take was that students could select which DLI to indicate and use the selected as a main DLI, considering they maintain FT enrollment at both and the on-campus work authorization would apply to the selected DLI. Could you please clarify if this is correct.
threads.answer:
In the case of a student who is attending two DLIs, their primary DLI would be the one where they are currently enrolled and pursuing the larger portion of their studies. Please note that for studies longer than 6 months, the student will require a second study permit for this DLI and program.
As ofNovember 8, 2024, students must be enrolled in the designated learning institution (DLI) named on their study permit. This means they can no longer change DLIs by letting IRCC know through their online account. To change DLIs, they will need to get a new study permit by applying to extend their current one.

Are these students required to take the General IELTS/CELPIP for their PGWP application, or will their current scores from the Academic test be accepted?
threads.answer:
If the applicant graduated with a bachelor's degree, master's degree or doctoral degree from a university, the applicant must prove their English or French language skills with a minimum level of Canadian Language Benchmarks (CLB) 7 in English or Niveaux de competence linguistique canadiens (NCLC) 7 in French in all 4 language areas: reading, writing, listening and speaking. The test results must be less than 2 years old at time of application submission.
Please note that applications are assessed on an individual basis, and officers must be satisfied that all requirements are met. The onus is on the applicant to provide sufficient documentation to satisfy an officer that they meet the requirements. An officer will review and make a decision based on the supporting documentation submitted by the applicant.

International students may work as part of a co-op or internship program only if work is an essential part of an academic, professional or vocational training program offered by a Designated Learning Institution. The Designated Learning Institution determines the co-op or intern study program requirements. If the student is eligible (that is, meets certain conditions), an open work permit can be issued with the Designated Learning Institution listed as the employer. A student can keep studying at the current DLI with an existing study permit as long as the student still meets the study permit conditions. However, if the student is changing schools, there is a new process for post-secondary study permit holders-Starting November 8, 2024, if a student wants to change the post-secondary school, they need to obtain a new study permit.
If the officer determines that a PGWP applicant did not meet the conditions of their study permit, they may be prohibited from being issued a work permit for 6 months from the date they stopped their unauthorized study or work, as per subparagraph R200(3)(e)(i) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations.
For further information: Find out more
In the context of stacking multiple programs towards the duration of the PGWP, on or after November 1, 2024, if a student completes two consecutive programs that are PGWP-eligible within two years of completion of the first program when applying for a PGWP, both programs could be considered for the purpose of determining the length of the PGWP.
To qualify for program stacking in relation to PGWP duration, both PGWP-eligible programs must be:
- a minimum of 8 months in duration; and
- completed at a PGWP-eligible DLI within 2 years of the completion of the first program
In determining whether a program is PGWP-eligible, the field of study requirement is applicable depending on the level of study and when a student applies for their student permit:
- If the student applies for a study permit extension under the same program for which they have study authorization via the study permit they applied for before November 1, 2024, then they do not need to meet the field of study requirement.
- If the student applies for a study permit extension under a different program from the one they were granted study authorization via the study permit they applied for before November 1, 2024, then their study permit extension application must meet the field of study requirements applicable to their study program to be eligible for a PGWP.

A2: Under R220.1(1)(a), a study permit holder is considered compliant as long as they are actively pursuing their course or program of study at a designated learning institution (DLI). If a student withdrew from their original DLI and switched to another DLI prior to November 8th, they would not be non-compliant under this provision, as long as they followed the appropriate process for transferring between institutions and remained enrolled at the new DLI.
Q2: Regarding R220.1(1)(a) and (b): does a SP-holder become non-compliant under this section if they had withdrawn from their original DLI and did not enroll into any new studies?
A2: Under R220.1(1)(a) and (b), a study permit holder becomes non-compliant if they withdraw from their original DLI and do not enroll in any new studies. The conditions state that the permit holder must be enrolled at the designated learning institution named in their permit and actively pursue their course or program of study. If they withdraw and do not enroll in a new program, they are no longer meeting these conditions and are considered non-compliant.
Q3: Regarding R222(1)(a): did the SP become invalid on November 8th if the SP-holder had withdrawn from the original DLI and switched to another DLI prior to this date?
A3: Based on R222(1)(a), a study permit becomes invalid 90 days after the permit holder completes their studies or is no longer enrolled at the DLI named in the permit. The 90 days do not apply in this scenario as the student has withdrawn from their studies, rather than completing their studies. If a student withdrew from their original DLI and switched to another DLI before November 8th, 2024, the student should have changed DLI via their IRCC Account. However, if the student changed DLIs after November 8th, they will need to apply for a new study permit extension.
Q4: Regarding R222(1)(a): did the SP become invalid on November 8th if the SP-holder had withdrawn from the original DLI and had not enroll into any new studies prior to this date?
A4: Under R222(1)(a), if a study permit holder withdrew from their original DLI and did not enroll in any new studies, they are breaching the conditions of their study permit as they are not actively pursuing studies.

Please note that we are not able to provide case-specific guidance. Under current instructions, a student on a leave from studies that was authorized by their designated learning institution (DLI), who did not resume their studies by the end of the authorized leave period, should either leave Canada, or change to visitor status or worker status. - avoir obtenu un permis d’études ayant été valide au cours des 180 derniers jours

Tandis que sur le site Permis de travail postdiplôme (PTPD) [R205c) - C43]- Programme de mobilité internationale-Canada.ca l’on voit que pour être admissible il faut absolument détenir un permis d’études valide.
Au Canada – permis d’études valide
Les permis d’études sont généralement délivrés pour 90 jours au-delà de la date de fin prévue du programme. Toutefois, les étudiants étrangers disposent de 180 jours à partir de la fin de leurs études pour présenter une demande de PTPD. Les demandeurs doivent conserver leur statut au Canada et leur capacité de présenter une demande depuis le Canada en vertu de l’article 199 du RIPR.
Les demandeurs peuvent présenter une demande de PTPD depuis le Canada si leur permis d’études est toujours valide (non expiré) ou s’ils satisfont à l’une des autres exigences énoncées à l’article 199 du RIPR au moment de présenter leur demande.
Conformément à l’alinéa 186w) du RIPR, le diplômé qui demande un permis de travail avant l’expiration de son permis d’études peut être autorisé à travailler sans permis de travail en attendant une décision relative à sa demande.
Important : Si un étranger a présenté une demande de prolongation de son permis d’études et qu’il étudie en vertu de l’article 189 du RIPR, l’article 199 ne s’applique pas à lui, et il doit attendre la réception de son nouveau permis d’études pour être
admissible en vertu de l’article 199.
Les délais de traitement des renouvellements de permis d'études ayant augmenté de manière exponentielle ces derniers mois, de nombreux étudiants finissants se retrouvent en statut conservé. Nous leur expliquons qu’ils doivent attendre que leur permis d'études soit approuvé avant de pouvoir déposer une demande de permis de travail postdiplôme au Canada, cependant les informations figurant sur le site web public les induisent en erreur.
Merci d'avance de l'attention que vous porterez à ce message.
Cordialement,

Distance learning
Distance learning can be through e-learning, correspondence, or Internet courses. Distance learning is a process by which technology is used in ways where the student does not have to physically be in the place where the teaching is taking place. Since by definition distance learning does not require one to be in Canada, a study permit cannot be issued for this type of course. For example, if a foreign national authorized to work in Canada is prohibited from engaging in studies as per a condition of their work permit, they are allowed to engage in distance learning courses. However, some distance learning courses include an in-Canada portion to the program (e.g., special tutorials or the writing of final exams). If the overall course of study is greater than six months, then the student requires a study permit for the in-Canada portion of the program, even if the in-Canada portion is less than six months. The duration of the study permit should be for the duration of the in-Canada portion only.

Merci pour votre réponse. Je souhaite préciser davantage ma demande initiale afin d’apporter plus de clarté à la situation.
1. Un Permis de séjour temporaire (PST)
2. Une fiche de visiteur, dont la durée de validité est alignée sur celle du PST.
Depuis son arrivée au Canada, cet enfant a obtenu un passeport ukrainien valide, ce qui élimine les motifs d’inadmissibilité ayant initialement justifié l’octroi du PST.
Actuellement, l’enfant souhaite prolonger son séjour au Canada et obtenir soit un permis de travail ouvert, soit un permis d’études.
Cependant, dans la pratique, les clients dans une situation similaire, titulaires d’un PST et d’un autre permis (soit d’études, soit de travail), voient systématiquement leurs demandes de changement de statut refusées. Les agents justifient ces refus en indiquant que le demandeur doit soumettre une nouvelle demande de PST, ce qui est incohérent puisque l’enfant possède désormais un passeport valide et n’est plus inadmissible.
Ainsi, selon ma compréhension de la situation actuelle, il est impossible de changer un PST vers un autre statut temporaire (par exemple, celui d’étudiant ou de travailleur) tout en restant au Canada. La seule option prévue dans la loi serait de quitter le Canada pour mettre fin au PST. Toutefois, cette solution n’est pas réalisable, car l’enfant ne dispose pas d’un visa de résident temporaire (VRT) apposé dans son passeport, ce qui rend tout retour impossible après son départ.
Je souhaite donc obtenir des précisions sur la procédure à suivre pour prolonger son statut temporaire en tant qu'étudiant ou travailleur, compte tenu du fait qu’il détient simultanément un PST et une fiche de visiteur, et qu’il n’existe pas de motifs valables pour demander un nouveau PST sans quitter le pays.
Cette problématique est fréquente parmi les personnes ukrainiennes arrivées au Canada sans passeport mais en ayant obtenu un sur place.
Je reste à votre disposition pour tout renseignement complémentaire et vous remercie pour votre assistance.

threads.question:
1. you have been working full-time for the employer on your work permit for at least 1 year (or an equal amount of part-time work)
Does this require applicants to have been working on the qualifying LMIA-exempt work permit itself for at least one year? Or does this criterion only require applicants to work for the employer listed on the current qualifying LMIA-exempt work permit for at least one year, regardless of how long they have held that work permit itself?
For example, if an applicant worked for an employer for 11 months on an open post-graduate work permit, and then for one month on an LMIA-exempt, employer specific work permit as free trade agreement professional for that same employer, would this be sufficient for obtaining points for an LMIA-exempt job offer assuming all other requirements are met?
threads.answer:
Yes, the applicant can count the 11 months on an open PGWP and the one month on the LMIA-exempt towards their one year of work experience for arranged employment. To obtain the points for arranged employment under 29 of the Ministerial Instructions respecting the Express Entry System, the applicant must have gained the work experience under the same employer, however there is no specification this work experience must be gained with an employer specific work permit, so that points would be granted. The work experience must still meet the requirements of the program. The applicant must still hold a valid work permit issued under the circumstances described in paragraph 204(a) or (c) or section 205 of the Regulations.
Please be advised that the assessment of an application is based on a case-by-case basis; each application will be considered on its own merits, with a final decision based on a review of all the information available to the officer at the time of decision. The onus is always on the applicant to provide sufficient documentation to satisfy an officer that they meet the requirements.

Operational instructions and guidelines-PR-EE-Assessing an electronic application on section A11.2:
After an e-APR is submitted, an application cannot be refused due to a change in circumstance unless

Family members can be added to the application at any time during the process, including after the visa is issued, but prior to obtaining permanent resident status.

threads.answer:
Please note that we do not answer case-specific questions. The Federal Skilled Worker program and the Category- based selection rounds require that qualifying work experience is obtained during continuous employment to be eligible towards the minimum selection criteria. The continuous requirement applies both to full-time work and its part-time equivalent. It is meant to make periodic, intermittent, seasonal, infrequent, or brief employment ineligible for the minimum selection criteria under these programs. Vacation periods, regular sick leave and other standard paid leave entitlements as provided for in collective agreements, workplace legislation and/or individual employer policies are not necessarily considered interruptions in continuous
For work experience to be considered continuous in the Express Entry system, work history must be entered without any gaps in employment, regardless of the job title entered. For work experience declared, an officer must be satisfied that the client was performing the duties listed in the lead statement of the occupational description in the National Occupational Classification, including most of the main duties listed. The assessment of an application is based on a case-by-case basis, considering the particular circumstances in conjunction with the supporting documentation available to the officer. The onus is on the applicant to provide sufficient documentation to satisfy an officer that they meet the requirements, and that they were able to successfully perform the duties of the NOC in two concurrent ful-time jobs. Les étrangers peuvent présenter une demande de permis de travail postdiplôme (PTPD) :

- * à l’extérieur du Canada (article 197 du RIPR).
Les demandeurs éligibles peuvent présenter une demande pour le PTPD à un moment donné au cours des 180 jours suivant l’obtention de leur diplôme.

De : Envoyé : 3 décembre 2024 16:55 À : Objet : Provincial Attestation Letters and Extensions
Dear ImmReps,
I am seeking clarity regarding whether Provincial Attestation Letters (PALs") are required for existing study permit holders who apply for changes in conditions (e.g. to attend a new DLI). This seems to be inconsistent with the legal basis for PALs as follows:
1. As far as I’m aware, PAL is a creature of MI 70. The MI sets out its scope as: These Instructions apply to applications for a study permit made under the student class, referred to in Part 12 of the Regulations, except for:
a. study permit applications referred to in subsection 215(1) of the Regulations;
b. study permit applications referred to in subsection 215(2) of the Regulations;
c. study permit applications from foreign nationals planning to study at the primary school or secondary school level; or
d. study permit applications from foreign nationals planning to study in a graduate degree program at the master's or doctorate level.
The MI, and therefore the PAL requirement, is not applicable to situations covered by IRPR 215(1) and (2) which basically involve all permitted SP applications from within Canada. This would include applications by existing SP holders whether for extensions or otherwise.
2. Students who change institutions after beginning study in Canada would presumably fall under IRPR 215(1). Of course, if their SP expires or is invalidated due to non-enrolment under IRPR 222(1)(a.1), then that would no longer bring them under IRPR 215(1), but let’s assume their SP is valid when they apply for a new SP.
3. The application for a new SP within Canada to attend another DLI would presumably be for a “change of conditions" and not necessarily an extension.
4. IRCC guidance regarding PALs indicates that the PAL 215(1) exemption is for extensions (somewhat unclearly, but the reference to extensions only is there). However, this distinction seems to only be made in the IRCC guidance and not in either MI 70 or IRPR 215(1). I wonder, therefore, how requiring a PAL for a valid SP holder applying for a SP within Canada for a new DLI would be supported in law?
Thank you
Kind regards,

As stated on our website, commercial transporters are legally required to ensure passengers are properly documented for travel to Canada. Section 148 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA) outlines the obligations of commercial carriers and section 259 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR) lists the prescribed documents that a person requires to enter Canada. A permanent resident (PR) that does not hold any of the prescribed documents outlined in section 259 of the IRPR should not be permitted to board a commercial carrier. Expired PR cards, Confirmation of Permanent Residence (CoPR) documents, and Records ofLanding (IMM 1000) are not valid for travel to Canada, but may indicate that a client held PR status at one point in time.
Section 11.3 of ENF 4 outlines the procedures for examining PRs at ports of entry (POEs). If a PR arrives at the POE without a valid PR card or PRTD, BSOs must first determine whether the person is a PR. When documentary evidence is not available, BSOs will refer the client for an Immigration examination to ask them questions about their identity and to check their status in the Global Case Management System (GCMS). The person is considered a foreign national until the BSO is satisfied that the person is a PR. The burden of proof lies on the person who is claiming to be a PR at a POE.
Paragraph 19(2) ofIRPA gives PRs the right to enter Canada once it is established that a person is a PR; however, as per paragraph 27(1) of IRPA, this right to enter and remain in Canada is subject to the provisions of the Act, and does not preclude the CBSA from ensuring that PRs are in compliance with IRPA and thus admissible to Canada. If the BSO believes that the PR is not in compliance with the residency obligation, they are to explain that while it has been established that they have a right to enter Canada, there is some reason to believe they could be the subject of a report under IRPA which could lead to the issuance of a removal order. If the BSO believes on a balance of probabilities that the PR has failed to comply with the residency obligation and there is sufficient evidence at the time of the examination to support the allegation, they may report the person (pursuant to A44(1)). If the PR refuses to provide any further information and enters Canada and where there is not sufficient evidence to support the writing of an inadmissibility report, the BSO may forward any available information to an inland office who will then determine whether an investigation is warranted.
Thank you,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

- The duration of the course or program of study is often a more important consideration than the number of months the foreign national intends to study. threads.answer:

threads.answer:
Please note that we are unable to provide case-specific information.
Students who applied for a study permit extension on or after November 1, 2024, to complete the same program of study as the study permit they applied for before November 1, 2024, do not need to meet the field of study requirement. a. Regarding the spouse:
i. Will the spouse also lose her authorization to work?
i. Our understanding is that in support of the spousal open WP application, because the SUV

Otherwise our understanding is that SUV entrepreneurs are considered to be employed in a high-skilled occupation and so if falling under the High-skilled worker" guidelines below, further evidence of being employed in a high-skilled occupation is not required. Which guideline should be referred to in the new three-year open work permit application, in support of the spouse's open work permit application? We believe the former.
b. To extend the time the SUV entrepreneur is authorized to continue working (and potentially the spouse as well) while the open WP application is pending, can they delay the withdrawal of the initial extension application? For instance, could they withdraw closer to the anticipated 166 day processing time for the initial extension application? Could the processing officer send a request through my rep portal to withdraw? Given the 166 day (5.5 months) published processing time for WP extensions, the entrepreneur could be forced to cease working for a very long
mmigration, Refugees
Lion period. Ifthe withdrawal can not be postponed, can IRCC introduce an interim authorization measure so SUV entrepreneurs can resume working much sooner?
c. Will the processing time for the new three-year open work permit (and spousal work permit) be a fresh 166 days from the date of submission or be 166 days from the date of the prior closed SUV WP extension application? threads.answer:
Please note that this service provides guidance and not case-specific advice.
With regards to your question, both an SUV work permit holder and their spouse may continue to work under the conditions of the existing work permit until IRCC makes a decision on their work permit extension applications, so long as they have maintained their status. As foreign nationals may hold more than one work permit application and thus, if they have applied for the new open work permit and spousal work permit, while the closed work permits were in effect, then they would have maintained their status as a result of their closed work permit.
As per section R186(u), a temporary resident may also be authorized to work without a permit until a decision is made on an application made by them under subsection 201(1), if they have remained in Canada after the expiry of their work permit and they have continued to comply with the conditions set out on the expired work permit, other than the expiry date.
For additional information specific to maintaining temporary resident status specific to SUV work permits — both employer-specific and open – please see “If you’re already in Canada as a temporary resident’ under “If you’ve applied for a Start-Up Visa work permit before October 3, 2024” which can be found here.
Regarding the second part of the question, a start-up visa are a high-skilled occupation visa and guidelines regarding family members of foreign nationals authorized to work in high-skill skilled occupations (TEER 0, 1, 2 or 3) can be found here.
As for the processing time of an open work permit, a new application currently being processed has no bearing on an existing employer-specific work permit extension; applications are assessed independently of each other.
Please visit our website for more information on maintained status during processing.
We hope this information is of assistance.
Thank you kindly,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

Family Class
There are two processes that must be completed for international adoptions: the adoption process and the immigration process.
Adoptions are the jurisdiction of the Canadian provinces and territories. For the immigration process, applications to sponsor a child to be adopted in Canada must meet the requirements under R117(1)(g)
For more information on domestic or intercountry adoption, please refer your client to contact the provincial or territorial authority for adoption where they live, who will guide them through the adoption process and requirements and answer any questions they may have. Please refer your client to the following link to find their provincial or territorial adoption authority: Adoption authorities-Canada.ca.
Humanitarian and Compassionate (H&C) Considerations
Foreign nationals who are inadmissible or who do not meet the requirements ofthe Immigration and Refugee Protection Act or Regulations may make a written request for Humanitarian and Compassionate consideration under subsection A25(1).
Humanitarian and compassionate (H&C) consideration: Intake and who may apply-Canada.ca
Permanent resident visa applicants who do not meet the applicable criteria or obligations ofthe inmigration class they are applying under and wish for H&C grounds to be considered must provide additional written information in support of their request for consideration under subsection A25(1) (H&C considerations). This must be included as part of their immigration application under the family class, economic class, or refugee class. Applicants are free to make submissions on any aspect of
and Citizenship Caneda
their personal circumstances that they believe are relevant to their request for H&C consideration. The applicant bears the onus of satisfying the decision maker that the H&C factors and their individual circumstances are sufficient to warrant the exemption(s) requested. Requests for H&C consideration are reviewed on a case-by-case basis. The H&C decision-making process is highly discretionary. The decision maker considers whether a special grant of an exemption from the requirements of the Act is warranted. Invoking sections A25(1) and A25.1 is an exceptional measure and not simply an alternate means of applying for permanent resident status in Canada.
It is important to note that only foreign nationals may put forth H&C requests.
If a positive H&C decision is made, the applicant must still satisfy the remaining requirements for permanent resident visas including medical, criminal records checks and security screening. Once all requirements are met, a permanent resident visa may be issued.
The guide (IMM 5196) for sponsorship of adopted children and other relatives indicates that applications must be submitted electronically.
The sponsor is unable to request H&C for a sponsorship application (IMM1344), however, they are able to indicate on the IMM1 344 form that they wish to continue processing if they don't qualify as a sponsor, so that the applicant's H&C request may be examined.
If you have any further questions, we recommend submitting your inquiries through IRCC's web form: IRCC Web form-Canada.ca
For more specific advice you may want to consult an immigration lawyer.

threads.question: I am seeking clarification regarding the newly implemented rules on Post-Graduation Work Permit (PGWP) eligibility. According to the updated guidelines: f0"If you submitted your study permit application on or after November 1, 2024, you must have graduated from an eligible field of study." My question concerns in-Canada extensions for students continuing in the same institution or program. For example: If a student initially received their study permit before November 1, 2024, but reduced their course load and now requires an extension, will they still need to meet the new eligibility criteria?
threads.answer:
If the student applies for a study permit extension under the same program of study as the study permit they applied for before November 1, 2024, then they do not need to meet the field of study requirement.
If the student applies for a study permit extension under a different program of study than the study permit they applied for before November 1, 2024, then their study permit extension application must meet the field of study requirements applicable to their study program to be eligible for a PGWP. Please note that all PGWP applications (except those from flight school graduates) submitted on or after November 1, 2024 must comply with the new language requirements, regardless of when the student applied for their study permit or when they started their program of study. We are in the process of updating the program manual instructions, in the meantime we have recently updated our website to provide clients with further details on the new PGWP eligibility requirements at the following link: Work in Canada after you graduate: Who can apply-Canada.ca

Question:
QUESTION: LAW –IRPR s.209.3(1)(a)(xiii) The employer is required to obtain and pay for private health insurance during the "period of employment” to ensure that the employee has emergency medical care for the FN, for “...any period during which the foreign national is not covered by the provincial or territorial health insurance system".
When does the “period of employment" begin?
For example, a FN arrives in Canada on August 1st, 2024 and is granted an employer specific work permit at the border, but their contract of employment has an official start date of August 15th, 2024. Does the period of employment begin on the date of arrival or their first day of work (as stated in the contract of employment)?
Response:
The “period of employment” generally begins on the start date specified in the employment contract between the employer and the foreign national (FN), as this date reflects when the FN expected to begin fulfilling their work duties.
While the work permit authorizes the foreign national to begin work upon arrival, the start date in the employment contract typically determines the formal beginning of the “period of employment." Employers are still res ponsible for providing private health insurance from the foreign national arrival date to cover any gap before they qualify for provincial or territorial health coverage. This ensures compliance with IRPR s. 209.3(1)(a)(xiii) and protects the FN during any waiting period for provincial or territorial health insurance eligibility.
Additionally, it is important to note that employer compliance inspections may be conducted to ensure adherence to all regulatory obligations. Staying compliant not only protects the rights of the foreign national but also helps employers avoid potential issues in the future.
For more information on employer compliance, please visit Employer compliance inspections-Canada.ca

Bonjour Mariana,
\sb160Merci pour votre courriel, et nous apprécions votre patience. Ces renseignements sont fournis à titre d'orientation générale et ne constituent pas une directive pour des dossiers individuels. Pour des demandes de renseignements sur des cas spécifiques, les demandeurs peuvent contacter le Ministère en soumettant le Formulaire Web d'IRCC. Veuillez trouver les réponses à vos questions ci-dessous :
Question 1
Je souhaiterais savoir si ce critère s'applique également aux codes de dispense d'EIMT et CAQ sous l’article R204a) pour les accords internationaux, par exemple le code T44 (personne mutée à l'intérieur d'une entreprise sous l'Accord économique et commercial global (AECG) entre le Canada et l’Union européenne).
Réponse 1
L'exigence selon laquelle l'entreprise étrangère doit être celle d'une multinationale existante ne s'applique qu'aux applications TIC spécifiquement codées C61 en vertu du R205(a).
Les demandes soumises en vertu du R204(a), bien que similaires, reflètent des engagements réciproques plus larges pris avec des partenaires commerciaux et impliquent donc certaines variations dans l'application.
L'attente en vertu du R204(a) est que l'entreprise puisse devenir une multinationale en établissant une succursale, une filiale ou une entreprise affiliée au Canada.
Question 2
La deuxième question concerne les dispenses C62 et C63. Si une entreprise a déjà été établie au Canada avant l’entrée en vigueur de la nouvelle exigence et qu’elle est active et génère déjà des revenus au Canada, doit-elle quand même répondre à cette nouvelle exigence d’être une multinationale ?
Réponse 2
Les dispositions relatives aux TIC spécifiées aux termes des C62 et C63 autorisent l'émission de WP TIC si l'une des opérations commerciales existantes est déjà établie au Canada, répondant ainsi à la définition d'une multinationale.
Nous reconnaissons que les récentes mises à jour des lignes directrices ont pu soulever des questions, et d'autres révisions sont en cours pour apporter des éclaircissements supplémentaires à ce sujet.

threads.answer:
Good day,
Thank you for contacting the Immigration Representatives Mailbox
Please note that this mailbox is intended for general guidance and does not provide responses to case-specific inquiries. If you have case specific questions about a file, you are encouraged to submit a Webform at: http//www.ircc.canada.ca/english/contacts/web-form.asp
Please see our response to your question.
\f0Question
I would like to ask about the legal status for students who are required to discontinue or RTD (also referred as “required to withdraw" at other DLIs). At our institution, student who do not meet academic progress expectation will be required to discontinue and cannot be re-admitted to any of our program for at least one academic term (usually 4 months). At the CBIE conference, it was discussed that such discontinuation is considered as authorized leave by IRCC. I would like to confirm correctness ofthe information that RTD, if instituted by DLI is considered as authorized leave.
If RTD is considered authorized leave by IRCC, we assume the following PDI section applies: [https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-) manuals/temporary-residents/study-permnits/assessing-conditions.htnl#leave
D. Leave from studies Students may be required or may wish to take leave from their studies while in Canada. For the purpose of assessing if a student is actively pursuing their studies, any leave taken from a program of studies in Canada should not exceed 150 days from the date the leave commenced and must be authorized by their DLI. A student on leave who begins or resumes their studies within 150 days from the date the leave commenced (that is, the date the leave was granted by the institution) is considered to be actively pursuing studies during their leave. If a student does not resume their studies within 150 days, they should do either of the following:
- change their status (that is, change to visitor status or worker status)
- leave Canada
If they do not change their status or leave Canada, they are considered non-compliant with their study permit conditions. In cases where a student has taken multiple periods of leave in Canada during their program of study, the officer should consider the student's reasons for the various periods of leave. If the multiple periods of leave do not appear to support the expectation that the student is making reasonable progress toward the completion of their course or program of study in the time allotted by the course or program of study, the officer may determine that the study permit holder has not fulfilled the condition to actively
mmigration, Refugees pursue their course or program of study.
Examples of reasons for leave include but are not limited to the following:
- medical illness or injury
- pregnancy
- family emergency
- death or serious illness of a family member
- change in program of study within the same institution, outside a regularly scheduled break
- dismissals or suspensions (dependent on degree of severity)
- postponed program start date (see Deferred enrolment for more information)
I would like to confirm impact on legal status for students while on RTD. The recent updates of R222(1) and (a.1), stated study permit becomes invalid 90 days after the permit holder completes their studies or the day on which the permit holder is no longer enrolled at the DLI that is named in the permit.
Since a student on RTD status cannot be enrolled with us during an RTD period, does this mean their study permit becomes invalid the day they are notified of withdrawal from their program? Or will the authorized leave will provide them a status of up to 150 days. Meaning they are not required change their status (that is, change to visitor status or worker status) or leave Canada if they will resume studies at our DLI within 150 days.
Answer
Students may, in exceptional circumstances, may take a leave from their studies. The student must resume classes within 150 days of the date on which they stopped studying. There are various examples of reasons listed on the IRCC website include illness or injury, pregnancy, family emergency, death or serious illness of a family member etc. As ofNovember 8, 2024, IRCC compliance reports are mandatory where the DLI must select the appropriate student's academic status at the DLI. IRCC’s website provides several enrollment status options such as leave of absence, deferred enrollment, academic suspension, no longer registered etc. We ask you that you carefully review each definition.
You may find additional information about students who are required to discontinue or a“ required to withdraw" on the IRCC website:
1)Academic suspension The student is suspended from your institution, due to poor academic performance or violation of the institution's policies. The student is allowed to return after the period of suspension. Any leave from a program of studies in Canada should not exceed 150 consecutive days from the date the leave started. If a student exceeds 150 days of leave from studies, they will need to change their status with IRCC or will be considered non-compliant with their study permit conditions. Please note that an academic suspension is different than being no longer registered.
2)No longer registered or enrolled Your institution sent the student a letter of admission, but they are no longer registered or enrolled because they have
- been dismissed
- withdrawn voluntarily
- transferred to another institution
This status should not be used for students who are academically suspended.
- 222 (1) A study permit becomes invalid upon the first to occur of the following days:
- (a.1) the day on which the permit holder is no longer enrolled at the designated learning institution that is named in the permit, other than as a result of completing their studies;
Sincerely,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

I am writing to request clarification on the interpretation of immigration rules concerning status in Canada after a work permit
If a foreign national (FN) enters Canada with a valid work permit and Temporary Resident Visa (TRV) one month before the work permit's expiry date, and does not apply for an extension or a change of status before the work permit expires, what is their
Does the FN automatically assume visitor status based on their valid TRV and recent entry to Canada or are they considered out of status despite having entered Canada before the work permit expired and have 90 days to restore their status? We are seeking a clear understanding of how an individual's status is determined in such cases, considering the interplay between
- If the foreign national did not apply to extend their work authorization after entry and before their work permit expires,
- The expiry date on the work permit is the date the foreign national must stop working in Canada. In most cases, it's also
- The expiry date of a TRV is the date by which the visa must be used to arrive at the port of entry (POE) and seek admission to Canada. The expiry date is not the suggested duration of the visit. A TRV does not guarantee entry to Canada, nor does it grant temporary resident status in Canada.
- The temporary resident status expires on the “Must leave Canada by” date, indicated on the work permit. This applies even if it's different (later) than the expiry date on the work permit.
- The authorized period of stay may be longer than the authorized period of work [R185(a) and R185(b)(iv)]. o If the border services officer authorizes the foreign national to stay as a visitor longer than the authorized period of work, the foreign national will continue to have a temporary resident status (as a visitor only). o If the authorized period of stay is equal to authorized period of work (for example, they were authorized to stay 6 months and work for 6 months), then when the work permit expires, the foreign national would lose their temporary resident status and will be required to restore it within 90 days.
Please refer to the following question and web pages for more details.
- My work permit expired and I did not apply to extend it. Can I stay and keep working in Canada? You can apply to restore your work permit in the first 90 days after it expires. There is no guarantee that your application will be approved. sb160Otherwise, you must leave Canada right away when your work permit expires. threads.answer:
Good day,
Thank you for contacting the Immigration Repres entatives Mailbox
Please note that this mailbox is intended for general guidance and does not provide responses to case-specific inquiries. If you have case specific questions about a file, you are encouraged to submit a Webform at: [http://www.ircc.canada.ca/english/contacts/web-form.asp](http://www.ircc.canada.ca/english/contacts/web-form.asp)
In order to work without a work permit pursuant to paragraph R186(1), this authority must be printed on their permit.
Otherwise, exemption code C32 (co-op for post-secondary international students), intended for foreign nationals who intend to perform work that is an essential part of a post-secondary academic, vocational or professional training program offered by a designated learning institution (DLI) in Canada would apply. The work cannot form more than 50% of the total program of study.
The acceptance letter provided by the DLI should clearly establish that the work is an essential part ofthe academic, vocational or professional training program that all participants enrolled in the program are required to complete in order to receive their degree, diploma or certificate. The most common example is undergraduate co-op programs at universities and colleges. If an unpaid internship or other activity for work experience is required to obtain the credits needed for graduation, an international student is required to apply and obtain a co-op work permit.
\cbpat4Students who are already in Canada and have applied for a co-op work permit may begin their co-op placement using their on-campus and off-campus work authorization, provided they meet all the eligibility requirements. There is no limit on work hours for on-campus work. A student may accept employment on the campus of the university or college at which they are a full-time student under paragraph 186(f).
\cbpat4\sb173For off-campus work authorization, as per paragraph R186(v), students can work a total of 24 hours per week during an academic term or semester while they are waiting for their co-op work permit; however, the 24 hours must include both the hours worked at their co-op job and those worked at their regular paid job (if they have one). They can work full-time during the regularly scheduled breaks.
\cbpat4\sb173If the co-op work permit application is refused, they must stop their co-op work immediately.
\sb173For more information, please see: Work related to a research, educational or training program– exemption codes C31, C32 and C33 (International Mobility Program) - Canada.ca
\sb240Thank you,
